**DEAR READER.**

This Work concerning the Advancement of the Sciences, if placed before the same Author's New Organon, not only provides it with necessary light, but also contains the divisions of the sciences which constitute the first part of the Great Instauration, and which the author therefore did not wish to revisit at the very outset of the Organon. I wanted you to know this.

[Rectangular stamp with a double border containing the text:]
ROYAL LIBRARY OF MUNICH.

AD LECTOREM.
lished, in his native tongue, distributed into only two Books, and dedicated to His Royal Majesty, which he does again now. Not so long ago he decided that it should be translated into the Latin Language. For he had heard that it was sought after by foreigners; moreover, he was accustomed to saying from time to time that books written in modern Languages would not much later become obsolete. Therefore, he now publishes its Translation, prepared by certain more distinguished Men of Eloquence, and also corrected by his own Revision. And the first Book certainly is, as it were, a mere Translation, changed in very few things; but the remaining Eight, which set forth the Divisions of the Sciences, and which were contained in a single Book before...

--- Page 7 ---
AD LECTOREM.
were contained, so that it now appears as a *new Work*, and now first published. But the principal reason which moved His Lordship to revise this Work and amplify it in many places, was this: That in the *Great Instauration* (which he published long afterwards) he established the *Divisions of the Sciences* as the first Part of the *Instauration*; which would be followed by the *New Organum*, then the *Natural History*, and so forth. Since therefore he found that part concerning the *Divisions of the Sciences* already worked out long ago (although less thoroughly than the Dignity of the Subject demanded), he thought it would be best if it were revised and brought into a proper and complete work. And in this way he understood his Promise to be fulfilled,

--- Page 8 ---
AD LECTOREM.
...understood his promise to be fulfilled, concerning the first Part of the *Instauration* having been delivered. As for the *work* itself, it is not for my humble ability to preface anything about it. The praise for it, which would be most fitting, I believe would be that which Demosthenes sometimes used to say concerning the deeds of the ancient Athenians: *That Time alone is a worthy praiser for them.* I earnestly pray to God, the Best and Greatest, that in accordance with the *Dignity of the Work*, abundant and lasting fruits may accrue to both the *Author* and the *Reader*.

they call: a capacity of intellect embracing so many and such great things, firmness of memory, swiftness of apprehension, penetration of judgment, and order, together with facility, of elocution. Indeed, that Platonic dogma sometimes comes to mind, by which it is asserted, *that knowledge is nothing other than* *Reminiscence; and that the soul naturally* *knows all things, being restored from time to time to its native light, which the cave* *of the body had obscured.* Certainly of this matter (if in any other) a remarkable example shines forth in Your Majesty; whose mind is so ready to conceive a flame, when even the slightest occasion presented has excited it, or the smallest spark of another's knowledge has gleamed. Therefore, just as Sacred Scripture relates concerning the wisest of kings, *that his heart was, as it were, the sand* *of the Sea:* whose mass, though very great, yet its parts are most minute; so God has endowed Your Majesty with a truly wonderful texture of mind, which, while it embraces the greatest things, yet apprehends the smallest, and does not suffer them to escape: whereas it seems very difficult, or rather impossible in Nature, that the same Instrument should aptly arrange both great Works and small. As for your Elocution, that saying of Cornelius Tacitus concerning Augustus Caesar comes to mind; *Augustus, he says, possessed a flowing* *eloquence, and such as befitted a prince.* Indeed, if we rightly weigh the matter,

--- Page 25 ---
L I B E R I. 3
—sider the matter, every discourse, whether laborious, or affe-
cted, or imitative, although otherwise excel-
lent, smells of something servile, and is not its own master.
But your style of speaking is truly Royal,
flowing as from a Fountain, and never-
theless, as the Order of Nature demands, drawn off into its own
streams, full of ease and felicity, imitating no one, inimitable by anyone.

And just as in your affairs, which pertain as much to the King-
dom as to your House, Virtue seems to contend with Fortune;
namely, the best morals with a fortunate rule;
your hopes formerly patiently and piously restrained,
with the propitious and opportune attainment of what was hoped for;
the holy faith of the Conjugal Bed, with the blessed
fruit of Matrimony, in a most beautiful Offspring;
your pious and most worthy inclination towards peace
for a Christian Prince, with a similar inclination of neighboring
Princes, happily concurring in the same wish: So also in the endow-
ments of your intellect no less a contention and rivalry arises,
if we compare those [endowments] which have been granted and
infused by Nature herself, with the most amply furnished treasury
of manifold Erudition, and the Knowledge of very many
Arts. Nor indeed would it be easy to find any King born
after Christ who could be compared to your Majesty
in the variety and cultivation of Divine and Human Letters.
Whoever wishes, let him run through the series of Emperors and
Kings, and he will agree with me. Certainly something
                                                                    great

4          DE AUGM. SCIENT.
dam Kings seem to achieve, if, by tasting lightly
the intellects of others, they gain wisdom concisely, or
if they stick somewhat to the surface of learning,
or finally if they love and elevate learned men.
But for a King, and a King by birth, to have drawn from the true
founts of Learning, indeed, to be himself the very fount
of Learning, is little short of a Miracle. But to Your
Majesty this also accrues, that in the same cabinet of your breast, Sacred
Letters are stored with profane ones, so that,
like that Hermes Trismegistus, you are distinguished by a triple glory:
by the Power of a King, by the Illumination
of a Priest, and by the Learning of a Philosopher. Since
therefore you far surpass other Kings in this praise (which is properly
yours), it is right that it be celebrated not
only by the fame and admiration of the present Age,
or even by the light of histories be transmitted to
posterity, but that it be engraved in some solid Work,
which both denotes the power of a Great King,
and reflects the Image of a King so remarkably Learned.
   Wherefore (to return to my undertaking), no
more fitting Offering seemed to me than some Treatise
directed to that end. The subject of this
consisted of two Parts. In the former (which
is lighter, yet by no means to be omitted),
the excellence of Science and Letters in all things
must be treated; and at the same time concerning the Merit of those
who strenuously and judiciously apply themselves to advancing them.
                                                                    Po-

--- Page 27 ---
L I B E R I. 5
But the latter Part (which is the main point) will set forth what has been done and perfected in this kind up to now; moreover, it will touch upon those things which seem to be lacking; so that although I may not dare to set aside or choose anything in particular to commend to your Majesty, nevertheless, by representing many and various things, I may be able to excite your Royal Thoughts, so that you may bring forth the treasures of your own Breast, and thence, according to your magnanimity and wisdom, draw forth the very best things for advancing the boundaries of Arts and Sciences.

In the very Vestibule of the former Part, for clearing the way, and as it were, proclaiming silence, so that the Testimonies concerning the Dignity of Letters may be better heard without the barking of silent Objections, I have decided in the first place to free letters from the reproaches and contempt with which Ignorance assails them; but Ignorance, under not one guise: now in the Jealousy of Theologians, now in the Arrogance of Politicians, now manifesting and betraying itself in the errors of the Literati themselves. I hear the first ones saying that Knowledge is among those things which are to be admitted sparingly and cautiously. That too much Appetite for Knowledge was the first Sin, whence the Fall of Man; and that even today something serpentine adheres to it, since, entering, it induces swelling; _Knowledge puffs up._ That Solomon judged: _Of making books there is no_
B

--- Page 28 ---
6	Dᴇ Aᴜɢᴍ. Sᴄɪᴇɴᴛ.
*of making many books there is no end, and much study is a weariness of the flesh; and elsewhere, In much wisdom there is much grief, and he that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow.* St. Paul warned, *Beware lest we be deceived by empty Philosophy:* Moreover, experience shows that the most learned Men, the leaders of Heretics; and the most learned Ages, have been prone to Atheism; and finally, that the contemplation of Secondary Causes detracts from the authority of the Primary Cause.

   Therefore, to reveal the falsity of this Dogma and its ill-laid Foundations, it is evident to anyone that these people do not perceive that the Knowledge which brought forth the Fall was not that pure, original Natural Knowledge, by the light of which Man imposed Names on the Animals brought to him in Paradise; but rather that proud knowledge *of Good and Evil*, through which he sought to cast off God and establish law for himself. Nor indeed does any power of Knowledge, however great, inflate the mind, since nothing can fill the Soul, much less distend it, except God and the contemplation of God. Wherefore Solomon, speaking of the two principal senses of Discovery (Sight and Hearing), says, *The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear with hearing.* And if there is no filling, it follows that the Container is greater than the Contained. No otherwise concerning Knowledge itself, and the human Mind (to which the Senses are like Emissaries)
                                                                    defi-

defines with these words, which he appends to his Calendar and Ephemeris, describing the times of all things, thus concluding: *God has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set the world in their heart, yet man cannot find out the work that God does from beginning to end.* By these words he not obscurely hints that God has fashioned the human mind like a mirror, capable of the whole world, and thirsting for it no less than the eye thirsts for light; nor merely eager to behold the varieties and changes of Times, but also ambitious to scrutinize and explore the unmoving and inviolable Laws and Decrees of Nature. And although he seems to imply that supreme economy of Nature (which he calls *the work that God does from beginning to end*) cannot be discovered by Man, this does not detract from human capacity, but should be attributed to the impediments of Learning; such as the brevity of life, the distractions of studies, the corrupt and unfaithful transmission of sciences, and many other inconveniences by which the human condition is entangled. Indeed, he teaches clearly enough elsewhere that no part of the Universe is alien from human inquiry, saying: *The spirit of man is the lamp of the Lord, searching all the innermost parts.* Therefore, if the amplitude of human capacity is so great, it is manifest that there is no danger from

quantity of Knowledge, however diffused, lest it induce either swel-

which, however small it may be, if taken without its proper Antidote,

This Antidote, or Spice (whose mixture tempers

Which the Apostle also adds to the former clause, saying,
*Knowledge puffs up, but charity edifies*. Consistent with
this is what he teaches elsewhere: *If, he says,*

Not that it is not something excellent to speak with the Tongues
of Angels and Men, but because if it is separated
from Charity, and is not directed to the common good
of the Human Race, it will rather exhibit empty
glory than solid fruit. As for Solomon's censure
concerning the excess of reading and writing Books, and
the vexation of spirit arising from Knowledge;
and also Paul's admoni-

*vain philosophy*: if these things are rightly explained,
they will best show the true bounds by which
human knowledge is enclosed, yet so that it is free
for it, without any restriction, to embrace the entire
nature of things. For there are three limits. The first, lest we so
place happiness in Knowledge that meanwhile
forgetfulness of our Mortality creeps in. Se-
                                                                cond,

--- Page 31 ---
L I B E R I.	9
Second, that we do not so use knowledge as to produce anxiety, not tranquility of mind. Third, that we do not think ourselves able, through the contemplation of Nature, to attain Divine Mysteries. For as to the first, Solomon explains himself excellently elsewhere in the same Book. "I have clearly seen enough," he says, "that Wisdom recedes from folly as much as Light from Darkness. The wise man's eyes are in his head, but the fool wanders in darkness; yet at the same time I have learned that the necessity of dying is common to both."

Concerning the second, it is certain that no anxiety or disturbance of mind arises from Knowledge, except only by accident. For all Knowledge, and Admiration (which is the seed of Knowledge), is pleasant in itself; but when conclusions are deduced from it, which, obliquely applied to our affairs, either generate weak fears or immoderate desires, then at last is born that Torment and Disturbance of mind of which we speak: for then Knowledge is no longer *dry light* (as that obscure Heraclitus wished, *dry light is the best soul*), but it becomes moist light, and soaked with the humors of the Passions.

The third rule demands a somewhat more accurate discussion, and must not be passed over lightly. For if anyone, from the contemplation of Sensible and Material Things, should hope to attain so much Light as to reveal the Divine Nature or Will

10      ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING.
suffice, lest he be deceived by empty philo-
sophy. For indeed, the Contemplation of Creatures,
as far as the Creatures themselves are concerned, produces Know-
ledge; as far as God is concerned, only Admiration;
which is, as it were, knowledge cut short. There-
fore, a certain Platonist most wisely said: that human
senses are like the sun, which indeed re-
veals the earthly globe, but seals off the heavens and the stars.
Thus the senses reveal natural things, they shut off Di-
vine things. And hence it comes about that some
from the company of the more learned have fallen into heresy,
when, relying on the waxed wings of the senses, they
strove to fly up to divine things. For those,
who maintain that excessive Knowledge inclines
the mind to Atheism; and that ignorance
of Secondary Causes assists piety towards the Pri-
mary: I would gladly address with
Job's question, Is it right to lie for
God, and is it fitting to speak deceitfully for his sake,
so that we may please him? For it is clear that God
ordinarily works nothing in nature, except through
secondary (causes). If they wished the opposite of this to be believed,
it would be pure imposture, as if to curry favor with God,
and nothing other than to sacrifice to the Author of truth an un-
clean offering of falsehood.
But rather, it is most certain, and proven by expe-
rience, that superficial tastes in philo-
sophy perhaps move one to Atheism,
but deeper draughts lead back to Religion.
For at the threshold of Philosophy, when
secondary causes, as if closest to the senses, are pre-

and alienate minds from business and action, instilling a love of leisure and retirement; then to introduce a relaxation of discipline into republics, while everyone is more ready to dispute than to obey. Hence Cato the Censor, one of the wisest of mortals, when Roman youth, captivated by the sweetness and majesty of his eloquence, flocked from all sides to Carneades the philosopher, who had come to Rome as an ambassador, advised in a full Senate that, once their business was dispatched, they should dismiss the man as soon as possible, lest he infect and bewitch the minds of the citizens; and, unbeknownst to them, introduce a change in their ancestral customs and manners. This also moved Virgil (while he postponed his own studies to the estimation of his country) to separate political arts from literary ones, claiming the former for the Romans, leaving the latter to the Greeks, in those celebrated verses;
       *Remember, Roman, to rule the peoples with your sway;*
       *These shall be your arts.*
We also see Anytus, the accuser of Socrates, charging him with the crime that by the force and truth of his speeches and disputations, he diminished the authority and reverence for the laws and ancestral customs among the young; and that he professed an art pernicious and full of danger, by which

But these accusations, and others of the same ilk, rather display a feigned Gravity than the Candor of Truth. For Experience testifies that just as one and the same men, so one and the same eras, have flourished with the glory both of Military Affairs and of the Best Arts.

As for men, let a noble pair of generals be an example: Alexander the Great, and Julius Caesar the Dictator; the one a Disciple of Aristotle in Philosophy, the other a Rival of Cicero in speaking. Or if anyone should rather seek learned men who became famous generals, than generals who were remarkably learned, there is at hand Epaminondas the Theban, or Xenophon the Athenian: of whom the former was the first who broke the power of the Spartans; but the latter the first who paved the way for the overthrow of the Monarchy of the Persians.

But that quasi-marriage of Arms and Letters shines forth more clearly still in Eras than in Persons, inasmuch as, of course, an Age is a grander Object than a Man. For indeed, the very same Eras, among the Egyptians, Assyrians, Persians, Greeks, and Romans, which are most celebrated for their Military Virtue, were also greatly ennobled by Letters; so much so that the most weighty

   But now, that learning is an impediment to politics
rather than an aid, nothing is less probable.
We all confess that it is a rash thing

Furthermore, the course of life in one man cannot supply a sufficiency of Examples for governing the events of life, even in one man. For just as it sometimes happens that a Grandson or Great-grandson resembles a Grandfather or Great-grandfather more than his Father: in the same way it not rarely happens that present affairs fit better with older Examples than with more recent ones. Lastly, the genius of one man yields as much to the Amplitude of Letters as a private income to the Treasury.

      But if it be granted that those corruptions and impediments, which are imputed to letters by politicians, have some force and truth: yet at the same time it must be observed that Erudition brings more Remedy than harm in individuals. For granted that Letters, by a certain silent force, render the Mind uncertain and perplexed; yet certainly they clearly prescribe how thoughts are to be disentangled, and how far deliberation should proceed, when finally

--- Page 39 ---
L I B E R I. 17
a decision must be made; nay, they show how

what things rest on Demonstrations, and what

use of Distinctions and Exceptions, than the
constancy of Canons and Principles.
Granted again, they lead and distort minds by
the inequality or dissimilarity of Examples.
I know not; but I know well enough that they
explain both the efficacies of circumstances,
and the errors of comparisons, and the cautions
of applications, so that on the whole they correct
minds more than they corrupt them. Moreover,
Literature everywhere insinuates these Remedies,
with great force and variety of Examples.
Let anyone weigh the Errors of Clement VII,
so clearly depicted by Guicciardini, who was, as

cut to the quick by his own hand in his letters

and frequent Changes of Counsel: Let him inspect
the Errors of Phocion; he will abhor Obstinacy:
Let him read the Fable of Ixion; and he will dispel
excessive hopes, and such Fumes and Mists.
Let him contemplate Cato the Younger; nor will
he ever migrate to the Antipodes, and fix his
footsteps contrary to the present Age.

--- Page 40 ---
18      On the Advancement of Learning.
...and that it imbues the mind with the sweetness of leisure and solitude, will make a strange assertion if those things which accustom the mind to perpetual activity should prove to be patrons of idleness. Whereas on the contrary it can truly be affirmed that among all types of men, no one loves business for the sake of business itself, except the man of letters. For some love affairs and business for the sake of gain, like hired workers [love] work for the sake of pay. Others for the sake of honor; for while they conduct affairs, they live in the eyes of men, and serve their reputation, which would otherwise vanish. Others for the sake of power, and the prerogative of fortune, so that they may reward friends and punish enemies. Others so that they may exercise some faculty of theirs, which they love, and often congratulate themselves and smile on this account. Finally, others so that they may achieve other ends of their own.

To such an extent that, what is usually said of the vainglorious, that their courage lies in the eyes of the beholders, so the diligence and strenuousness of such men seems to aim at this: either that others may applaud, or that they themselves may exult within themselves.

Only men of letters delight in business and occupations, as actions agreeable to nature, and no less wholesome for the mind than exercise is for the body, looking at the thing itself, not the profit; so that they are the least weary of all, if only the matter is of such a kind that it may engage the mind according to its dignity.

fill, and occupy it. But if sometimes some are found who are diligent in reading, but sluggish in acting, this does not originate from learning, but from a certain weakness and softness of Body or Mind; such as Seneca observes. "Some," he says, "are so reclusive that they think whatever is in the light is in turmoil." It might perhaps happen that those conscious of such a disposition devote themselves to learning; but learning itself by no means implants or produces such dispositions. But if anyone nevertheless stubbornly maintains that learning consumes too much time, which could otherwise be more properly spent; I say that no one is so engrossed in business but that he has his intervals of leisure, until the turns and tides of action recede, unless he is either very dull in dispatching business, or too little ambitious with dignity in seizing business of any kind. It remains therefore to be asked, in what, and how, these spare hours ought to be employed; in studies or pleasures, should one indulge one's inclination or one's intellect? Just as Demosthenes rightly replied to Aeschines, a man devoted to pleasures. When Aeschines had reproachfully objected that his orations smelled of the lamp, Demosthenes said: "By Pollux! there is a great difference between what you and I do by lamplight." Therefore, it is by no means to be feared that learning might eliminate business; but rather they reclaim the mind from idleness and pleasure, which otherwise gradually, to both

   Next, the objection they raise, that Letters undermine the Reverence for Laws and Empire, is a mere calumny, not even probably brought forward for accusation. For whoever would contend that blind obedience binds more strongly than enlightened duty, would at the same time assert that a blind man led by hand walks more surely than one who uses Light and Eyes. Indeed, beyond all controversy, the Arts soften manners, render them tender, compliant, pliable, and amenable to the commands of the Empire; Ignorance, on the contrary, makes them stubborn, refractory, seditious. Which is most clearly evident from history, inasmuch as the most unlearned, uncultivated, barbarous times have been most prone to tumults, seditions, and changes.

   Concerning the judgment of Cato the Censor, let this be said: that he suffered the most deserved penalties for his blasphemy against Letters, when, older than seventy, as if becoming a boy again, he most eagerly learned the Greek Language. From which it is clear that that former censure of Greek Literature flowed rather from an affected seriousness than from what he truly felt deep down. But as for Virgil's poems, however much it pleased him to insult the whole world, by asserting for the Romans the Arts of Ruling, while leaving the others, as if common, to others; in this, however, he is clearly held (to account), that the Romans never (achieved) the height of Empire—

--- Page 43 ---
LIBER I. 21
had ascended to the summit, until they had simultaneously reached the peak of the Arts. For, to the two first Caesars, men most skilled in ruling, were contemporaries that very best Poet, Virgil Maro, the best Historian, Titus Livius, the best Antiquarian, Marcus Varro, the best or next-to-best Orator, Marcus Cicero; certainly leaders, from all memory, each in his own field. Finally, as to the Accusation of Socrates, I say only this; Let us remember the times in which it was brought; namely, under the Thirty Tyrants, the cruelest, most wicked of all mortals, and most unworthy of rule. After that cycle of affairs and times had revolved, that Socrates (the supposed criminal, of course) was numbered among the Heroes, and his memory was heaped with all honors, both Divine and Human: moreover, his disputations, previously held as Corrupters of Morals, were celebrated by all Posterity as the most effective Antidotes for Mind and Morals. And let these things suffice for responding to the Politicians, who, with supercilious severity, or feigned gravity, have dared to attack letters with insults; which refutation, however, for the present, might seem less necessary, unless we consider whether our labors will endure to posterity; since the Countenance and Favor of two most learned Princes, Queen Elizabeth, and Maje-

Now we come to the third kind of disparagement, which redounds from the learned themselves upon Letters, and usually sticks deeper than the others. These (criticisms) derive their origin either from Fortune, or from Morals; or from their own Studies. Of which the first is beyond their power, the second is beside the point; so that only the third properly seems to come into question. However, because the discourse is to be established not so much about the true Weight of Things, as about the estimation of the Common People, it will not be amiss to hint at a few things concerning the other two as well.

Therefore, the diminutions of dignity, and as it were, disgraces, which are imposed upon Letters by the Fortune of the learned, are taken either from their poverty and want, or from an obscure and shadowy kind of life, or from the not very noble subject of the occupations in which they are engaged.

As far as poverty is concerned, and because it frequently happens that the learned are poor, and for the most part of humble origin, nor do they grow rich as quickly as others who only gape after gain: it would be advisable to hand over this topic, concerning the praise of poverty, to the mendicant friars (with their leave, I would say) to adorn; to whom Machiavelli

*“Long ago it would have been over with the kingdom of priests,*
*if reverence for the friars and monks had not compensated for the*
*luxury and excess of the bishops.”*
Similarly one might say that the happiness and magnificence of Princes and nobles could long ago have fallen back into barbarism and squalor, if they did not owe to these poor learned men the cultivation and adornment of civil life. But leaving aside these pursuits of praise, it is worthy of note how sacred and venerable a thing poverty itself was considered among the Romans for several centuries; though that Republic drew nothing from paradoxes. For thus T. Livy prefaces: *“Either the love of the task I have undertaken deceives me,*
*or no Republic ever was greater, nor more righteous, nor richer in good*
*examples, nor into which avarice and luxury immigrated so late, nor where*
*such great and long-lasting honor was paid to poverty and frugality.”*
Indeed, even after Rome had already degenerated, we read that when Caesar the Dictator professed that he would restore the collapsed Republic, one of his friends put forth the opinion that nothing was so expedient for what he was undertaking as if the honor of riches were abolished in any way. But (he said) *“these, and all evils, will cease together with the honor*
*of money, if neither magistracies, nor other things commonly desired, are for sale.”*

    What need is there to speak of that private and obscure life, which they object to scholars? So worn a theme it is, and cast about by all, to prefer leisure and retirement (provided idleness and luxury are absent) to a public and busy life, on account of security, liberty, sweetness, dignity, or at least immunity from indignities, that no one treats this topic without treating it well: so much does it accord with human concepts in experience, and with general agreement in approval. I will only add this, that learned men, hidden in states and living least under the eyes of men, are like the images of Cassius and Brutus, concerning whom, when they were not carried in Junia's funeral procession, while many others were, Tacitus says, *By that very fact they shone forth, because they were not seen.*

From this it is clear that the principal care is concerned with the beginnings of things and bodies. Lend an ear, if you please, to the Rabbis: "Your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams." From this text they gather that youth is a more worthy age, inasmuch as, of course, revelation comes more clearly through visions than through dreams. But this is altogether worthy of note: that although pedagogues, like apes of tyranny, are the laughingstock of the stage, and the carelessness of the times, as it were, has fallen asleep in their selection, yet there is an old complaint, handed down from the best and most prudent ages, that the Commonwealth indeed busies itself too much with laws, but is negligent concerning education. This most noble part of ancient discipline has been recalled to some extent, as if by right of postliminy, in the Colleges of the Jesuits; when I contemplate their industry and skill, both in cultivating doctrine and in forming morals, that saying of Agesilaus to Pharnabazus comes to mind: "Since you are such a man, I wish you were ours." And thus far concerning the reproaches from the learned...

    As for the morals of learned men, this is a matter pertaining more to individuals than to studies. Without doubt, among them are found, just as in all orders and kinds of life, both bad and good; nor is it therefore untrue (as is asserted) that studies pass into morals; and that learning, unless it falls into very depraved minds, entirely corrects nature and changes it for the better.
    Nevertheless, as I diligently and honestly assess the matter, no disgrace occurs to me as adhering to learning from the morals of learned men, insofar as they are learned; unless perhaps this is considered a fault (of which Demosthenes, Cicero, Cato the Younger, Seneca, and many others are accused): that since generally the times about which they read are better than those in which they live, and what is taught is better than what is done, they contend beyond what is proper, [to bring] the corruptions of morals to the precept.

Another fault, which perhaps not undeservedly is objected to the learned, is of this kind: that they have postponed their own fortunes or safeguards to the honor or advantage of their own countries or dominions.    Another fault common to learned men, which can be more easily excused than denied, is this, namely, that they do not easily apply and accommodate themselves to the persons with whom they do business or live. Which defect arises from two causes: The first is the greatness of the mind itself, on account of which they can with difficulty humble themselves to the deference of any single man. These are the words of a lover, not a wise man: *We are a sufficiently large theater for another.* Nor, however, will I deny that he who cannot equally contract and expand the keenness of his mind, like an eye, is deprived of a remarkable faculty for managing affairs. But the second cause is integrity of morals and simplicity; which nevertheless indicates a discernment of judgment, not a defect, in them. For the true and legitimate limits of deference towards any person do not extend further than to know their manners in such a way that one can associate with them without offense, and, if necessary, assist them with counsel, and meanwhile for ourselves in

For the custom of the East, by which it is considered impious to fix one's eyes on Kings, is indeed barbarous in rite, but good in its meaning: for it is not fitting for subjects to pry too curiously into the hearts of their Kings, which the Sacred Scriptures teach are inscrutable.
      There remains yet another vice (with which I shall conclude this part), often imputed to learned men, namely that in small and external matters (in countenance, gesture, gait, daily conversations, and suchlike) they fail in observing decorum; whence inexperienced men, from these minute and trivial errors, form a conjecture as to how capable they are in handling greater matters. But such a judgment usually deceives them; indeed, let them know that Themistocles' answer applies to them. For when he had been asked to play the lyre,

And therefore, learned men are not to be condemned when, as the situation demands, they relax something of their dignity, whether compelled by necessity or prompted by opportunity; which, although it may seem humble and servile at first glance, nevertheless, to one more truly judging the matter, they will be judged not to serve the person, but the time itself.

Let us proceed now to the errors and vanities which intervene and mix themselves in the very studies of learned men; this especially and properly pertains to the present argument. In this matter, it is not our purpose to champion the errors themselves, but through their censure and separation, to shake out what is sound and solid, and to vindicate it from calumny. For we see that it is customary, especially among the envious, because of those things which are depraved, also to disparage those things which are uncorrupted and have remained in their proper state; just as the Heathens in the primitive Church used to bespatter Christians with the vices of heretics. Nor is it my intention, however, to institute some more accurate examination concerning the errors, and

A somewhat sounder kind of style exists, yet not entirely devoid of vanity itself, which almost immediately succeeds that abundance and luxury of speech in time. It consists entirely in this: that the words be pointed, the sentences concise, and the speech, in short, rather crafted than diffused; hence it happens that all things, through such artifice, seem more ingenious than they really are. Such a style is found more profusely in Seneca, more moderately in Tacitus and Pliny the Younger; and recently began to be suited to the ears of our time. But this very thing is usually pleasing to mediocre intellects, so much so that it procures a certain dignity for letters; nevertheless, it is deservedly disdained by more refined judgments, and can be considered a kind of intemperance

of doctrine, since it is also a kind of pursuit of words and their elegance. And let these things be said concerning the first literary intemperance.

There follows that intemperance in the subject matter itself, which we placed in the middle, and designated by the name of _contentious subtlety_. And that one is somewhat worse than the one about which we just spoke. For just as the dignity of subject matter excels the elegance of words, so on the contrary, vanity is more hateful in things than in words. In this regard, that Pauline rebuke can be referred no more to his own age than it can be extended to subsequent times; and it seems to regard not only Theology, but also all sciences. _Avoid profane novelties of words, and oppositions of falsely named knowledge._ For by these words he proposes two signs and indications of suspected and counterfeit knowledge. The first is, novelty and unusualness of words; The second, the rigidity of dogmas, which necessarily introduces opposition, and then altercations and questions. Certainly, just as many natural bodies, while they are whole and strong, are often corrupted and turn into worms, in the same way sound and solid knowledge of things very often putrefies and dissolves into subtle, vain, unhealthy, and (if I may so speak) worm-eaten questions; which seem to be endowed with a certain movement and some vivacity, but they are rotten and of no use. This kind of doctrine, being less sound and corrupting itself,

--- Page 61 ---
L I B E R I. 39
ting itself, prevailed especially among many of the Scholastics, who, abounding in extreme leisure and sharp in intellect, but deficient in reading (since their minds were confined within the writings of a few authors, especially Aristotle their dictator, no less than their bodies in the cells of monasteries), and for the most part ignorant of the history of both nature and time; from a not great warp of matter, but by a very great agitation of spirit, as if of rays, they wove the most elaborate webs, which are extant in their books. For, the human mind, if it acts upon matter, contemplating the nature of things and the works of God, operates according to the measure of the matter, and is determined by it; but if it turns in upon itself (like a spider weaving a web), then at last it is boundless, and certainly produces certain webs of doctrine, admirable in the fineness of their thread and workmanship, but as to use, frivolous and empty.

This useless subtlety or curiosity is twofold: and is observed either in the matter itself: such as vain speculation, or controversy, of which kind not a few are found both in Theology and in Philosophy: or in the manner and method of treating [a subject]; this among the Scholastics was generally of this kind. In this, indeed, shines forth Aristotle's wisdom and integrity; who, although he wrote a diligent and accurate history of animals, so sparingly mixed in fictitious or fabulous things: but rather, he collected admirable reports, which he judged worthy of mention, into a single small commentary: wisely considering that clearly true things (which, as a solid basis of experience, can be laid beneath philosophy and sciences) ought not rashly to be mixed with things of suspected credibility: and again, also rare and unusual things, which seem incredible to most, ought not to be entirely suppressed, nor denied to the memory of posterity.

The arts themselves, which have more from imagination and faith than from reason and demonstrations, are principally three: Astrology, Natural Magic, and Alchemy; whose ends, however, are not ignoble. For Astrology professes to reveal the influence and dominion of superior things over inferior things. Magic aims to recall Natural Philosophy from the variety of speculations to the greatness of works. Alchemy undertakes to separate and extract the heterogeneous parts of things which lie hidden and are entangled in natural bodies; and to purify the defiled bodies themselves, to free the impeded, to perfect the immature. But the ways and methods which are thought to lead to these ends, both in the theory of those arts and in practice, are full of error and trifles. Nor indeed is their tradition, for the most part, straightforward, but riddled with artifices and concealments.    That credulity, however, which fortified certain authors of sciences with a certain dictatorial power, so that they might decree, not as senators to consult, inflicted immense damage on the sciences, as the principal cause which so greatly afflicted and depressed them, that without any significant augmentation they lay lifeless. Hence indeed it happened that in the Mechanical arts, the first inventors devised few things, while time supplied and perfected the rest; but in the sciences, the first authors penetrated very far, while time wore away and corrupted many things. Thus we see Gunnery, Navigation, and Typography to have been imperfect and almost formless at their beginnings, and burdensome to those practicing them, but by the progress of time, refined and suitable. But on the contrary, the philosophies and sciences of Aristotle, Plato, Democritus, Hippocrates, Euclid, and Archimedes flourished in those very authors, but rather degenerated with the passage of time, and lost no small part of their splendor: Of which matter there is no other reason than that in the Mechanical arts, the talents of many converged into one, [whereas] in the liberal arts and sciences, the talents of many succumbed under one; whom, however, his own followers very often rather corrupted than illuminated.

For just as water will not rise higher than the source from which it flows; so doctrine derived from Aristotle will never rise above the doctrine of Aristotle. And therefore, although the rule, "the learner must believe," is not displeasing; yet to this must be joined, "*the one already taught must use his own judgment.*" For disciples owe to their Masters only temporary faith and suspension of judgment, until they have thoroughly imbibed the arts, but not a full renunciation of liberty and perpetual servitude of intellect. Wherefore, to conclude this part, I will only add this; let great authors thus retain their due honor, that the Author of authors, and Time, the parent of truth, may not be disparaged.

We have finally explained three distempers, or diseases, of learning; besides which there are some, not so much confirmed diseases, as vicious humors: which, however, are not so obscure or hidden, but that they fall under the notice and censure of many, and therefore are by no means to be omitted.

The first of these is the immoderate study of two extremes, antiquity and novelty. In which matter the daughters of time badly imitate their father: for just as time devours its offspring, so do these (devour) each other; while antiquity envies new advancements, and novelty is not content to add recent things, unless it utterly eliminates and rejects the old. Certainly the counsel of the Prophet true in

--- Page 69 ---
LIBER I.                     47
the true counsel of the Prophet in this matter is: _Stand ye in the old ways, and see which is the straight and good way, and walk therein._ Antiquity deserves such reverence that men should for a while stop their step, and stand upon it, and look around everywhere to see what is the best way: but when the way has been well established, then at last one must not hesitate, but proceed eagerly. Indeed, to speak the truth, _Antiquity of the age, youth of the world._ Our times are truly the ancient times, since the world has now grown old, not those which are reckoned in retrograde order, taking their beginning from our age.

  Another error arising from the former is a certain suspicion and distrust, which supposes that nothing can now be discovered which the world could have lacked for so long: as if that objection were applicable to time, by which Lucian assails Jupiter and the other pagan gods: For he wonders, _why they begot so many children in the past, but none now_

--- Page 70 ---
48      ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING.
It had not been. Thus Alexander's expedition into Asia was considered at first as a vast and very difficult undertaking; yet afterwards it pleased Livy to elevate it so much that he said of Alexander, *'He dared nothing else than to bravely scorn vain things.'* The same happened to Columbus concerning the Western navigation. But in intellectual matters, this happens much more frequently; as can be seen in most propositions in Euclid: which before they are demonstrated, seem wonderful, and to which one would not easily assent; but after the demonstration has been made, the mind grasps them by a kind of 'retraction' (as jurists speak), as if previously seen and known.

Another error akin to the previous one, is that of those who think that of all ancient sects and heresies, after they had been examined and sifted, the best always prevailed, with others being set aside. Therefore they think that if someone were to institute an inquiry and examination anew, he could not but fall upon some of the rejected opinions, and those lost and obliterated after their rejection: as if indeed the multitude, or even the wise for the sake of deluding the multitude, have not often approved that which is more popular and superficial, rather than that which is solid and deeply rooted. For time indeed is like a river, which carries down to us light and inflated things, but submerges solid and weighty things.

--- Page 71 ---
LIBER I. 49

Another error, different from the rest, is the premature and presumptuous reduction of doctrines into arts and methods; which being the case, science for the most part profits either little or nothing. Indeed, just as youths, after the limbs and features of their bodies are perfectly formed, scarcely grow any more: so science, as long as it is scattered in Aphorisms and observations, can grow and rise, but once circumscribed and concluded by methods, it can perhaps be polished and illustrated, or fashioned for human uses, but not further increased in bulk.

Another error succeeding the one we last noted, is that after individual sciences and arts have been distributed into their classes, universal knowledge of things and First Philosophy are soon renounced by most; which is indeed most hostile to the progress of doctrines. Views are made from towers, or very high places: and it is impossible for anyone to explore the more remote and inner parts of any science, if he stands on the plain of that same science, and does not ascend, as it were, to a watchtower of a higher science.

Another error flows from an excessive reverence and, as it were, adoration of the human intellect: whence men have withdrawn themselves from the contemplation of nature and from experience, wallowing up and down in their own meditations and fancies of the mind. But these renowned theorists

--- Page 72 ---
50      ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING
But these excellent theorists, and (if I may so speak) Intellectualists, who are nevertheless usually considered the most sublime and divine philosophers, Heraclitus rightly criticized. "Men," he said, "seek truth in their own Microcosms, not in the greater world." For they reject, as it were, the ABC of nature and the first apprenticeship in divine works; which if they did not do, they might perhaps gradually and slowly, after simple letters, and then syllables, ascend to readily reading the very text and volume of creatures. But they, on the contrary, by constant agitation of mind, urge and as it were invoke their Geniuses, that they may prophesy to them and utter oracles, by which they are deservedly and pleasantly deceived.

    Another error, akin to this latter one, is that men too often imbue and infect their meditations and doctrines with certain opinions and their own concepts, which they especially hold in admiration; or with arts to which they are most addicted and consecrated, infecting and as it were tinging all other things with these delights, though with a very deceptive dye. Thus Plato mixed Theology into his Philosophy, Aristotle Logic, the second School of Plato (Proclus, namely, and the rest) Mathematics. philosophy they hammered out. And Gilbert, our countryman, drew out another philosophy from the Magnet. Another error is the impatience of doubting, and a blind haste in deciding, without a due and [small red mark] mature suspension of judgment. For the crossroads of contemplation is not unlike the crossroads of action, often mentioned by the ancients: of which one path was at first smooth and easy, but at the end impassable; the other was rough and rugged to the one entering, but when you had proceeded a little, it was clear and level. No differently in contemplations, if one begins from certainties, he will end in uncertainties; but if he begins from doubts, and patiently endures them for a while, he will find an outcome in certainties.

A similar error shows itself in the method of transmitting doctrine, which, for the most part, is imperious and magisterial, not open and liberal, so composed in the end that it rather commands belief than submits itself to examination. I would not deny that in summary treatises, destined for practice, this form of writing can be retained; but in proper treatises on the sciences I consider both extremes to be avoided: both that of Velleius the Epicurean, fearing nothing so much as lest

--- Page 74 ---
52 Dᴇ Aᴜɢᴍ. Sᴄɪᴇɴᴛ.
...lest he should seem to doubt about anything: than that of Socrates and the Academy, who left everything in doubt. Rather, one should strive for candor, and things should be delivered with greater or lesser assertiveness, according as they have been proven more sparingly or more fully by the weight of reasons.

	Other errors are in the aims which men set for themselves, and towards which they direct their efforts and labors. For while the more diligent leaders of letters ought especially to aim at this, that they may add something excellent to the art which they profess: these (others), on the contrary, are content merely to stand in secondary roles, seeking the name either of a subtle interpreter, or of a vehement and vigorous antagonist, or of a methodical abbreviator: whence the revenues and income of the sciences can be increased, but the patrimony and capital by no means.

	But the gravest error of all consists in the deviation from the ultimate end of doctrines. For men desire knowledge, some from an innate and restless curiosity: others for the sake of amusement, and delight: others for the sake of reputation: others for the sake of contention, and that they may be superior in disputation: most because of gain and livelihood: very few, that they may employ the gift of reason, divinely given, for the uses of the human race. Clearly, as if in doctrine one sought a couch, in which a restless and fervent intellect might repose: or a Xystus or Portico, in which the mind might freely wander.

--- Page 75 ---
L I B E R I. 53
free, and wandering: or a high and lofty Tower, from which an ambitious and proud mind might look down: or a fortress and bulwark for contentions and battles: or a workshop for gain, and trade: And not rather a rich storehouse, and Treasury, for the glory of the maker of all things, and the relief of human life. For this is what would truly adorn and elevate learning and the arts, if contemplation and action were joined by a closer bond than hitherto. And certainly such a conjunction would be like the Syzygy of the two supreme Planets, when Saturn, the Leader of quiet and contemplation, conspires with Jupiter, the Leader of Society and action. Although when I speak of practice and action, I by no means allude to professional and lucrative learning. For it does not escape me how much this very thing hinders the progress and amplification of learning. Now I seem to have explained, and as it were, opened up with a kind of dissection, those vicious humors, or at least their principal ones, which not only hindered the progress of letters, but also gave occasion for blaming them. If indeed I have done this too much to the quick, it is necessary to remember, *Faithful are the wounds of a lover, but deceitful* *the kisses of a malicious one.* However this may be, I certainly seem to have achieved this, that I may merit trust in the following commendation, since I have acted so freely in the preceding censure. Nor is it my intention, however, to write a panegyric of letters, or to sing a hymn to the Muses, although perhaps it has been a long time since their sacred rites were duly celebrated: but the plan is, without embellishments and hyperboles, to take up and weigh the true importance of doctrine against other things, and to seek out its true value and price from divine and human testimonies.

Furthermore, the first actions of man, which he exercised in Paradise, embraced two summary parts of knowledge: these were, the inspection of creatures, and the imposition of names. For that knowledge which introduced the fall (which we also previously noted) was not natural science concerning creatures, but moral science concerning good and evil; from this supposition, that God's commands, or prohibitions, were not the principles of good and evil, but that they had other origins; the knowledge of which man sought, namely, that he might totally defect from God, and rely entirely on himself and his own will.

Let us come to those things which happened immediately after the fall. We see (as there are innumerable Mysteries of the sacred scriptures, always preserving historical and literal truth) the image of two lives, namely contemplative and active, delineated in the persons of Abel and Cain, and in their institutions, and primitive ways of living: of whom one was a Shepherd (who, because of leisure and quiet, and a free view of the sky, is a type of the Theoretical life) the other an agriculturist (wearied, namely, by labors, with his gaze fixed on the earth.) Where it is to be observed that divine favor and election came to the shepherd, not to the farmer.

  Nor indeed did God arrange these things differently after our Savior had come into the world. Thus also we know that many of the ancient Bishops and Fathers were excellently versed in all Gentile learning. So much so that Julian's edict, by which it was decreed that Christians should not be sent to Schools and Gymnasia, was considered a more pernicious device for overthrowing the Christian faith than the bloody persecutions of previous Emperors. Nor was the zeal and ill-will of Gregory I, Bishop of Rome (otherwise an excellent man), who strove to obliterate the memory of Gentile authors and antiquities, well-received, even among pious men. Moreover, the Christian Church alone, amidst the inundations of the Scythians from the northern regions and of the Saracens from the eastern ones, preserved in its bosom and lap the precious remnants of Gentile learning, which were already on the verge of utterly perishing. Recently also one can observe the Jesuits (who, partly from their own zeal, partly from rivalry with adversaries, strenuously applied themselves to letters) how much aid and strength they brought to restoring and establishing the Roman See.

As for human testimonies and arguments, so wide a field is opened that in this brief and concise treatise, it is more fitting to employ selection rather than abundance. First, therefore, the highest degree of honor among the Heathens was to achieve divine veneration and worship: (Which indeed for Christians is as a forbidden fruit:) But now we speak separately of human judgments. Therefore (as we began to say) among the Heathens, that which the Greeks called *Apotheosis*, the Latins *Enrollment among the Gods*, was the supreme honor that could be bestowed by man upon man: especially when it was not conferred by any decree or edict of the empire (as for the Caesars among the Romans), but was spontaneously bestowed from the opinion of men and internal faith. Of such an exalted honor, there was a certain degree and an intermediate stage. Indeed, above human honors, heroic and divine honors were reckoned. In their distribution, the ancients observed this order. Founders of commonwealths, Legislators, Tyrannicides; Fathers of the Fatherland, and those who deserved best in civil affairs, were distinguished by the title of Heroes only, or Demigods, such as *Theseus, Minos, Romulus*, and others: On the other hand, inventors and authors of new arts, and those who endowed human life with new conveniences and additions, were always consecrated among the greater Gods themselves; which to *Ceres, Bacchus, Mercury, Apollo*, and others was con-

But indeed this is seen more clearly when Kings themselves, or Magnates, or Governors are endowed with learning. For however much he may seem too devoted to his own party, who said, *then at last will states be happy, when either philosophers rule, or kings philosophize*; this, however, is known by experience, that under learned Princes and guardians of the State, ages have been most happy. For although Kings themselves have their own errors and vices,

   This happiness of times under learned Princes (as I always strive for brevity, using only the most select and most illustrious examples) is especially seen in that age which flowed from the death of Emperor Domitian up to the reign of Commodus; embracing a succession of learned princes, or certainly those intensely favoring learning; and (which was) by far the most flourishing of all (ages), if we consider temporal goods, that Rome, then the epitome of the whole world, ever saw. This had been foretold to Domitian in a dream, on the day before he was killed. For he seemed to see that *a golden head had grown for him behind his neck.* Which prophecy was indeed fulfilled in those subsequent golden ages. In natural philosophy, let that be observed which he frequently asserted: *'That he most perceived his mortality in two things, sleep and desire:'* which saying was indeed drawn from the deepest natural philosophy, wise not so much for Alexander, as for Aristotle or Democritus, since both the need and the excess of nature, designated by those two, are as it were pledges of death.

In Poetics, let that saying be observed, when, with blood flowing from his wounds, he summoned one of his flatterers, who used to attribute divinity to him, and said, *'Look, this is the blood of a man, not such a liquid as Homer said flowed from the hand of Venus, wounded by Diomedes;'* by this saying ridiculing both the poets, and his flatterers, and himself.

In politics, note that most weighty and most prudent distinction (which all posterity has embraced) by which he distinguished two of his principal friends, Hephaestion and Craterus, when he said, "One loves Alexander, the other loves the King:" establishing a dissimilarity of the greatest importance, even among the most faithful servants of kings, that some pursue the persons of their masters with true affection, while others are moved rather by duty towards the principate itself. Let it also be observed how excellently he refuted an error common to the counselors of princes, who for the most part suggest counsels according to the measure of their own mind and fortune, not their masters'. As for Julius Caesar, there is no need for us to make conjectures about the excellence of his learning, either from his education, or from his acquaintances, or from his own responses. For this indeed stands out in his writings and books: some of which are extant, others are unfortunately missing. had been, but acquired from the precepts and institutions of learning, his book on _Analogy_ testifies:
which was nothing else than a certain Grammatical Philosophy;
in which he diligently strove that arbitrary speech should be rendered speech according to rule; and that the custom of speaking in any way whatsoever should be recalled to the propriety of speaking correctly; and that words, which are images of things, should agree with the things themselves, and not entirely follow the arbitrary will of the common people.
    Thus also, as a monument of learning, no less than of power, we have his computation of the year, corrected by his edict; which clearly testifies that he considered it equally glorious for himself to know the laws of the stars in the heavens, as to give laws to men on earth.
    Also from the book, to which he prefixed the title _Anti-Cato_, it is readily apparent that he was inflamed with as much zeal for the victory of intellect, as for that of war and arms, to be obtained; then undertaking a contest of the pen against the greatest champion of that time, Cicero the Orator.
    Again, in the book of Apophthegms, which we see he collected, he thought it more honorable for himself if he were to transform himself as it were into Tablets or Notebooks, into which the wise and weighty sayings of others might be recorded; than if his own sayings were consecrated as oracles, as some foolish Princes, corrupted by flattery, eagerly desire to have done for themselves. First then, he must be a master of speech, who could suppress a mutiny in the army with a single word. And the matter stood thus. It was the custom for Romans, when commanders addressed the army, to call them soldiers; when a magistrate addressed the people, *Quirites*. Caesar's soldiers were rioting, and seditiously demanding their discharge; not because they themselves desired this, but so that by this demand they might force Caesar to other terms. He, unmoved and unshaken, having made silence, thus began: *I, Quirites:* By which word, he signified that they were already discharged. Struck by this, and utterly astonished, the soldiers thereafter continually interrupted him as he harangued, and setting aside that demand for discharge, on the contrary, earnestly begged that the appellation of soldiers be restored to them.

The second was of this kind. Caesar greatly desired the title of King. Therefore, some were suborned to greet him as King with popular acclamation as he passed by. He, perceiving that the acclamation had been faint and rare; dismissed the matter with a joke, as if a mistake had been made in the surname, "*I am not King,*"
                                             he said,

he said, "but Caesar." A saying indeed of this kind, that if it is diligently examined, its vigor and weight can scarcely be expressed. For first, it presented a refusal of the name, but by no means serious: Then it showed a certain immense confidence and magnanimity; as if the appellation of Caesar were a more illustrious title than that of King; which indeed turned out to be true, and has held true even to this day. But what most concerned him, this saying, with supreme artifice, pursued its goal. For this implied that the Senate and People of Rome were contending with him about a trivial matter, that is, merely about a name (for he had long since possessed royal power), and about such a name as many even from obscure families bore: For the surname 'Rex' was hereditary for many Romans, just as we also have something similar in our own idiom.

The last thing which it pleases to repeat in this place was as follows. When Caesar, after the war had begun, had occupied Rome and had opened the sacred Treasury, in order to take the money collected there for the uses of war, Metellus resisted, as he was at that time Tribune; to whom Caesar [said], *"If you persist,"* he said, *"you are dead."* Then, restraining himself a little, he added, *"Young man, it is harder for me to say this than to do it."* A saying so wonderfully forged from terror and clemency, that nothing could be more so.

Furthermore, learning takes away, or at least diminishes, the fear of death and of adverse fortune, than which nothing is more accustomed to harm virtues and morals. For if the mind of anyone has been imbued and steeped in the contemplation of mortality and the corruptible nature of things, he will feel just as Epictetus; who, when going out the day before, he saw a little woman weeping over a broken pot, and going out also the next day, he saw another woman lamenting her dead son, said; "Yesterday I saw a fragile thing broken, today I saw a mortal die." Therefore, most excellently and very wisely, Virgil coupled the knowledge of causes with the vanquishing of all fear, as if they were Concomitants.
*Happy is he who has been able to know the causes of things,*
*And who has placed all fears, and inexorable fate*

It would be too long to go through each remedy which learning
supplies for individual diseases of the mind; sometimes pur-

times aiding digestion, at other times exciting appetite, not
infrequently healing its wounds and ulcers, and similar things.
Therefore I will conclude with this, which seems to contain the
reason of the whole: namely, that learning so disposes and bends
the mind that it never immediately acquiesces and as it were
freezes in its defects, but rather always incites itself and breathes
progress. The unlearned man does not know what it is to descend
into himself, or to take account with himself, or how sweet a life
it is which daily feels itself becoming better; if by chance he is
endowed with any virtue, he will certainly boast of it and display
it everywhere to be seen, and perhaps use it conveniently, but
neglects to cultivate and increase it. Again, if he labors under
any vice, he will apply art and industry to concealing and hiding
it, but by no means to correcting it; like a bad reaper who
perpetually reaps but never sharpens his sickle: the learned man,
on the contrary, not only uses his mind and exercises virtue, but
continually amends himself and makes progress in virtue. Indeed,
to speak in sum, it is certain that truth and goodness are distin-

From virtue let us pass to power and dominion, and let us consider if anywhere is found such power and kingdom as learning invests and crowns human nature. We see that the dignity of commanding follows the dignity of him who is commanded. Dominion over wild beasts and cattle, such as that of herdsmen or shepherds, is a base thing; dominion over boys, such as that of schoolmasters, is less honorable; dominion over slaves is rather a disgrace than an honor. Nor is much more excellent the rule of tyrants over a servile people, stripped of spirit and noble character. Whence this judgment has always flowed, that honors in free Monarchies or Republics are sweeter than under tyrants; because honorable rule is more over those who are willing than over those who are unwilling and compelled. And therefore Virgil, when with profound art he wished to bring forth by far the best among human honors, which he might assign to Augustus Caesar, speaks in these very words,
                --- And as victor he gives laws
  To willing peoples, and aims his way
      To Olympus.
But the dominion of knowledge is far loftier than dominion over the will, even if free and unconstrained. For that rules over reason, faith, and the intellect itself, which is the
                E 4             highest

--- Page 106 ---
84 ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING
most exalted part of the soul, and governs the will itself. For without doubt, there is no earthly power that erects and establishes its throne, and as it were, its chair, in the spirits of men, and in their souls, and in their thoughts, and fantasies, and also in their assent and faith, except doctrine and knowledge. And therefore we see that detestable and immense delight with which Heresiarchs, false Prophets, and great impostors are imbued and carried away, after they have perceived that they have begun to reign in the faith and consciences of men: so great indeed, that whoever has once tasted it can scarcely be compelled by any persecutions or torments to abdicate this kingdom. But just as this is what is said in the Apocalypse, *the Abyss or depths of Satan*: so, on the contrary, a just and legitimate dominion over the minds of men, established by the very evidence of truth and the sweetest commendation, certainly approaches very closely to the likeness of divine power.
   As for fortunes and honors, the munificence of learning does not thus enrich entire kingdoms and republics,

whether arms or letters have established the fortunes of many. Moreover, if we speak of supreme power, we see that if arms, or the right of inheritance, have conferred a Kingdom, yet the priesthood, which was always a rival to the kingdom, has more often yielded to the power of letters.

  Furthermore, if you consider the delight and pleasure of knowledge, it certainly surpasses all other pleasures by a great deal. What then? Do the pleasures of the affections perhaps exceed the delights of the senses by such a great interval, as the happy attainment of a wish (exceeds) a little song or a dinner? And will not the pleasures of the intellect, by a similar gradation, transcend those of the affections? In other delights, satiety is close at hand, and after they have grown a little old, their flower and charm wither; by which we are taught that those were not truly real and sincere pleasures, but only shadows and deceptions of pleasures, pleasant not so much by their own quality as by their novelty; whence also voluptuaries often become Monks, and the old age of ambitious princes is almost sadder and beset by melancholy. But of knowledge there is no satiety, but a perpetually and repeatedly recurring alternation of enjoying and desiring; so that it must be that the good of this delight is simple, not accidental, or with fraud. Nor does that pleasure, which Lucretius depicts, obtain the ultimate place in the mind;

So truly, knowledge seemed to them an immortal thing,

Although these things are so, I by no means take this upon myself, nor do I trust that I can achieve it, that by any pleading or action for this cause of learning, I might overturn the judgments: either of *Aesop's Cock*, who preferred a grain of barley to a jewel; or of *Midas*, who, when he had been made judge between Apollo, patron of the Muses, and Pan, the President of the sheep, awarded the palm of wealth; or of *Paris*, who, despising wisdom and power, gave the first place to pleasure and love; or of *Agrippina*, choosing, '*Let him kill his mother, provided he rules*', preferring empire even with a detestable condition; or of *Ulysses*, who preferred an old woman to immortality, certainly types of those who prefer the accustomed to the best: and many such popular judgments. For these will hold their ancient sway: But that also will remain, upon which learning has always rested as its firmest foundation

Among these things, however (unless my zeal for letters deceives me), nothing is more worthy, or nobler, than if the world were endowed with solid and fruitful *Augmentations of Sciences*. For how long, pray, shall we finally set up a few writers for ourselves as *Pillars of Hercules, lest we advance further* in doctrines; when we have Your Majesty, like a bright and benign Star, which may guide and and prosper us while we navigate?

Therefore, to return to the matter: Let us now recall, and weigh with ourselves, what leading Men, and others, have hitherto contributed to the amplification of letters, and what they have omitted? Let us, however, examine this precisely and distinctly, in a certain Active and Masculine discourse, nowhere digressing, nothing amplifying.

Let it therefore be posited, (which anyone would concede) that all the greatest and most difficult works are overcome either by the amplitude of rewards, or by the prudence and soundness of counsels, or by the conjunction of labors: Of which the first stimulates effort, the second removes ambiguities and errors, the third succors the fragility of mortals.    And first, the Works which pertain to the *Seats of the Muses* are four in number: The structure of Buildings; The endowment of Revenues; The granting of Privileges; The Law and Institution of Discipline; All of which contribute (for the most part) to retreat and leisure, and to freedom from cares and troubles: such as those things which Virgil requires for establishing Beehives, for the use of honey;

Furthermore, the works which concern the *Persons of Learned Men* (besides the fact that they themselves are to be honored and promoted) are also two: The remuneration and appointment of Lecturers, in arts long since invented and known; and the remuneration and appointment of writers, concerning those parts of doctrine which have not hitherto been sufficiently cultivated or elaborated.

These, in summary, are the works and deeds in which the merits of illustrious Princes and other distinguished men, towards the literary realm, have become clear. When thinking about the particular commemoration of anyone who has deserved well of Letters, that saying of Cicero comes to mind, which impelled him, after his return, to give thanks indiscriminately; *It is difficult to include anyone ungrateful.* Rather (following the counsel of the scriptures), let us look at the space that still remains to be run in the race, than turn our eyes back to those things which we have long since left behind.

First therefore, among so many Colleges throughout Europe, most splendidly founded, I am astonished that all of them are destined for certain Professions, none dedicated to free and universal studies of arts and sciences. For if anyone judges that all Doctrine should be referred to *Use and Action*, he is wise: Nevertheless, it is easy in that way to fall into error.

For it is especially important for the progress in Sciences, that Lecturers in each kind be chosen from the best and most learned: inasmuch as their work is applied not for transient use; but for supplying the Offspring of Science, for ages. This cannot happen, unless such rewards and conditions are established, by which each most eminent person in that Art can be plainly content; so that finally it may not be burdensome for him to die in the same office, nor to think of Practice. Therefore, for Sciences to flourish, the Military law of David must be observed; *That the share of him who goes down to battle, and of him who remains with the baggage, should be equal;* Otherwise, the baggage will be poorly provided for. Finally, I complain about this (concerning which I have previously made some preliminary remarks), that either never, or very rarely, has there been any public designation of suitable men, who would either write, or institute an inquiry, concerning those parts of the sciences in which sufficient work has not yet been done.

For this purpose, it will be most useful if a survey of doctrines is established, and a census is taken, to determine which of them are rich and greatly augmented, and which are poor and destitute.

For the opinion of abundance is among the causes of poverty; and the multitude of books presents itself as an indication of luxury rather than of scarcity.

This redundancy, however (if one judges correctly), should by no means be removed by destroying books written previously, but by publishing new and better ones, which are of such a kind that, like the serpent of Moses, they devour the serpents of the Magicians.

As for which [works], the efforts and industry of any private individual are almost like Mercury at the Crossroads, who can point a finger towards the road, but cannot set foot upon it. But that speculative part, which pertains to the examination of doctrines (what indeed is lacking in each), is also open to the industry of a private individual. Therefore, it is my intention to undertake a survey of doctrines, and a general and faithful review, especially with a diligent and accurate inquiry into which of their parts lie neglected and uncultivated, not yet subdued by human industry and converted to use; so that a delineation and registration of this kind may light a torch both for public initiatives and for the spontaneous labors of private individuals. In which, nevertheless, the plan is, at this time, only to note omissions and desiderata; but not to refute errors and infelicities. For it is one thing to point out uncultivated places, another to correct the method of cultivation.

Indeed, for this task, as I prepare myself and gird myself for action, I am not unaware how great a work I undertake, and how difficult an undertaking I sustain; also how little my strengths are equal to my will: nevertheless, I entertain great hope, if a more ardent mind, a love for letters, has carried me further, I will use the excuse of passion; because it is not granted to anyone at the same time, *to Love and to be Wise*. Indeed, I am well aware that the same freedom of judgment

As far as the first two are concerned, the things themselves will plead their own cause; concerning the last point, regarding impossibility, I thus determine: All those things are to be considered possible and achievable which can be accomplished by some, although not by just anyone; and which by many jointly, although not by one; and which in the succession of ages, although not in the same age; and finally, which by public care and expense, although not by the wealth and industry of individuals. If there is anyone, however, who would prefer to use that saying of Solomon, *The sluggard says, There is a lion in the way;* rather than that of Virgil, *They can, because they seem to be able:* it will be enough for me if my labours are held merely among wishes or aspirations of a better kind. Nor do we think any other partition is necessary for *Theology*.             C H A P. I I.

*Division of History into Natural and Civil, Ecclesiastical and Literary comprehended under Civil. Division of Natural History into the History of Generations, Preter-Generations, and Arts.*

H Istory is either *Natural* or *Civil*: In *Natural* [History], the actions and deeds of Nature are recorded; in *Civil*, those of men. Undoubtedly, *Divine* [matters] shine forth in both, but more

--- Page 129 ---
LIBER II. 107
more in *Civil* [History], so that they even constitute a distinct species of *History*, which we are accustomed to call *Sacred* or *Ecclesiastical*. But to us, the dignity of *Letters* and *Arts* also seems such that a distinct *History* should be separately attributed to them; which we understand to be comprised under *Civil History* (just as *Ecclesiastical* History is).

We undertake the partition of *Natural History* from the state and condition of Nature itself, which is found to exist in a threefold state, and as it were undergoes a triple governance. For either nature is free, explaining itself in its accustomed course, as in the heavens, animals, plants, and the entire apparatus of nature; or it is thrust from its state by the depravities and insolence of stubborn matter, and by the violence of impediments, as in Monsters; or finally, it is constrained and shaped by human art and labor, and as it were renewed, as in artificial things.

Let therefore the partition of *Natural History* be into the *History of Generations*; *Preter-Generations*; and *Arts*; Which last we are also accustomed to call *Mechanical* and *Experimental*. Of these, the first treats the *liberty of nature*, the second its *errors*, the third its *bonds*. We willingly, however, constitute the *history of arts* as a species of natural history: because the opinion has entirely grown old, as if art were something different from nature, artificial things from natural ones: whence that evil, that most
