Therefore, nature governs all things: but those three are subordinated; *the course of nature*; *the digression of nature*; and *art*, or man added to things: And therefore, in natural history, it is proper that those three be comprehended; which C. For as the matter now stands, if by chance some falsehoods concerning natural things have gained acceptance and become celebrated (whether because the reverence for antiquity can do so much, or because it is troublesome to subject them again to examination, or because they are indeed thought to be wonderful ornaments of speech, on account of similarities and comparisons), they are never afterwards eradicated or retracted.
    The purpose of this kind of work, which Aristotle adorned with his example, is by no means to gratify curious and empty minds, as wonder-mongers and prodigy-makers do: But for two reasons, both serious and weighty; one, that the unsoundness of axioms may be corrected, which for the most part have their foundation in worn-out and common examples: The other, that a ready and open passage may be made from the wonders of nature to the wonders of art.
    For there is no more difficulty in this matter than that you sagaciously pursue the traces of nature, when she herself spontaneously deviates: so that in this way afterwards, when you wish, you may be able to lead and compel her to the same place. Nor indeed would I prescribe that from this history of wonders, superstitious narratives concerning witchcraft, fascinations, incantations, dreams, divinations, and similar things, should be entirely excluded, where the fact and the event are clearly established.

in this kind, experiments familiar and common in individual arts are always neglected and rejected; yet these contribute equally or more to the interpretation of nature than less common ones. For a certain stain seems to be cast upon learning, if perchance learned men submit themselves to the inquiry or observation of mechanical things, unless it be of those things which are considered as secrets of art, or as very rare or subtle things. This vice of such empty and supercilious arrogance, Plato rightly ridiculed, when he introduces the boastful Sophist Hippias disputing with Socrates, a sincere and solid investigator of truth: Who, when the discussion was about beauty, according to his vague and free manner of disputing, first introduced the example of a beautiful maiden, then a beautiful mare, and finally a beautiful and skillfully made earthenware pot. Hippias, moved by this last example, said: "*I would certainly be indignant (unless the consideration of humanity compelled me to it) to dispute with anyone who would adduce such vile and sordid examples.*" To whom Socrates replied, "*Indeed, it suits you so, since you are clothed in such splendid garments and beautiful shoes:*" and other things ironically. Indeed, it can be asserted for certain that grand examples do not provide the best or safest information. This is expressed not foolishly in that well-known fable about the Philosopher: who, when observing the stars

--- Page 135 ---
LIBER II. 113

...with uplifted eyes, fell into the water: For if he had lowered his eyes, he could have immediately seen the stars in the water; but looking up at the sky, he could not see the water in the stars. In the same way, it often happens that small and humble things contribute more to the knowledge of great things than great things to the knowledge of small ones. Indeed, Aristotle rightly observed, *that the nature of anything is best discerned in its smallest parts.* For this reason, he first investigates the nature of the Commonwealth in the family, and in the simplest combinations of society (namely, husband and wife, parents and children, Master and Servant), which occur in any humble dwelling. By a precisely similar reasoning, the nature of this great city (namely, the universe of things) and its administration must be investigated in every primary symbolization and in the smallest portions of things: as we see happens, that secret of nature (held to be most important), concerning the polarity of iron, excited to the poles by the touch of a magnet, revealed itself not in iron bars, but in needles.

But I, if there is any weight to my judgment, thus plainly declare; that the use of *Mechanical History* towards Natural Philosophy is most radical and fundamental. I understand such a Natural Philosophy which does not vanish into the smoke of subtle or sublime speculations; but which operates effectively, towards the advancement of...

alleviating the inconveniences of human life. For just as you would not know or prove someone's character well, unless you provoke him; nor was Proteus accustomed to transform himself into various shapes of things, unless tightly grasped by manacles; similarly, nature, irritated and vexed by art, reveals herself more clearly than when she is freely permitted to herself.
    But before we dismiss this branch of natural history (which we call mechanical and experimental), that must be added; the body of such a history ought to be compiled not only from the mechanical arts themselves, but also from the operative part of the liberal sciences, and at the same time from many Practices (which have not coalesced into an art), so that nothing useful is omitted which helps to inform the understanding. And this is the *first division of natural history.*

[Large initial H] *Natural History, as it is threefold in Subject*
*(as we have said), so it is twofold in Use:*
For it is employed either for the *Knowledge of the things themselves*, which are committed to history; or as *the primary Material of Philosophy*. And that former kind, which either delights with the pleasantness of *Narrations*, or aids with the utility of *Experiments*, and has been sought for the sake of such pleasure or fruit, is to be considered of a far inferior rank, compared to that which may be the forest and furniture for true and legitimate *Induction*, and may offer the first nourishment to Philosophy. Therefore, we again divide *natural history into Narrative and Inductive:* And this latter we place among the *Desiderata*. Nor indeed should the keenness of anyone's mind be dazzled by the great names of the ancients, or the great volumes of the moderns. C A P. V.

*Concerning the Dignity and Difficulty of Civil History.*

**T**here follows *Civil History* in particular, whose dignity and authority stand out among human writings. For to its trust are committed the examples of our ancestors, the vicissitudes of things, the foundations of Civil Prudence, and finally the name and fame of men. To the dignity of the subject is added no less difficulty. For to draw back the mind in writing to past events, and as it were to make it ancient; to diligently scrutinize the movements of times, the characters of persons, the hesitations of counsels, the courses of actions (as of waters), the inner workings of pretexts, the secrets of empire; to relate them with fidelity and freedom; and finally, to place them before the eyes with the light of words, is certainly a work of great labor and judgment; especially since older matters are found to be uncertain, and more recent ones exposed to danger. For this reason, many faults also surround this Civil History: while most people [produce] certain meager narratives, and ple-

--- Page 144 ---
122      DE AUGM. SCIENT.
and common, and plainly disgraceful histories they write;
others patch together particular accounts and small
commentaries with hurried work and in an uneven style;
others only skim the main points of events, while others, on
the contrary, pursue every smallest detail, and things
contributing nothing to the main actions; some, with
excessive indulgence towards their own talents, boldly
invent many things; but others impress upon events not so
much the image of their own talents as that of their
passions, and add things, mindful of their own parties,
being witnesses little faithful to the facts: some everywhere
inculcate politics, in which they take pleasure, and seeking
digressions for ostentation, too lightly interrupt the
narration of events: others are excessive in the prolixity
of speeches, and sermons, or even of the acts themselves,
with little judgment; so that it is sufficiently clear that
nothing is found more rarely among the writings of men
than a legitimate history, perfect in all its parts. But we at
present are instituting a division of doctrines, so that things
may be omitted; not a censure, so that faults may be noted.
Now we will pursue the divisions of *Civil History*, and those
of different kinds: For the Species will be less entangled if
diverse divisions are proposed, than if one division is
curiously drawn out through its members.

[Large decorative initial H] ISTORY *Civil* is tripartite, not unlike three

In these kinds of *Imperfect History*, I do not think any defect should be pointed out, since they are, as it were, *Imperfectly Compounded*, so that a defect of this kind is from their very Nature. As for *Epitomes* (indeed the woodworms and moths of Histories), we wish them to be banished; which we do also with very many who were of the soundest judgment; inasmuch as they have eaten away and corroded many bodies of the noblest Histories, and finally reduced them to useless dregs.

CAP VII.
*Division of Just History into Chronicles, Lives, & Relations; and an explanation of those parts.*

[Large decorative initial A]T *Just History* is of three kinds, according to the nature of the *Object* which it proposes to represent. For either it represents some *Portion* of time; or a singular *Person* worthy of memory; or some *Action* or *deed* from among the more illustrious. The first we call *Chronicles* or *Annals*; the second, *Lives*; the third, *Relations*. Among these, *Chronicles* seem to excel in renown and name; *Lives*, however, in benefit and examples; *Relations*, again, in sincerity and truth. For *Chronicles* propose the scope of public actions, and the external aspects of persons, and those turned towards the public; Minor
G matters,

--- Page 148 ---
126      OF THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING.
but minor things, which pertain both to affairs and to persons, they omit and wrap in silence. But since it is characteristic of divine art to suspend the greatest from the smallest, it often happens that history of this kind, having pursued only the greater things, shows rather the pomp and solemnities of affairs than their true origins and more subtle textures; furthermore, even if it adds and intermingles the counsels themselves, nevertheless, delighting in grandeur, it sprinkles upon human actions more gravity and prudence than they truly possess; so that some Satire can be a truer picture of human life than some of these kinds of Histories. On the contrary, Lives, if they are written diligently and with judgment (for we are not speaking of Elogies, and such barren Commemorations), since they propose a single Person as their Subject, in whom it is necessary for actions, no less trivial than grave, small than great, private than public, to be composed and intermingled; they certainly exhibit more vivid and faithful narratives of events, and which you can transfer to example more safely and happily. But special Relations of Actions (such as the Peloponnesian War, the Expedition of Cyrus, the Conspiracy of Catiline, and similar things) it is altogether fitting that they be clothed in a purer and more sincere candor of truth than the just Histories of times; because in them an argument can be chosen and taken that is suitable and definite; and of such a kind, that concerning it, know-

--- Page 149 ---
L I B E R II. 127
knowledge, and good certainty, and full information can be had, whereas, on the contrary, the *History* of a period (especially one which is much older than the age of the writer) necessarily often fails in the memory of events, and contains, as it were, empty spaces; which have been accustomed to be filled and supplied quite freely by ingenuity and conjecture. This very thing, however, which we say concerning the sincerity of *Relations*, must be understood with an exception. For it must certainly be confessed (since all human things are imperfect in part, and advantages are almost perpetually conjoined with disadvantages) that relations of this kind, especially if they are published at the very time of the events, (since they are often written either for favor or for ill-will,) are deservedly the most suspect of all narratives. **C H A P. VIII.**

*Division of the History of Times, into Universal*
*and Particular History, and the Advantages*
*and Disadvantages of each.*

The History of Times is either Universal
or Particular; The latter embraces the deeds
of some Kingdom, or Republic, or Nation,
the former those of the Whole World. Nor indeed have
there been wanting those who wish to appear to have
written the History of the World even from its Origin;
presenting a jumble of things, and abridgements of
narratives, instead of History: Others have been confident
that they could embrace the memorable events of their
own time, throughout the whole world, as a proper
History, an attempt certainly magnanimous, and with
no small fruit. For human affairs are not so divided
by Empires or Regions, that they do not have many
things connected; Wherefore it is certainly helpful to
view the destinies appointed to any age or era, as if
contained and described on a single tablet. It also
happens that many writings not to be scorned (such
as those Reports, of which we spoke before), which
might otherwise perhaps perish, and not often to
undergo printing, or at least their main points, are
received into such a General History, and in this way
are fixed and preserved. Nevertheless, if one considers
the matter more correctly, one will notice that the
Laws of a proper History are so severe, that to exercise

--- Page 156 ---
134      ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING
...it is scarcely permissible to exercise them; so much so that the Majesty of History is rather diminished by the grandeur of its bulk, than amplified. For it will happen that he who pursues so many varied things from all sides, with the scrupulousness of information gradually relaxed, and his diligence, which extends to so many matters, languishing in individual instances, will catch popular ears and rumors; and from relations not very authentic, or some such trivial material, will compose history. Moreover, it will be necessary for him (lest the work grow to an immense size) to deliberately omit many things worthy of relation, and to often descend to the methods of epitomes. Another not small danger also arises, and one diametrically opposed to the utility of universal history. For just as universal history preserves some narratives which otherwise perhaps would have perished; so on the contrary, it very often destroys other sufficiently fruitful narratives, which would have otherwise survived, because of the summaries of things pleasing to mortals.

            CHAPTER IX.
Another Division of the History of Times, into Annals, &
            Journals.

Also the History of Times is rightly divided into Annals, & Journals: Which division, although it takes its names from periods of time, nevertheless also pertains to the selection of matters. For rightly Cornelius Tacitus, when he came to mention the Magnificence of certain structures.

--- Page 157 ---
**BOOK II. 135**
he rarely mentions it, immediately adding, '*It was found to be in keeping with the dignity of the Roman people to commit illustrious matters to the Annals, and such things to the daily acts of the city:*' Applying to the *Annals* matters which pertain to the *State of the Republic*; but the lighter *Acts* and *Occurrences* to the *Diaries*. In my judgment, at any rate, it would be fitting for a certain heraldic discipline to prevail, in arranging the dignities no less of books than of persons. For just as nothing detracts more from *Civil Affairs* than the confusion of Orders and Ranks; so also it detracts not a little from the authority of serious history, if matters of lesser moment are mixed with *Politics*; such as pomp, and solemnities, and spectacles, and things of this kind. And indeed it would be desirable that that very distinction should come into common practice. In our times, however, *Diaries* are only in use for voyages and military expeditions. Among the Ancients, certainly, it was given to the honor of Kings that the acts of their Palace should be recorded in *Diaries*; which we see was done under *Ahasuerus, King of the Persians*; who, when he spent a sleepless night, called for the *Diaries*; where he recognized the conspiracy of the Eunuchs: But in *Alexander's Diaries,* such trivial matters were contained, that even if he happened to fall asleep at the table, it would be recorded in the acts: For neither did *Annals* only comprise weighty matters, nor *Diaries* only light ones; but all things indiscriminately and cursorily were received into *Diaries*, whether of greater or lesser moment.

C H A P. X.

*Second Division of Civil History, into Pure,*
*& Mixed.*

THE last division of Civil History, however, is that it be divided into Pure, or Mixed. There are two notable mixtures. One from Civil Science. The other principally from Natural [Science]. For a kind of writing has been introduced by some, that one should compile certain narratives, not continued in the series of history, but selected by the author's choice: then recall them, and as it were, ruminate upon them; and taking occasion from them, discourse on Political matters. Which kind of *ruminated history* we indeed greatly approve, provided that such a writer does this, and confesses that he is doing this. But to one writing *just* history professionally, to insert politics everywhere, and by those means to interrupt the thread of history, is something untimely and troublesome. For although every more prudent history may be, as it were, impregnated with political precepts and warnings, yet the writer himself ought not to act as his own midwife.
Also mixed is *Cosmographical history*, and that in many ways: For it has from *Natural history*, the Regions themselves, and their *Sites*, and *Fruits*; From *Civil history*, *Cities*, *Empires*, *Customs*: From *Mathematics*, *Climates*, and *Configurations of the Heavens*, by which the tracts of the world

--- Page 159 ---
LIBER II. 137
are subject to. It is in this kind of *History*, or Science, that we have cause to congratulate our age. For in this our age, the globe of the earth has been remarkably opened up and made accessible. The Ancients certainly knew the Zones and Antipodes,
( *And where the rising sun with panting horses first breathed upon us,*
*There the late reddening evening kindles its lights.* )
And this very knowledge more through demonstrations than through travels. But that some small *Keel* should emulate heaven itself; and should have circled the entire terrestrial globe with a journey even more oblique and winding than celestial bodies are accustomed to, that is the prerogative of our age: so that the present age can rightly adopt in its motto, not only that *Plus ultra* (Further beyond), where the Ancients adopted *Non ultra* (No further); and moreover that *Imitable lightning*, where the Ancients (adopted) *Non-imitable lightning*;
( *Madman who (imitates) clouds, and non-imitable lightning;* )
but also that, which surpasses all admiration, *Imitable Heaven*; on account of our navigations, by which it has often been granted to be rolled and carried around the entire circuit of the earth, in the manner of celestial bodies.
And this splendid success in nautical matters and in exploring the Globe can create great hope concerning even further progress and Augmentations of the Sciences; especially

--- Page 160 ---
138          ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING.
tim since it seems to have been decreed by divine Counsel that these two things should be coeval: For thus Daniel the Prophet, speaking of the last times, foretells, *Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be increased*; as if the passing through, or exploration of the world, and the manifold Augmentation of the Sciences, were destined for the same age: As we now see largely accomplished; inasmuch as our times, in learning, do not much yield to those two earlier periods or revolutions of doctrines (one among the Greeks, the other among the Romans), but rather in some things far surpass them.

C H A P. XI.

*Partition of Ecclesiastical history, into special Ecclesiastical history, history pertaining to Prophecies, & history of Nemesis.*

[Large initial H]*Ecclesiastical history* in general undergoes almost the same divisions as *Civil history*. For there are *Ecclesiastical Chronicles*, there are *lives of the Fathers*, there are *Relations concerning Synods*, & other things pertaining to the Church. But properly speaking, it is rightly divided into *Ecclesiastical history* (the generic name being retained), & *history pertaining to Prophecies*, & *history of Nemesis or Providence*. The first commemorates the *times* & *diverse state of the Church Militant*: whether it fluctuates, like the *Ark in the deluge*: or journeys, like the *Ark in the wilderness*: or stands still, like the *Ark*—

--- Page 161 ---
            BOOK II.           139
as the _Ark_ in the temple: that is, the state of the _Church_
in persecution, in movement, and in peace. In this
part, I find no defect, but rather that many things
are present in it than are lacking: I would certainly
wish that to so great a mass, the quality and sincerity
of the narratives would also correspond.
   The second part, which is the _history relating to Prophecies_,
consists of two Relatives, the _Prophecy itself_, and its
_Fulfillment_. Therefore, such ought to be the design of this
work, that with each of the _Prophecies_ from the scriptures,
the truth of events may be joined; and this through all ages
of the world, both for the confirmation of faith, and
for establishing a certain discipline and skill, in the
interpretation of _Prophecies_, which still remain to be
fulfilled. Nevertheless, in this matter, that latitude must

that their fulfillments may occur, both continuously and

The Third Part, which is the *History of Nemesis*,
has indeed fallen into the pens of some pious men, but not without partisan bias: it is occupied, however, in observing that divine congruence which sometimes intervenes between God's Revealed Will and His Secret Will. For although the Counsels and Judgments of God are so obscure that they are utterly inscrutable to the *natural man*, and indeed often withdraw themselves from the eyes of those who look forth from the tabernacle; nevertheless, it has seemed good to Divine Wisdom, sometimes at turns, for the confirmation of His own, and the confusion of those who are, as it were, without God in the world, to propose these things, as if written in larger characters, thus to be seen, so that (as the Prophet speaks) *anyone may read them even in running*; that is, that merely sensual and pleasure-seeking men, who hasten to pass by those divine Judgments, and never fix their thoughts upon them, nevertheless, although they run quickly and are doing something else, are compelled to acknowledge them. Such are late and unexpected vengeances; sudden and unhoped-for salvations; divine counsels, through tortuous windings of things and amazing spirals, at last clearly unfolding themselves; and similar things: which are powerful, not only for comforting the minds of the faithful, but for striking and convincing the consciences of the wicked.

CAP. XII.

*On the Appendices of history: which concern the Words of men (just as history itself concerns facts): Their division into letters, and apophthegms.*

But not only of the deeds of the human race, but also of its sayings, memory ought to be preserved. Nor is there any doubt, however, that those sayings are sometimes inserted into history itself, insofar as they clearly and weightily contribute to and serve the narration of events. But sayings or *Human* words are properly preserved by *Books of Orations, Letters, and Apophthegms.*

And indeed, the Orations of prudent men, delivered on grave and arduous affairs and causes, are very valuable both for the knowledge of the matters themselves and for eloquence. But even greater aids are provided for instructing civil prudence by *Letters*, which have been sent by great men concerning serious affairs. For from the words of men, nothing is sounder or more excellent than *Letters* of this kind. For they have more native sense than Orations; and also more maturity than sudden conversations. The same, when continued according to a series of times, (as happens in those which are sent by *Legates, Governors of Provinces, & other Ministers of the Empire, to Kings, or Senates, or their other Superiors; or conversely*

--- Page 164 ---
142 ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING.
(and conversely from Rulers to ministers,) are
certainly, for *history*, above all, a most precious
store. Nor do *Apophthegms* themselves serve
only for delight and ornament, but also for the
conduct of affairs, and civil uses. For they are
(as he used to say) like *Axes* or *Spear-points of
Words*, which cut and penetrate the knots of
things and affairs with a certain sharpness: But
occasions return in a cycle, and what was once
useful, can again be applied and be profitable;
whether one brings them forth as one's own, or
as ancient. Nor indeed can there be any doubt
about the utility of this matter for civil affairs,
which Caesar the Dictator honored with his own

those things which are anywhere found in this
kind, seem to us to be collected with too little
selection.
    And let these things have been said concerning

   And concerning *Narrative Poetry*, whether it

and in some way to satisfy the mind with shadows of things,
when solid things cannot be had.
For if anyone looks into the matter more acutely, a
firm argument is drawn from *Poetry*, that a more
illustrious greatness of things, a more perfect order,
and a more beautiful variety, please the human soul,
than it can in any way find in nature itself, after the Fall.
Therefore, since deeds and events, which are
subject to true history, are not of such magnitude
in which the human soul may satisfy itself, *Poetry*
is at hand, which invents more Heroic deeds:
Since true history narrates the successes of things
by no means according to the merits of Virtues
and Crimes; *Poetry* corrects it, and exhibits
outcomes and fortunes, according to merits, and
by the law of Nemesis: Since
                                                     true,

--- Page 167 ---

(true history), by the obvious satiety and similarity of things, becomes a weariness to the human soul; Poetry refreshes it, singing of things unexpected, varied, and full of changes. So much so that this Poetry contributes not only to delight, but also to greatness of soul and to morals. Wherefore and deservedly it can even seem to partake of some divinity; because it raises the soul and snatches it to the sublime; by accommodating the images of things to the soul's desires, not by submitting the soul to things (which reason and history do). And by these allurements, and by the suitability with which it soothes the human soul, with the added companionship of Music (whence it can be more sweetly insinuated), it opened a way for itself, so that it was held in honor even in plainly rude ages, and among barbarous nations, when other Doctrines were entirely excluded.

Dramatic Poetry, however, which has the Theater as its world, is excellent in use, if it were sound. For not small could be the Theater's Discipline and Corruption: And of Corruptions, in this kind, there is abundance; discipline is plainly neglected in our times. Nevertheless, although in modern Republics theatrical action is held as a trivial thing, unless perhaps it draws too much from Satire and bites; yet among the Ancients it was a concern that it should instruct the minds of men towards virtue. Moreover, by prudent men and great Philosophers, it was considered as a kind of plectrum for the soul. And indeed

--- Page 168 ---
146 ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING
indeed it is most true, and as a certain Secret of Nature, that the minds of men, when they are gathered together, are more open to affections and impressions than when they are alone.

But *Parabolic Poetry* stands out among the rest, and seems like a sacred and august thing; especially since Religion itself very often uses its agency, and through it carries on the commerce of divine things with human. Nevertheless, this also is found to be corrupted by the levity and indulgence of intellects concerning Allegories. Its use, however, is ambiguous, and it is applied to contrary purposes. For it serves for *Envelopment*; it also serves for *Illustration*. In the latter, a certain *Method of Teaching*; in the former, an *Artifice of Concealing* seems to be sought. This *Method of Teaching*, however, which serves for *Illustration*, was very much used in ancient centuries. For since the inventions and conclusions of human reason (even those which are now trite and common) were at that time new and unaccustomed, human intellects scarcely grasped that subtlety, unless they were brought nearer to the senses through such images and examples. Wherefore all things among them were full of all kinds of fables, and Parables, and Enigmas, and similitudes. Hence the symbols of Pythagoras, the Enigmas of the Sphinx, the Fables of Aesop, and similar things. Moreover, the Apophthegms of the ancient Sages almost always demonstrated the matter through similitudes. Hence Menenius Agrippa
                                                                    among

--- Page 169 ---

among the Romans (a people in that age very
unlettered) a fable suppressed sedition. Finally,
as hieroglyphs were older than letters, so parables
were older than arguments. And even today and
always, the power of parables has been and is
outstanding, since neither arguments can be so clear,
nor true examples so apt.
   There is another use of *Parabolic Poetry*, almost
contrary to the former, which serves (as we said) for

But since what has hitherto been attempted concerning the interpretation of these Parables, namely by unskilled men, nor beyond learned commonplaces, in no way satisfies us; it seemed good to include Philosophy according to ancient Parables among the Desiderata. Of this work, however, we will subjoin one or two Examples. Not that the matter is perhaps of such great importance, but that we may maintain our purpose. This is as follows: that concerning those works which we place among the Desiderata (if anything is a little obscure), we perpetually propose either precepts for guiding that work, or Examples: lest anyone perhaps think that only some slight Notion concerning them has touched our mind, and that we, like Augurs, only measure regions with our mind, and do not know the ways of entering them. We do not find any other part in Poetry to be desired; but rather, since Poetry is a plant which, as it were, from a luxuriant earth, has germinated without a specific seed, it has grown above other doctrines and has spread widely. But now we will propose examples, only three in number: one from Natural Philosophy, one from Politics, and finally one from Morals.

First Example of Philosophy according to Ancient Parables,
in Natural Philosophy. Concerning the Universe, according
to the Fable of Pan.

The ancients leave the generation of *Pan* in doubt.
For some say he was begotten by *Mercury*;
Others attribute to him a far different mode of generation.
For they say that all the Suitors had intercourse with *Penelope*,
from which promiscuous union *Pan* was born as a common son.
Nor should that third explanation of his generation be omitted:
For some have reported that he was the son of *Jupiter* and *Hybris*
(that is, *Contumely*). However he was born, the *Fates* are said
to have been his sisters: who dwelt in a subterranean cave:
but *Pan* dwelled under the open sky. The effigy of *Pan* is
described by antiquity as such: Horned, with horns rising to a point,
and tapering up to the sky; his whole body shaggy and hairy;
his beard especially long; his form twofold, human as to the upper
parts, but half-beast and ending in goat's feet. He bore, moreover,
insignia of power; in his left hand a pipe made of seven reeds,
in his right a shepherd's crook or staff, curved and bent at the top.
He was clothed in a cloak of *Leopard* skin. Powers and functions
of this kind are attributed to him: that he is the God of hunters,
also of shepherds, and in general of country-dwellers; likewise
the President of mountains. He was also, next to *Mercury*,

The *Fates*, truly called the *sisters of things*, are said to belong to the Nature of things, and are posited. For the *Fates* are called

is so great that it does not depend on something else; so

embraces every event both smallest and greatest;

Indeed, *Epicurus* seems not only to utter profane discourse, but also to be foolish, when he said, *It is better to believe the fable of the Gods than to assert Fate*, as if anything in the universe could exist like an Island, separated from the chain of things. Moreover, horns are attributed to the world, broader at the base, sharp at the top. For all nature of things is pointed like a Pyramid. Indeed, Individuals, in which the base of nature extends, are infinite; these are gathered into species, and these themselves are manifold; species in turn rise into genera, and these also, ascending, are contracted into more general categories; so that finally nature seems to converge into one; which is signified by *that pyramidal Figure of Pan's Horns*. But the *Body of Nature* is most elegantly and most truly depicted as *shaggy*, on account of the rays of things. For rays are like the hairs or shaggy fibers of nature; and almost all things are more or less radiant: which is most manifest in the faculty of sight; nor less in every magnetic virtue, and operation at a distance. For whatever operates at a distance, can also rightly be said to emit rays. But most prominent of all is *Pan's Beard*, because the rays of celestial bodies, and especially of the Sun, operate and penetrate most powerfully from afar. So much so that the upper parts of the earth, and even the inner parts, have plainly changed and subdued, and filled with spirit, to some distance. But a more elegant figure is that of *Pan's Beard*, because the Sun itself, when its upper part is enveloped in a cloud, and rays burst forth below, is seen to be *bearded* in appearance.

Pan is also the God of country-dwellers in general, because such people live more according to nature, whereas in cities and courts, nature is corrupted by excessive refinement, as that amorous saying of the poet, true, on account of such delights, is also about Nature:

But Pan is especially called the *President* of *Mountains*, because in mountains and elevated places the nature of things is revealed, and is more subjected to the eyes and contemplation. That Pan is another *messenger of the Gods, like Mercury*, is a plainly divine allegory, since, immediately after the Word of God, the very image of the world is a proclamation of divine power and wisdom. Which the divine Poet also sang: *The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament shows His handiwork.*

But as for the *Audacity of Pan*, and the *Fight by challenge with Cupid*; this points to the fact that matter is not without an inclination and appetite for the dissolution of the world, and a relapse into that ancient Chaos, unless the very strong harmony of things (signified by *Love or Cupid*) were to restrain its malice and impetus, and compel it into order. And so it happens by a very good fate for men and things (or rather by immense divine goodness) that *Pan* experiences that adverse contest, and departs vanquished. To the very same point belongs also that about *Typhon* entangled in *nets*, because however vast and unusual the swellings of things may sometimes be (which is what *Typhon* signifies), whether the seas swell, or the clouds swell, or the earth swells, or other things, nevertheless the nature of things entangles and restrains such exuberances and unruliness of bodies in an inextricable net, and binds them as if with an adamantine chain.

*Another Example of Philosophy, according to Ancient*
  *parables in Politics. On War according to the fable*
  *of Perseus.*

**P**erseus, since he was an *Oriental*, is said to have been
sent by *Pallas*, to cut off the head of *Medusa*,

stones. Now *Medusa* was one of the *Gorgons*,

choosing, the fable proposes three precepts, exceedingly sound and weighty. The first is, that one should not greatly strive for the subjugation of neighboring nations. For the method of enlarging patrimony and empire is not the same. For in private possessions, the proximity of estates is regarded, but in extending empire, Opportunity, and the ease of waging war, and profit, ought to be in place of proximity. Therefore *Perseus*, although an *Easterner*, nevertheless by no means declined such a distant expedition, even to the farthest *West*. A notable example of this matter is in the different method of waging war of the father and son Kings, *Philip* and *Alexander*. For he, occupied in neighboring wars, added few cities to his Empire, and that not without the greatest struggle and danger. Indeed he who both at other times, and especially in the *Battle of Chaeronea*, was brought into ultimate danger: But *Alexander*, having well dared a distant expedition against the *Persians*, subjugated countless nations, more tired by journeys than by battles. This very thing is seen still more clearly in the extension of the *Roman Empire*. who, for a time, from the part of the *West*, had scarcely penetrated beyond *Ligurian* territory with arms, at the same time encompassed the provinces of the *East* as far as *Mount Taurus* with arms and Empire. Also *Charles VIII, King of France*, having not found the *British War* (which was finally settled by marriage) very easy, an expedi-

Distant wars certainly have this advantage,
that one contends with those who are least accustomed to military service and
the arms of an invader. This is otherwise the case with
neighbors. Also, the preparation
in expeditions of this kind is usually more diligent
and better equipped; and the terror among the enemies
from the very daring and confidence is greater. Nor can it
easily happen in those distant expeditions,
that the enemies, to whom one arrives by such a long journey,
can make any diversion or reciprocal invasion,
which is more often employed in the method of warfare with
neighbors. The main point, however, is,
that in subjugating neighbors, the choice of opportunities
is limited; but if one does not shrink from more distant undertakings,
one can, at one's discretion, transfer the war
to where either military discipline is most enervated, or the nation's
strength is greatly worn out and consumed, or
civil dissensions have opportunely arisen, or other advantages of this
kind present themselves. Secondly,
it is important that there is always a just,
pious, honorable, and favorable *Cause for War*: For this
adds alacrity, both to the soldiers and to the people
contributing expenses, and opens and conciliates alliances,
and finally has very many advantages.

Finally, in the very actions and assaults of war, that *Gaze into the mirror of Pallas* must be employed. For many, before the dangers themselves, can keenly and attentively examine the enemy's affairs; but at the very moment of *Danger*, either they are overwhelmed by terror, or they view dangers too rashly and from the front: whence they rush into them rashly, mindful of conquering, forgetful of avoiding. But neither of these ought to happen, but into the *mirror of Pallas*, with neck bent back, one must look, so that the attack may be rightly directed, without either terror or fury.

   From a completed war and victory, two effects follow. First, that generation and emergence of Pegasus, which quite clearly denotes Fame, which flies everywhere, celebrates victory, and makes the remnants of war easy and compliant with one's wishes. Second, the carrying of Medusa's Head on the Shield; indeed, no kind of protection can be compared to this in terms of its excellence. For a single, signal and memorable deed, successfully carried out and accomplished, makes all movements of enemies stiffen, and renders malevolence itself stupid.

*Third Example of Philosophy according to Ancient Parables, in Morals. On Cupidity, according to the fable of Dionysus.*

**T**hey relate that Semele, Jupiter's mistress, after she had bound him by an inviolable oath to an indefinite wish, asked that he should approach her embraces in the same form as he was accustomed to with Juno. And so she perished in the conflagration. The infant, however, whom she was carrying in her womb, was taken by the Father and sewn into his thigh, until he should complete the months destined for the fetus. From this burden, however, Jupiter meanwhile limped somewhat. And so the Boy, because he burdened and pricked Jupiter while he was carried in his thigh, received the name Dionysus. After he was born, he was nourished by Proserpina for several years. When he was grown, with a face almost womanly

he was seen, so that his sex seemed as if ambiguous. He was also once dead and buried for a time, and not long after, he revived. And in his early youth, he first discovered and taught the cultivation of the vine, and indeed the making and use of wine. From this, having become famous and renowned, he subjugated the world and proceeded to the furthest boundaries of the Indians. He was carried in a chariot drawn by Tigers; around him leaped deformed *Dæmones*, called *Cobali*, *Acratus*, and others. Moreover, even the *Muses* joined his retinue. But he took *Ariadne* as his wife, abandoned and forsaken by *Theseus*. The *Ivy* was sacred to him. He was also considered the inventor and institutor of sacred rites and ceremonies; of that kind, however, which were both fanatical, and full of corruptions, and moreover cruel. He also had the power to inflict madness. Certainly, in his *Orgies*, two distinguished men are said to have been torn apart by women driven mad: *Pentheus* and *Orpheus*: The former, while he had wished to be a curious spectator of what was being done, having climbed a tree; the latter, while he was playing the lyre sweetly and skillfully. And the deeds of this God are almost confused with the deeds of *Jupiter*.

The fable seems to pertain to *morals*, so that hardly anything better can be found in Moral Philosophy. But under the *Person of Bacchus* is described the *Nature of Cupidity*, or of the *affections* and *perturbations* of the mind. But especially noble is that Allegory, *that Bacchus poured out his loves upon her who had been abandoned and disdained by another.* For it is most certain, *that affections seek and pursue that which Experience has long since repudiated.* And let all be aware, who, serving and indulging their affections, greatly increase the price of obtaining (it) (whether they seek honors, or loves, or glory, or knowledge, or whatever else), *that they seek things abandoned, and dismissed and repudiated by many, through almost all ages, after trial.* Nor is it without Mystery, that *Ivy was sacred to Bacchus.* For this is fitting in a twofold manner. First, because *Ivy flourishes in winter;* then, because it *creeps around so many things (trees, walls, buildings),* and spreads itself around, and raises itself up. For as to the first point, *every Desire, through Resistance and Prohibition,* and as it were *Antiperistasis (just as Ivy through the cold of Winter) flourishes,* and acquires vigor: Secondly, *a predominant affection in the human soul encircles all its actions and decrees, like Ivy;* nor will you find almost anything pure, where it does not impress its tendrils. But that story about Pentheus and Orpheus, torn apart amidst the Orgies of Bacchus, has an evident Parable; since every powerful affection is most harsh and most intolerant towards two things: one of which is curious Inquiry into it, the other, salutary and free Admonition. Nor will it be of help if that inquiry is made only for the sake of contemplation or observation, as if having climbed a tree, without any malice of mind; nor again, if that admonition is applied with much gentleness and skill; but in any case, the Orgies tolerate neither Pentheus nor Orpheus. Lastly, that Confusion of the Persons of Jove and Bacchus can rightly be translated into a Parable; since noble and famous deeds, and distinguished and glorious merits, sometimes arise from Virtue and right reason and magnanimity, but sometimes from a latent affection and hidden Desire (although both things equally rejoice in the celebrity of fame and praise): so that it is not easy to distinguish the deeds of Dionysus from the deeds of Jove.

But we linger too long in the Theater; let us pass to the Palace of the Mind, whose threshold it is fitting to enter with greater veneration and care.

[Decorative initial H] All History (O excellent King) walks on the ground, and performs the office of a guide rather than a light: *Poetry* however is like a dream to doctrine: A sweet, and varied thing, and wishing to seem to have something Divine in itself; which dreams also claim. But now it is time for me to awaken, and lift myself from the ground, cutting through the clear ether of *Philosophy & the Sciences*.

*Knowledge* is like waters. Some waters descend from heaven, others emanate from the earth. Also, the primary division of *Sciences* must be taken from their sources. Of these, some are situated on high, others here below. For all *Knowledge* receives a twofold

    *Philosophy*, moreover, has a threefold Object: *God*,

For *Nature* strikes the intellect with a *direct* Ray;
*God*, however, because of the unequal medium (namely, *Creatures*),
with a *refracted* Ray; *Man*, truly, shown and exhibited to himself,

C A P. II.
Concerning Natural Theology: and the Doctrine of Angels & Spirits; *which is an Appendix of the same.*

[Large initial C]Therefore, the *Common Parent of the Sciences* having been placed in its proper seat, like Berecynthia rejoicing in such a heavenly offspring;
*All heavenly dwellers, all who hold the heights above;*
let us return to that division of the three *Philosophies, Divine, Natural, & Human.* For *Natural Theology* is also rightly called *Divine Philosophy*. Now this is defined as being such a *Science*, or rather a spark of *Science*, as can be had concerning God, through the light of Nature, and the Contemplation of created Things: and by reason of its Object it can certainly be considered Divine, by reason of its information, natural. The limits of this *Science* are truly marked out in such a way, that they extend to refuting and convincing Atheism, and to informing the law of nature; but they do not extend to establishing religion. For this reason, God never performed a miracle by which an Atheist might be converted; because he could be led to the knowledge of God by the very Light of nature; but miracles [are] for conver-

--- Page 208 ---
186      ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING.
were designed for converting idolaters and superstitious people, who acknowledged a Divine Being, but erred in His worship; because the Light of Nature is not sufficient for declaring God's will, or for revealing His legitimate worship. For just as the works of a craftsman show his power and skill, but by no means his image; so the Works of God, the Creator, show His omnipotence and Wisdom, but by no means depict His Image. And in this matter, the opinion of the Heathens deviates from sacred truth. For they held the World to be the Image of God, and Man to be the image of the World. But the Sacred Scriptures do not deem the World worthy of such honor, that it should anywhere be called the Image of God, but only the Work of His Hands; but Man, on the other hand, they immediately substitute as the Image of God. Wherefore, that God exists, that He governs the reins of things, that He is supremely Powerful, that He is Wise and Prescient, that He is Good, that He is a Rewarder, that He is an Avenger, that He is to be Adored, can also be demonstrated and proven from His works: and many wonderful hidden attributes of His, and much more concerning His governance and dispensation over the universe, can also be soberly deduced and manifested from the same; and this argument has been usefully handled by some. But from the contemplation of natural things, and the principles of human reason, either to reason about the mysteries of faith, or even to persuade more vehemently, or again to examine them more curiously, and to ventilate them, and to inquire into the manner of the Mystery, would not be safe in my judgment. Give to faith what belongs to faith

--- Page 209 ---
LIBER III. 187

which are God's. For even the Pagans, in that famous and divine fable of the golden chain, concede this very thing: that *neither men nor gods could draw Jupiter from Heaven to Earth; on the contrary, Jupiter could draw them from Earth to Heaven*. Therefore, he will have toiled in vain who tries to adapt the heavenly mysteries of Religion to our reason: It will be more fitting, rather, to raise our minds to adore the Throne of heavenly truth. In this part, therefore, of *Natural Theology*, so far am I from observing any defect, that I rather find an excess; to note which I have digressed a little, because of the very great disadvantages and dangers which threaten both Religion and Philosophy from it; inasmuch as it both forges Heretical Religion and Fantastic and Superstitious Philosophy.

It is otherwise concerning the nature of *Angels and Spirits*; which is neither inscrutable nor forbidden; to which access is largely opened, also, due to the affinity it has with the human soul. Sacred Scripture certainly commands: *Let no one deceive you in loftiness of words, and in the worship of Angels, intruding into those things which he has not known*. Yet if you diligently weigh this warning, you will find only two things forbidden in it; namely, the adoration of Angels, such as is due to God; and fanatical opinions about them, either exalting them beyond the lot of a creature, or peddling a greater knowledge of them than one has truly acquired. But a sober inquiry concerning them, which either through things

--- Page 210 ---
188 D E A U G M. S C I E N T.
the ladder of corporeal things to thoroughly know their nature; or contemplates it in the human soul, as in a mirror, is by no means forbidden. The same is to be established concerning *Unclean* Spirits, who have fallen from their state. Fellowship with them, and the use of their service, is illicit, much more any kind of worship or veneration. But the contemplation and knowledge of their nature, power, illusions, not only from passages of Sacred Scripture, but from reason, or experience, is by no means the least part of spiritual wisdom. Thus certainly the Apostle (said), *We are not ignorant of his devices*. And it is no less permitted *to investigate the Nature of Demons in Natural Theology* than *of Poisons in Physics*, or *of Vices in Ethics*. This part of Science, however, concerning *Angels and Demons*, it is not permitted to number among the *Desiderata*, since it has been attempted by not a few: It would be more just that not a small part of the writings in this genre be accused of either vanity, or superstition, or useless subtlety.

C A P. I I I.
*The Division of Natural Philosophy into Speculative &*
*Operative: and that these two ought to be separated, both in the intention*
*of the Author, and in the Body of the Treatise.*

[M] Therefore, having dismissed *Natural Theology* (to which we have attributed the inquiry concerning Spirits, as an appendix), let us proceed to the second part, namely that concerning *Nature, or Natural Philosophy.*

--- Page 211 ---
**BOOK III. 189**

natural philosophy. Democritus said it best: that the knowledge of Nature lies submerged in the depths of mines or wells. Not badly do the Chemists say: that Vulcan is a second Nature, and indeed accomplishes quickly what Nature usually does through circuitous ways and delays of time. Why then should we not divide Philosophy into two parts, the Mine and the Furnace; and establish two offices for Philosophers, Workers in the Mines, and Smiths? Indeed, however much we may seem to speak these things in jest; nevertheless, we consider this kind of division to be most useful when it is proposed in familiar and scholastic terms; that is, that the Doctrine of Nature be divided into the investigation of causes and the production of effects; Speculative and Operative. The one scrutinizes the inner workings of Nature, the other shapes Nature as if upon an anvil. Nor does it escape me by how close a bond Cause and effect are joined, so that their explanation must to some extent be connected. Yet, since all solid and fruitful Natural Philosophy employs a double scale, and that a diverse one; Ascending and Descending; From Experience to Axioms, and from Axioms to new Inventions, I judge it most advisable that these two Parts, Speculative and Operative, be separated both in the intention of the Author and in the body of the Treatise.

Therefore, it can rightly be asked, what finally is left to Metaphysics? Certainly nothing beyond Nature, but the most excellent part of Nature itself. And indeed, without detriment to truth, it may thus far be permitted to answer according to the opinion of the ancients, that Physics treats those things which are deeply immersed in Matter and are Mobile; Metaphysics [treats] things more Abstract and Constant. Again, that Physics in Nature presupposes only existence, and motion, and natural necessity: But Metaphysics also [presupposes] mind and Idea. For perhaps the matter we are about to discuss returns to this point. But we, setting aside the sublimity of discourse, will propose it clearly and familiarly. We have divided Natural Philosophy into the inquiry into causes, and the production of effects. The inquiry into Causes we have placed in Theory. This we have divided into Physics and Metaphysics. Therefore it is necessary that the true difference between these be taken from the nature of the causes which they investigate. And so, without any obscurity or circumlocution, Physics is that which inquires concerning the Efficient Cause and Matter; Metaphysics, that which [inquires] concerning Form and End. [marginal note: 189.]

Physics, therefore, is vague and uncertain in its Causes, and according to the nature of the subject, embraces mobile things; it does not attain the constancy of causes.

aggregated, constitute those *Composite Motions*, or *Sums of Motions*, which are accepted, or similar to them. The *Sums of motions* are those celebrated motions: *Generation, Corruption, Augmentation, Diminution, Alteration, & Local Motion*; Also *Mixture, Separation, Conversion*. There remain only, as *Appendices of Physics, the Measure of Motions*: *What can Quantity do, or the Dose of Nature? What can Distance do?* (that which is not improperly called the Sphere of Virtue or Activity). *What can excitation & slowness do? What can short or long delay do? What can the force or dullness of a thing do? What can the stimulus of circumstance do?* And these are the genuine parts of *true Physics of Abstracts*. Indeed, in the *schematisms of matter*, in *Simple Motions*, in the *sums or Aggregations of motions*, & in the *measures of motions*, *Physics of Abstracts* is completed. For *Voluntary Motion in animals*; *Motion that occurs in the actions of the Senses*; *Motion of imagination, appetite & will, Motion of mind, decree, & Intellectual things*, we relegate to their proper *Doctrines*. We warn again, however, that all these things which we have mentioned are not treated further in *Physics* than as their *Matter & Efficient Cause*: for they are reconsidered in *Metaphysics*, regarding their *Forms & Ends*.
     To *Physics* we will subjoin two notable *Appendices*, which pertain not so much to matter, as to the method of inquiry: *Natural Problems*, & the *Tenets of Ancient Philosophers*. The former (pertains to) *Nature manifold or scattered*.

...scattered *Appendix* is: The second [Appendix] is of unique *Nature*, or *of Summaries*. Both pertain to skillful doubt, which is a not-to-be-despised part of *Science*. For *Problems* embrace particular doubts; *Tenets* [embrace] general [doubts] concerning *Principles* & *Structure*. A noble example of *Problems* is in the books of *Aristotle*; which kind of work certainly deserved not only to be celebrated by the praises of posterity, but also to be continued by their labors, since new *doubts* arise daily. However, in this matter, a caution of certainly great importance must be applied. The *commemoration and proposition of doubts* has a twofold fruit in itself: One, that it fortifies *Philosophy* against errors, when that which is not plainly clear is not judged or asserted (lest error should generate error), but judgment concerning it is suspended, and it does not become positive; The other, that *Doubts*, recorded in notebooks, are so many sponges, which perpetually suck and attract the increments of *Science* to themselves.

to the end that *Doubt* may rather be nourished than terminated or resolved. Examples of which are found everywhere, both among Jurists and among Academics: whose custom it is that, once *Doubt* has been admitted, they wish it to be perpetual, and they embrace the advantages of *Doubting* no less than those of *Asserting*: Whereas, however, that alone is the legitimate use of the intellect which makes *Certainties* out of *Doubts*, not which calls *Certainties* into *Doubt*. Wherefore, I assert that a *Calendar of Doubts*, or of *Problems* in Nature, is desired, and I approve of its being undertaken: provided care is taken that, as *Science* increases daily (which will undoubtedly happen if men listen to us), those *Doubts* which have been clearly discussed may be deleted from the Register. To this *Calendar* I would wish another, no less useful, to be added: For since in every inquiry these three things are found: *clearly True, Doubtful, clearly False*: it would be most useful to add to the *Calendar of Doubts* a *Calendar of Falsehoods*, and of popular errors, whether in Natural History or in prevailing Dogmas: lest those (falsehoods and errors) should trouble the Sciences any longer.

As to the *Tenets of the ancient Philosophers*, such as were those of *Pythagoras, Philolaus, Xenophanes, Anaxagoras, Parmenides, Leucippus, Democritus*, and others: (which men are accustomed to skim over contemptuously:) it would not be amiss to cast one's eyes upon them a little more modestly. For although Aristotle, in the manner of the Ottomans, thought he could not reign safely unless all his brothers .

--- Page 235 ---
L I B E R III. 213
all [his brothers] had destroyed: nevertheless, to those who propose to themselves not a kingdom or mastery, but the inquiry and illustration of truth, it cannot but seem a useful thing to view the diverse opinions of diverse people, concerning the natures of things, under a single aspect. Nor, however, is there hope that any purer truth, from those, or similar Theories, is to be hoped for in any way. For just as the same Phenomena, the same calculations, are consistent with both Ptolemy's Astronomical principles and Copernicus's: so that common experience, which we use, and the obvious appearance of things, can apply itself to many diverse Theories: where for the right investigation of truth, a far different severity will be needed. For Aristotle elegantly [says]: *Infants, at first babbling, call any women mothers, but afterwards discern their own mother.* Thus certainly childish experience will call every *Philosophy* a mother: but adult [experience] will recognize the true Mother. Meanwhile it will be helpful to read through differing *Philosophies*, as if diverse *Glossaries of Nature*, (of which one is perhaps more accurate in one place, another in another,). I would wish, therefore, from the ancient philosophers, from Plutarch's collection concerning their Opinions, from Aristotle's citations, from scattered mention, which is found in other books, both Ecclesiastical and Pagan, (Lactantius, Philo, Philostratus, & others) a work to be compiled, with diligence and judgment, concerning *Ancient Philosophies.* For I see that such a work does not yet exist. Nevertheless, here I advise that this be done distin-

distinctly: so that individual Philosophies may be composed separately and continued, not extracted by titles and fascicles (which Plutarch did). For every complete Philosophy sustains itself; and its doctrines mutually add both light and strength to each other; but if they are pulled apart, they sound foreign and harsh. Certainly, when I read the Deeds of Nero or Claudius in Tacitus, clothed in the circumstances of Times, Persons, and Occasions, I see nothing that utterly deviates from probability; but when I read the same in Suetonius Tranquillus, presented by chapters and commonplaces, and by no means in chronological order, they seem like certain monstrosities, and utterly incredible. Nor is the case of Philosophy dissimilar, when it is presented whole, and when it is cut and dissected into fragments. As for *Metaphysics*, we have already assigned to it the inquiry into *Formal* and *Final Causes*; which assignment, as far as *Forms* are concerned, may seem to have been made in vain. For indeed, an opinion has prevailed and become inveterate, that *the essential forms of things*, or *true differences*, cannot be discovered by any human diligence. This opinion, meanwhile, grants and concedes to us that *the Invention of Forms* is the most worthy of all parts of Science to be investigated, if only it can be done, so that they may be found. But as for the possibility of invention, there are certainly lazy explorers of regions who, where nothing but Sky and Sea is seen, utterly deny that there are lands beyond. But it is manifest that Plato, a man of sublime genius (and who, as if from a high rock, surveyed all things around), in his doctrine of Ideas, saw that *Forms are the true object of Science*; however, he lost the fruit of this most true opinion by contemplating and grasping *Forms* as entirely abstracted from matter, not determined within matter: Whence it happened that he turned to Theological speculations; which infected and polluted all his natural Philosophy. But if we diligently, seriously, and sincerely turn our eyes to action and use; it will not be difficult to inquire and attain knowledge of what those *Forms* are, the knowledge of which can enrich and bless human affairs in wonderful ways. For the *Forms* of Substances (with the exception of man, concerning whom Scripture says, *He formed man from the dust of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life;*)

For order pertains to illustration, and is not of the substance of the Sciences. But this inversion of order has brought forth a significant defect, and has introduced the greatest calamity to Philosophy. For the treatment of *final causes* in *Physics* has expelled and cast down the inquiry into *physical causes*, and has caused men to acquiesce in such specious and shadowy causes, nor vigorously to pursue the inquiry into *real*, and truly *physical causes*, to the great detriment of the Sciences. Indeed, I find that this has been done not only by Plato, who always casts anchor on this shore, but also by Aristotle, Galen, and others, who very often run aground on those shoals. Indeed, whoever has adduced causes of this kind: *that eyelids with hairs are for a fence and rampart, for the protection of the eyes; or that the firmness of the skin in Animals is for repelling heat and cold; or that bones are introduced by nature as columns and beams, upon which the fabric of the body may rest; or that the leaves of trees are put forth, so that fruits may suffer less from the Sun and Wind; or that clouds are formed on high, so that they may water the earth with rains; or that the Earth is made dense and solid, so that it may be a station and dwelling place for Animals; and other similar things:* such a one would not have badly alleged these things in *Metaphysics*, but by no means in *Physics*. remoras) as they imagine (clinging to ships) have retarded the quasi-sailing and progress of the Sciences, lest they hold their course and proceed further; and long ago they brought it about that the *inquiry into physical causes*, neglected, should fail and be passed over in silence. Therefore, the *natural philosophy* of Democritus, and of others, who removed God and mind from the fabric of things; and attributed the structure of the universe to infinite preludes and attempts of Nature (which they called by one name *fate* or *fortune*); and assigned the *causes* of particular things to the necessity of matter, without the intermixture of *final causes*; seems to us (as far as one can conjecture from the fragments and remnants of their philosophy), as far as *Physical causes* are concerned, to have been much more solid, and to have penetrated deeper into Nature; than that of Aristotle and Plato: For this sole reason, that the former never wasted effort on *final causes*; while the latter perpetually inculcated them. And in this respect Aristotle is more to be accused than Plato: inasmuch as he omitted the source of *final causes*, namely *God*, and substituted *Nature* for *God*, and embraced *final causes themselves*, more as a Lover of Logic than of Theology. Nor do we say this because *those final causes* are not true, and very worthy of inquiry in the speculations of *Metaphysics*, but because while they run out and rush into the possessions of *Physical Causes*, they miserably depopulate and lay waste that province. Otherwise, if

Nor indeed does this matter call divine providence into doubt, or detract anything from it: but rather confirms and exalts it in wonderful ways. For just as in civil matters political prudence would be much higher and more wonderful, if someone could use the works of others for his own ends and desires, to whom nevertheless he imparts nothing of his counsel, (so that meanwhile they do what he himself wishes, but by no means understand that they are doing this,) than if he were to communicate his counsels with the Ministers of his will: So God's Wisdom shines forth more wonderfully, when Nature does one thing, and providence elicits another; than if the characters of providence were impressed upon individual schemes and natural motions. that Nature does nothing in vain, and always achieves its purpose (if impediments were absent), and had posited many such things pertaining to it, there was no further need for God. So far is it from the case that *Physical Causes* lead men away from God and Providence, that on the contrary, those philosophers who were occupied in discovering them, find no solution to the matter, unless they ultimately take refuge in God and Providence. And let these things be said concerning *Metaphysics*: a part of which, concerning *Final Causes*, I would not deny has been treated in both *Physical* and *Metaphysical* Books, in the latter correctly, in the former wrongly, because of the inconvenience that followed from it.

Indeed, in my judgment, hardly anything in Nature can be fundamentally changed or innovated, either by some fortuitous accidents, or by experimental trials, or from the light of Physical Causes, but only through the *invention of forms*. If therefore we have posited that that part of *Metaphysics* which *deals with forms* is wanting; it follows that *Natural Magic* also, which is relative to it, is similarly wanting. But in this place it seems necessary to demand that this word *Magic*, long since accepted in a pejorative sense, be restored to its ancient and honorable meaning. For *Magic* among the Persians was understood as sublime wisdom, and the science of the universal harmonies of things; and also those three Kings who came from the East to adore *Christ* were called by the name of *Magi*. But we understand it in that sense, that it is a science which leads the knowledge of *hidden forms* to admirable works, and, as is usually said, *by joining actives with passives*, reveals the great works of Nature. For as to *Natural Magic* (which flits about in the books of most people) it contains certain credulous and superstitious traditions and observations concerning *Sympathies*

For it is manifest that Caesar truly accomplished greater things than they dared to invent about their Heroes; but by methods of doing that were by no means fabulous.

The Fable of Ixion well shadowed forth such doctrines; Who, when he mentally desired cohabitation with Juno, the Goddess of Power, had the deed with an evanescent cloud; from which he begot Centaurs and Chimaeras.

...men are no longer stirred up and awakened to discover and investigate true Causes, but acquiesce in such idle and credulous opinions. Then indeed it insinuates innumerable pleasing fictions, and such as one would most wish for, like dreams. And it is worth noting that in those sciences which draw too much from fantasy and faith (such as this light *Magic* of which we are now speaking, *Alchemy*, *Astrology*, and other similar ones), their means and Theory are usually more monstrous than the End and the action towards which they tend. The transmutation of silver, or quicksilver, or any other metal into gold, is a thing hard to believe: Yet it is far more probable that gold could at last be produced by much sagacious effort by a man who has known and understood the natures of *Weight*, *Yellow Color*, *Malleability* and *Extensibility*, and also of *Fixedness* and *Volatility*; and who has similarly diligently examined the primary seeds and menstrua of minerals; than that a few grains of *Elixir* could, in a few moments, turn other metals into gold through the activity of the same *Elixir*, which is supposedly able to perfect nature and free it from every impediment. Similarly, the retardation of old age, or the restoration of some degree of youth, may not easily find belief: Yet it is far more probable that by a man who thoroughly understands the nature of *Desiccation* and the *depredations of Spirits upon solid bodies*, and who has grasped the Nature of *assimilation* and *alimentation*, whether more perfect or more corrupt, and *also the Nature of Spirits*,

Again, that fates can be drawn from the stars, men will not immediately or easily agree: But that the hour of birth, (which very often, by several natural accidents, is either accelerated or deferred,) should rule the fortune of the whole life, or that the hour of a question should be co-fated with the thing itself that is sought, you would call mere trifles. Yet such impotence and intemperance afflict the human race, that they not only promise themselves what cannot be done, but also trust that they can attain the most arduous things, without trouble or sweat, as if on holiday. But of this *Operative* part, namely concerning *Nature*, there are two *Appendices*, both of great value. The first is, that an *Inventory of human resources* be made, in which all human goods and fortunes may be received and briefly enumerated, (whether they are from the fruits and products of Nature, or of art) which are now possessed, and which men enjoy, with the addition of those things which are known to have been known in the past, but have now perished: to this end, that those who

--- Page 251 ---
L I B E R   I I I. 229
who prepares himself for new inventions should not trouble himself with things already discovered and existing. But this *Inventory* will be more ingenious and even more useful, if you add those things which are considered *impossible* by common human opinion in each category: and at the same time, you connect those things *closest to the impossible* which are nevertheless possessed, so that the one may sharpen human invention, the other may direct it to some extent, and so that from these *Desirables & Potentials, Actives* may be more readily deduced. The second is, that a *Calendar* be made of those experiments which are most *Polychresta* (multi-useful), and which contribute to, and lead to, the invention of others. For example, the *experiment of artificial congelation of water*, by ice with black salt, pertains to countless things: For this reveals a secret method of condensation, than which nothing is more fruitful for man. For fire is readily available for rarefactions; but in condensations, there is labor. Moreover, it greatly contributes to the efficiency of discovery, if such *Polychresta* are set aside in their own catalog.

...as well as the Operative part of the *Doctrine* of *Nature*, it is now time to speak of *Mathematics*, which is an auxiliary science to both. Indeed, in accepted Philosophy, this is added as a third part to *Physics* & *Metaphysics*. But for us, reconsidering and reviewing these matters, if it were our intention to designate it as a *substantive* and principal *science*, it would seem more consistent, both with the Nature of the thing itself and with the clarity of order, that it should be constituted as a portion of *Metaphysics*. For *Quantity* (which is the subject of *Mathematics*), when applied to matter, is, as it were, a dose of Nature, and causative of very many effects in Natural things; and therefore is to be numbered among the *Essential Forms*. But *Figure* and the power *of numbers* seemed to hold so much sway among the ancients, that Democritus chiefly placed the *principles of the variety of things* in the *figures of atoms*; And Pythagoras asserted that the *Nature of things* is constituted *from numbers*. Meanwhile, it is true that quantity, among *natural forms* (as we understand them), is of all things most abstract, and separable from matter: This very fact was the cause why it has been both more diligently cultivated and more keenly investigated by men, than any other *forms* whatever, all of which are more immersed in matter. For since it is plainly ingrained in the minds of men (certainly with very great detriment to the sciences) that they delight more in the *free fields, as it were, of generals*, than in the *woods and enclosures of particulars*, nothing has been found more agreeable and pleasant to *Mathematicians*, by which to appe-

Which we are also compelled to do in a certain way, because of the delights and pride of *Mathematicians*, who desire that this science should almost rule *Physics*. For I do not know by what fate it happens, that *Mathematics* and *Logic*, which ought to behave as handmaidens towards *Physics*, nevertheless, boasting their certainty before it, presume to exercise dominion against it. But concerning the place and dignity of this science, less attention should be paid: let us see about the thing itself.

Division of the doctrine concerning man, into the Philosophy of Human-

Division of the doctrine concerning the person of man, into the doctrine
concerning the miseries of man, and concerning his prerogatives. Division
of the doctrine concerning the union, into the doctrine concerning indica-

IF anyone (most excellent King) on account of anything
of those things which I have proposed, or shall here-
after propose, should attack or wound me,
(besides that I ought to be safe within the safeguards of your Majesty,)
let him know that he acts contrary to the custom and discipline of warfare.
For I am only a Trumpeter, I do not enter the battle,
perhaps one of those of whom Homer says:
Rejoice

--- Page 257 ---
L I B E R IV. 235
Hail, heralds, messengers of Zeus, and of men.
For these, even among the most hostile and bitter enemies, passed everywhere inviolate, going to and fro. Nor indeed does our Trumpet summon and rouse men to tear each other apart with contradictions, or to fight and contend among themselves; but rather that, having made peace among themselves, with united forces, they may prepare themselves against _the Nature of Things_, and capture and conquer its Works and Fortifications, and extend the boundaries of human empire (as far as God, Most Good, Most Great, in His Goodness shall permit).

Let us now come to that _Science_ to which the ancient _Oracle_ leads us: namely, to _the Science of ourselves_. To which, the more it concerns us, the more diligently must we apply ourselves. This _Science_ is for man the end of _Sciences_, but only a _portion of Nature itself_. And let this be laid down as a general _Rule_: That all divisions of the Sciences be so understood and applied, that they rather mark or distinguish the sciences, than cut and tear them apart, so that the _solution of continuity in the sciences_ may be perpetually avoided. For the contrary of this has rendered particular Sciences sterile, empty, and erroneous, while they are not nourished, sustained, and rectified by a common source and stimulus. Thus we see Cicero the Orator complaining about Socrates and his school, that he was the first to separate _Philosophy from Rhetoric_, whence _Rhetoric_ became a verbose and empty art. It is likewise evident, Senten-

--- Page 258 ---
236 ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING.
It is similarly clear that Copernicus's theory concerning the Earth's system (which now also prevails), because it does not conflict with phenomena, cannot be refuted by Astronomical Principles; but it can be, by the *Principles of Natural Philosophy*, rightly established. Finally, we see that the Medical Art, if it is abandoned by *Natural Philosophy*, does not much surpass the practice of empirics.

This, therefore, being established, let us proceed to the *Doctrine concerning Man*. It is twofold; for it either contemplates *Man as an individual*, or *Man in a group*, and in *Society*. We call one of these the *Philosophy of Humanity*; the other, *Civil Philosophy*. The *Philosophy of Humanity*, or *Human* Philosophy, consists of parts similar to those of which man himself consists: Namely, from Sciences which concern the *Body*, and from Sciences which concern the *Soul*.

But before we pursue the Particular distributions, let us establish *one general Science, concerning the nature and state of man*: For it is certainly a worthy thing that this *Science* be emancipated, and into a *Science*
