The *doctrine concerning the person of man* chiefly comprises two things; namely, contemplations concerning the *miseries of the human race*; and concerning its *prerogatives, or excellencies*. And the lamentation of *human woes* has been elegantly and copiously treated by many, both in Philosophical and Theological writings. And it is a thing both sweet and salutary at the same time.

But that [part] concerning *prerogatives* seemed to us a thing worthy to be proposed among the *Desiderata*. Most elegantly certainly Pindar (as he usually does) when praising Hiero says, "That he plucks the *summits from all virtues*." Indeed, I would think it could contribute very much to magnanimity and human dignity: if the *Ultimates* (as the Scholastics speak) or *Summits* (as Pindar) of human nature were collected; especially from the trustworthiness of history. That is, what has been the *Ultimate and Supreme* point to which human nature has ever ascended by itself, in each of the endowments of both body and mind. How great a thing is that which is related of Caesar, that he was able to *dictate* to five scribes simultaneously? Moreover, those exercises of the ancient Rhetoricians, Protagoras, Gorgias; and also of the Philosophers, Callisthenes, Posidonius, Carneades, that they were able to discuss elegantly and copiously on any theme on both sides extemporaneously; these not a little ennoble the *powers of human intellect*. In this matter, we approve the plan of Valerius Maximus and C. Pliny, and we require their diligence and judgment.
    As for the *doctrine of the covenant*, or of the *Common bond of soul and body*: This can be divided into two parts. For just as between allies there exist both a mutual communication of their affairs and mutual duties; so this covenant of soul and body is similarly contained in two things: Namely, that it be described; *how these two (namely, soul and body) reveal themselves to each other, and how they act upon each other; by knowledge or indication, and by impression.* Of these

--- Page 262 ---
240	ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING.
...the former of which (namely, a description of how knowledge of the soul may be had from the disposition of the body, or of the body from the manifestations of the soul) has produced for us two *arts*, both of prediction: one adorned with the investigations of Aristotle, the other with those of Hippocrates. Although more recent times have polluted these arts with superstitious and fantastic mixtures, yet, purged and restored to their integrity, they have a solid foundation in nature and yield fruit useful for common life. The first is *Physiognomy*, which, through the lineaments of the body, indicates the propensities of the soul: The other is the *interpretation of natural dreams*, which reveals the state and disposition of the body from the agitations of the soul. In the former of these, I perceive a certain part to be lacking. For while Aristotle ingeniously and skillfully treated the fabric of the body while it was at rest, he omitted the same in motion (namely, the gestures of the body); which nevertheless are no less subject to the observations of art, and are of greater use. For the lineaments of the body show the general inclinations and propensities of the soul; but the movements and gestures of the mouth and other parts, moreover, declare the approaches, and times, and signs of the present disposition and will. For, to use the most apt and elegant words of Your Majesty, *The tongue strikes the ears, but Gesture addresses the eyes.* This, indeed, many ancients and astute men, whose eyes dwell on the countenances and gestures of others, and turn it to their own advantage,

For it considers two things: *Either how and to what

and humiliation. They regard these as things not merely ritual, but also fruitful.
But the root of all such precepts, besides the ceremony itself and the exercise of obedience, consists in this matter of which we speak: Namely, that the soul sympathizes with the body. But if anyone, weaker in judgment, should think that these Impressions of the Body on the Soul either call into doubt the Immortality of the Soul, or detract from the Soul's Dominion over the Body; a light answer will suffice for a light doubt. Let him seek examples, either from an Infant in the Mother's Womb: who sympathizes with the Mother's Affections, and yet is excluded from the mother's body in due time: or from Monarchs, who, though powerful, are sometimes swayed by the impetuosity of servants, while their Royal Majesty remains intact.
      Now as to the reciprocal part, (concerning the *soul and its affections acting upon the body*) that also finds a place in medicine. For no physician who is even a little prudent fails to consider and treat the *accidents of the mind*, as a matter of the greatest importance for his cures, and one which greatly either aids or hinders all other remedies. But something else, which pertains to this, has been inquired into very sparingly, and not in proportion to the subtlety or utility of the matter; namely, to what extent (setting aside affections) the *imagination of the soul itself*, or a very fixed thought, and as it were exalted into a kind of *faith*, is capable of changing the body of the one imagining? For although it has a manifest power to harm, yet not from that

--- Page 266 ---
244    ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING
it therefore follows that it is endowed with equal power to help. No more, by Hercules, than if someone concluded that because some air is found so pestilential that it suddenly kills, there ought also to be some air so salubrious that it suddenly restores a sick person. And this inquiry would certainly be of noble use; but (as Socrates says) it needs a *Delian Swimmer*, because it sinks into the deep. Again, among these *doctrines concerning the covenant, or agreements of the soul and body,* no other would have been more necessary than that *arrangement concerning the proper seats and dwellings which the individual faculties of the soul have in the body and its organs.* Those who have pursued this kind of *Science* are not lacking, but what is held by most is either controversial or lightly investigated; so that greater diligence and acumen are needed. For the opinion introduced by Plato, by which the intellect is placed in the brain as if in a citadel, *spiritedness* (which he rather unskillfully called anger, though it is more akin to swelling and pride) in the heart, and *concupiscence and sensuality* in the liver, is neither to be entirely despised nor eagerly accepted. Again, nor is the assignment of those intellectual faculties (*Imagination, Reason, Memory*) according to the ventricles of the brain free from error. And we have explained the *Doctrine concerning the undivided Nature of Man, and also concerning the Covenant of Mind and Body.*

CAP. II.

The division of the doctrine concerning the human body into medicine;
and the voluptuary art. The division of medicine into three offices,
namely: the Preservation of Health, the Cure of
Diseases, and the Prolongation of Life. And that the
last part concerning the Prolongation of Life ought to be separated from
the other two.

**D**octrine concerning the human body receives the same
division as the goods of the body itself,
which it serves: the goods of the human body are four:
Health, form or beauty, strength, pleasure.
Therefore, there are as many Sciences: Medicine,
Cosmetics, Athletics, and the Voluptuary art, which
Tacitus calls "Erudite luxury."
Medicine is an art noble in the first place, and from the most
generous lineage, according to the Poets. For they
introduced Apollo as the primary God of Medicine;
to whom they gave a Son, Aesculapius, likewise a God,
and a Professor of Medicine: Indeed, since
the Sun in Natural things is the author and source of life, the
Physician is the preserver of the same, and as it were, another
spring. But a far more illustrious glory accrues to
Medicine from the works of the Savior, who was a Physician
both of the soul and of the body: And just as he constituted
the soul as the object of his heavenly doctrine, so he constituted
the body as, as it were, the proper object of his miracles.
For nowhere do we read of any miracle performed
by him concerning honors or money (except for the
single one by which tribute was rendered to Caesar),
but only concerning the human body, either to be preserved,
or to be sustained, or to be perfectly healed.

Solomon in a more serious matter; *If there is one outcome for both the fool and me, what good does it do me that I applied myself more to wisdom?* Indeed, I am less angry with physicians if they very often devote themselves to some other study, which they love more than their own proper Art. For you will find among them Poets, Antiquarians, Critics, Rhetoricians, Politicians, Theologians, and more learned in these Arts than in their own profession. Nor does this happen, as I believe, because (as a certain Declaimer against the Sciences objects to physicians) they have objects confronting them so foul and sad that it is absolutely necessary for them to divert their minds to other things; (*For being human, they should think nothing human alien to them;*) But because of this very thing, which we are now discussing; namely, that they think it matters little to them, either for reputation or for profit, whether they achieve mediocrity in their art or greater perfection in it.

For the weariness of disease, the sweetness of life, the deceptiveness of hope, and the recommendation of friends, cause people to easily place trust in any kind of physician. But if anyone considers these things more attentively, they point rather to the fault of physicians than to an excuse for their fault. For they ought not to have abandoned hope, but rather to have exerted their strength. For if anyone chooses to awaken their observation, and gradually look around, even from obvious and familiar examples, they will easily discover how much power *subtlety and sharpness of intellect* obtains over the variety of things, whether of *Matter* or of *Form*. Were physicians to set aside these generalities for a little while, they would wish to confront Nature and become masters of it, concerning which the Poet says:
   *And since diseases vary, we shall vary our arts;*
   *A thousand kinds of ill, a thousand kinds of healing there were.*
They ought to do this all the more, because the philosophies themselves, upon which physicians rely, whether Methodists or Chemists (for medicine not founded on philosophy is a weak thing), are in reality of little value. Wherefore if generalities that are too broad (even if they were true) have this fault, that they do not effectively guide people to action, certainly there is greater danger from those generalities which are inherently false: and, instead of leading, they mislead.

Medicine therefore (as we have observed) has hitherto been so constituted that it has been more for show than for substance: also more worked upon than expanded, since the labors expended on it have revolved in a circle rather than advanced. For I see very many things in it repeated by writers, and few additions made. We will divide it into three parts, which we will call its three functions. The first is *The Preservation of Health*, the second *The Cure of Diseases*, the third *The Prolongation of Life*. But this last, physicians do not seem to have recognized as a principal part of their art, but rather to have quite unskillfully mingled it with the other two. For they think that if diseases are repelled before they attack, and cured after they have invaded, the Prolongation of life will follow of its own accord.

--- Page 274 ---
252           OF THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING.
Although this is by no means doubtful, yet they perceive too little acutely that both of these pertain only to diseases, and only to that *prolongation of life* which is shortened and cut short by diseases. But to prolong the very thread of life, and to remove death, creeping on gradually through simple dissolution and senile atrophy, for a time, is a subject which no physician has treated with due dignity. Nor indeed should that scruple enter the minds of men, as if this matter, committed to fate and divine Providence, were now for the first time recalled by us into the office and function of art. For Providence undoubtedly governs all deaths whatsoever, whether from violence, or from diseases, or from the course of age, equally; yet it does not therefore exclude preventions and remedies. But art and human industry do not command nature and fate, but minister to them. But we will speak of this part a little later; having only said this in the meantime, lest anyone unskillfully confuse this third office of Medicine with the two former ones (with which it has almost always been dealt until now).

    As for the office of *preserving Health* (the first of the aforesaid offices of Medicine), many have written about it, though in other matters quite unskillfully, and, as we think, attributing too much to the choice of foods, and less than is proper to their quantity. Nay, even in quantity itself, like moral philosophers, they have praised moderation too much; whereas both customary fasts, and a liberal diet, to which one who has accustomed himself,
                                                              better

But since this part, *concerning the preservation

    As for *the Cure of Diseases*, that finally is
the part of *Medicine* in which the greatest labor

*Diseases* to which the human body is subject,

Yet it is no less true (as was noted by the Ancients) that many pores and passages, and perfusions, which are of the more subtle kind, do not appear in anatomical dissections; since these are closed and hidden in cadavers; whereas in living beings they are dilated, and can be conspicuous. Therefore, so that both utility and humanity may be consulted at the same time, the *Anatomy of the Living* is not to be entirely rejected, nor to be relegated to the fortuitous inspections of surgeons (as Celsus did): since this very thing can be well accomplished through the dissection of living brutes, which, notwithstanding the dissimilarity of their parts to human ones, can satisfy this inquiry, with judgment applied.

Likewise, in the *Cures of Diseases*, I find that this is generally *lacking*: That the physicians of this age, although they do not badly pursue the *general intentions of Cures*, yet particular Medicines, which pertain to the cures of individual diseases by a certain property, they either do not know well, or do not scrupulously observe. For physicians have destroyed and removed the fruit of traditions and proven experience by their authoritative prescriptions; by adding, and subtracting, and changing about Medicines, as it pleased them; and almost in the manner of apothecaries substituting *Quid pro Quo* (something for something else); so proudly commanding Medicine, that Medicine no longer commands the Disease. For, with Theriaca, and Mithridaticum, and perhaps Diascordium, and Confection of Alkermes, and a few other Medicines removed, they bind themselves scrupulously and strictly to almost no certain remedies. For those Medicines which are available for sale in the shops are rather ready for general intentions, than suited and proper for particular cures; since they specifically do not greatly regard any disease, but generally pertain to opening obstructions, strengthening digestions, altering distempers. But lest we pursue individual points more scrupulously than is fitting either for our purpose or for the nature of this Treatise, we will close this part with the enumeration of another certain defect, which seems to us of the greatest importance: Namely, that the *method of healing* which has prevailed is *far too compendious* for it to be able to achieve anything significant or difficult. For in our judgment, it would be an opinion more flattering than true, if anyone were to imagine that some medicine could be made so potent or efficacious that its simple use would suffice for some greater cure. Truly wonderful would be a Discourse which, pronounced, or even often repeated, could correct or remove some fault, deeply ingrained or inveterate in the mind. Far from it indeed. But what are exceptionally powerful and effective in Nature are order, sustained application, sequence, and skillful alternation. Which, although they require a somewhat greater judgment in prescribing and greater constancy in obeying, yet they abundantly compensate for the requirements by the magnitude of their effects. And although from the daily work of physicians, which they perform for the sick by visiting, attending, and prescribing, someone might think that they diligently pursue the cure and adhere to a certain path in it: Yet if anyone should look more keenly into those things which physicians are accustomed to prescribe and administer, he will find most things full of vacillation and inconsistency, and which are devised on the spur of the moment and come into their minds, without any certain or foreseen path of Cure. But they ought also

Nor yet do we wish this, that every scrupulous and superstitious method of healing be held in esteem as the best (no more than every *narrow way is the way to Heaven*): but that the way be as straight, as it is narrow and difficult. But that is not for this Treatise.*

      Firstly, we *admonish*, that among writers concerning this Subject, no one has found anything great, let alone anything sound. Aristotle certainly published a very small Commentary on this, in which there is something acute: which he wants to be everything, as is his custom. But recent authors have written so carelessly and superstitiously about this, that the Subject itself, because of their vanity, has begun to be considered as vain and senseless.
      Secondly, we *admonish*, that the very intentions of physicians which relate to this, are things of no value, and rather lead men's thoughts away from the matter, than direct them towards it. For they discourse that death consists in the lack of heat and moisture:

For there are some things which are beneficial for the alacrity of the spirits, and the strength of functions, and for warding off diseases: yet these detract from the sum of life, and accelerate senile atrophy without diseases: And there are others which help towards the Prolongation of life, and the further postponement of senile atrophy: but these are not used without risk to health; So much so that those who use them for the Prolongation of life, ought at the same time to counteract the inconveniences which might otherwise arise from their use. And *thus far we have given warnings.*

We *prescribe* first, that the Prolongation of life should be expected rather from established Diets, than from any familiar regimen of living; or even from the excellence of particular medicines. For, those things which possess such great power as to be able to reverse nature; are generally stronger and more potent for altering, than that they could be compounded simultaneously in some Medicine, much less interspersed in familiar diet. It remains therefore that they should be applied serially, and regularly, and at certain times, and recurring at certain intervals.
    Secondly, we *prescribe*, that *Prolongation of Life* should be expected rather from operation on the Spirits, and from the Softening of the parts, than from modes of alimentation. For, since the human Body, and its Structure (external things being omitted) suffers from three things; namely, Spirits; Parts; and Aliments; the Way of prolongation of life through modes of alimentation is long; and through many windings and circuits: But the ways through operations upon the Spirits, and upon the parts, are much shorter, and by which the desired end is reached more quickly; because the Spirits suffer suddenly, both from vapors, and from affections, which can enter them by these methods: likewise the parts, by Baths, or Ointments, or Plasters, which also make sudden impressions.

**CAP. III.**

*Division of Human Philosophy concerning the soul, into the Doctrine of the breath; and the doctrine of the sensible or produced soul. Second division of the same Philosophy into the Doctrine of the substance and faculties of the soul, and the doctrine of the use and objects of the faculties. Two appendices to the doctrine of the faculties of the soul; The Doctrine of natural divination, and the doctrine of fascination. Distribution of the faculties of the sensible soul into motion and sensation.*

[Large initial V]Let us come to the *doctrine of the human soul*; from whose treasures all other doctrines are drawn. It has two parts; One treats of the *rational soul*, which is Divine; The other of the *irrational* [soul], which is common with Brutes. We noted a little earlier (where we spoke of *forms*) those two different emanations of *souls*, which present themselves to be observed in the first creation of both; Namely, that one had its origin from the *breath of God*, the other from the *wombs of the Elements*. For concerning the primitive generation of the *rational soul*, thus says Scripture, "*He formed man from the dust of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life*." But the generation of the *Irrational soul*, or of Brutes, was made by those words, "*Let the water bring forth, Let the earth bring*
                                  N 3                                 *forth*."

--- Page 296 ---
...let the earth bring forth. But this *soul* (such as is in man) is only an organ to the *rational soul*, and it too has its origin, just as in *Brutes*, from the dust of the earth: For it was not said, "He formed the body of man from the dust of the earth," but "He formed man"; that is, the whole man, except for the *breath*. Wherefore we shall call the first part of the *general doctrine* concerning the *human soul*, the *doctrine concerning the breath*; and the second, the *doctrine concerning the sensible or produced soul*. Nor yet, since we have hitherto treated *Philosophy* alone (for we have placed *Sacred Theology* at the end of the work), would we borrow this division from *Theology*, unless it also agreed with the principles of *Philosophy*. For there are very many and very great excellences of the *human soul* above the *souls of Brutes*, manifest even to those philosophizing according to sense. But wherever a *Symbol of so many and so great Excellences* is found, there a *specific difference* ought always to be rightly established. Therefore, we are not too pleased with that confused and indiscriminate treatment by philosophers concerning the *functions of the soul*; as if the *human soul* were distinguished from the *soul of Brutes* by degree rather than by species: no differently than the *Sun* among the *Stars*, or *Gold* among the *Metals*.

Another division of the *general doctrine* concerning the *human soul* must also be subjoined, before we speak more fully of its species. For what we shall say later concerning the species, both...

--- Page 297 ---
L I B E R IV. 275

...both partitions simultaneously, both that one which we just now set forth, and this one which we will now propose. Therefore, let the second partition be into the doctrine concerning the substance and faculties of the soul, and the doctrine concerning the use and objects of the faculties.

Therefore, these twin partitions having been set forth, let us proceed to the species. The doctrine concerning the breath, and likewise concerning the substance of the rational soul, embraces those inquiries concerning its Nature; Whether it is native or adventitious: separable or inseparable: mortal or immortal: to what extent bound by the laws of matter, to what extent not at all: and similar things.

But things of this kind, although even in Philosophy they might undergo a more diligent and profound inquiry than is currently held, nevertheless, in the end, we deem it more proper that they be transmitted to Religion to be determined and defined: For otherwise, they will be entirely exposed to not a few errors and illusions of the senses. For, since the Substance of the soul, in its creation, was not extracted or deduced from the mass of Heaven and earth, but immediately inspired by God; and since the laws of Heaven and earth are the proper subjects of Philosophy; how can knowledge concerning the substance of the rational soul be sought and obtained from philosophy? Rather, let it be drawn from the same Divine inspiration from which the substance of the soul first emanated.

But the doctrine concerning the sensible, or produced, soul, even as far as its substance is concerned, is truly inquired into: But that inquiry seems to us, as it were, to be wanting

N 4

--- Page 298 ---
276      On the Advancement of Learning.
wanting. For what do *the doctrine of the substance of the soul,* *the ultimate act, and the form of the body,* and such *logical trifles* contribute? For *the sensible soul, or that of brutes,* is plainly to be considered a corporeal substance, attenuated by heat, and rendered invisible; an *aura* (I say) composed of a fiery and airy nature, endowed with the softness of air for receiving impressions, and with the vigor of fire for vibrating into action; nourished partly by oily, partly by watery substances; clothed by the body, and in perfect animals located chiefly in the head; running through the nerves, and refreshed and repaired by the spiritual blood of the arteries. just as *Bernardinus Telesius,* and his disciple *Augustinus Donius,* have asserted in some part, not entirely uselessly. Therefore, let a more diligent inquiry be made concerning this *doctrine*: all the more so, because this matter, not well understood, has given rise to superstitious and plainly contaminated opinions, and those most cruelly trampling upon the dignity of the human soul, concerning *Metempsychosis, and the purifications of souls through periods of years,* and finally concerning the too close *kinship of the human soul with the souls of brutes in all respects.* Now this *soul in brutes is the principal soul,* of which the body of brutes is the organ; but in man, it is only an organ, and can itself be designated rather by the appellation of *rational soul, and spirit,* than soul. And so much for *the substance of the soul.*
      But *the faculties of the soul* are very well known; *Intellect, Reason, Imagination, Memory, Appetite,*

     *Divination* has been divided by the Ancients, and not badly, into
two parts; *Artificial*, and
*Natural*. *Artificial* collects prediction by reasoning, from the indication
of signs. *Natural*,
predicts from the soul's own internal premonition, without
the aid of signs. *Artificial*
is twofold: One argues from *causes*; The other
from *experiments* only, with a certain blind authority.
The latter, for the most part, is superstitious.
Such were the disciplines of the Pagans,
concerning the *inspection of entrails, the flight of birds*, and
similar things. Even the more solemn *Astrology* of the Chaldeans
is not much better. But *artificial Divination*,
both kinds, is scattered among different Sciences.
The *Astrologer* has his predictions from the position of the
stars. The *Physician* also has his; concerning impending death;
concerning recovery; concerning symptoms—

But *Natural Divination*, having its origin, namely,

from the proper power of its essence, some pre-knowledge

in dreams, ecstasies, the confines of death; more

and strong. Indeed, such a state of mind
is almost always brought about, or aided by abstinences,
and by those things which most withdraw the soul from
performing the functions of the body, so that its own
nature may rejoice without external impediments.
But *Divination* through *influx*,
rests on this other foundation of supposition;
That the soul, like a mirror, receives a certain
secondary illumination, from the Prescience

--- Page 301 ---

...except that in *Divinations* by *Influx* the soul is seized by a certain fervor, and as it were, an impatience of a present Deity (which among the Ancients was called by the name of *Sacred Fury*); but in *Native Divination*, it is rather closer to quiet and rest.

   But *Fascination* is an intensive power and act of imagination upon the body of another: (for we have briefly touched upon the power of imagination over the imaginer's own body above.) In this kind, the school of Paracelsus, and the followers of spurious *natural Magic*, were so immoderate that they almost equated the impulse and apprehension of imagination with *faith that works miracles*. Others, approaching closer to the likeness of *truth*; when they more acutely observed the hidden energies and impressions of things, the irradiations of the senses, the transmissions of contagions from body to body, the conveyances of magnetic virtues; came to the opinion that much more from Spirit to Spirit (since Spirit is above all things, and strenuous in acting, and tender and soft in suffering) impressions, and conveyances, and communications could occur. Hence opinions became widespread, as it were popular, concerning a superior Genius, concerning certain unlucky and ominous people, concerning the darts of love and envy, and others similar to these. And to this is joined the inquiry, *how Imagination can be intensified and strengthened?* For if strong imagination is of such great powers, it would be worthwhile to know by what means
                               N 6                      dis

--- Page 302 ---
280          On the Augmentation of Sciences.
by what means can it be exalted and made greater than itself? And here, obliquely, and no less dangerously, a certain palliation and defense for a very large part of *Ceremonial Magic* insinuates itself. For a plausible pretext would be that ceremonies, characters, incantations, gesticulations, amulets, and similar things do not derive their power from any tacit or Sacramental contract with evil Spirits; but pertain only to this, that the Imagination of him who uses them may be strengthened and exalted: just as also in Religion, the use of images has prevailed for fixing the minds of men in the contemplation of things, and for exciting the devotion of those praying.

Nevertheless, my opinion is this: Even if it be granted that the power of imagination is indeed potent, and moreover that Ceremonies intensify and strengthen that power; supposing finally that Ceremonies are employed for this intention sincerely, and as a Physical remedy, without any or the slightest thought of inviting the aid of Spirits through them: they ought nevertheless to be held as illicit, because they are repugnant to and kick against that Divine sentence pronounced against man because of Sin; *In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat thy bread*. Inasmuch as Magic of that kind proposes to obtain those excellent fruits, for which God has appointed Labor as the price, by a few, and those easy, and least laborious observances.

In the former of these, though otherwise investigated rather meagerly, almost one entire part is missing. For concerning the function and convenient structure of nerves and muscles, and of other things which are required for this motion; and what part of the body rests, while another is moved; then that the imagination is the director and, as it were, charioteer of this motion; so much so that, if the image towards which the motion is directed is dismissed, the motion itself is immediately intercepted and stopped (as when we walk, if another sharp and fixed thought arises, we immediately stop); and some other not bad subtleties, have long since come into observation and inquiry. But how the compressions, and dilatations, and agitations of the Spirit (which is undoubtedly the source of motion) bends, excites, or impels the corporeal and gross mass of the parts, has not yet been diligently inquired into and treated. Nor is it strange, since the sensitive soul itself has hitherto been regarded rather as a kind of entelechy and function, than as a substance. But when it shall now be known that it is a corporeal and material substance, it is also necessary that it be inquired by what efforts such a tiny and tender breath can put such gross and hard bodies into *motion*. Therefore, concerning this part, since it is *lacking*, let an inquiry be made.

That a due inquiry concerning the *Form of Light* has not been made (especially since men labored strenuously in *Perspective*) could be considered a certain astonishing negligence. CHAPTER I.

Division of doctrine concerning the use and objects of the
human soul's faculties, into Logic and Ethics. Division
of Logic, into the Arts of Inventing, Judging, and Trans-
-mitting.

The doctrine concerning the Intellect, (O best
of Kings) and that other concerning the Will
of man, in their birth are as Twins. For indeed
the purity of illumination, and the liberty of will,
began together, together they fell. Nor is there
given in the Universe of Things, so intimate a Sym-
pathy, as that of Truth and Goodness. Wherefore the more
it will be a shame to learned Men, if Sciences are as
winged Angels, but to Lusts as Serpents that
crawl on the ground; carrying souls about, like a
mirror indeed, but stained.
We have now come to the doctrine concerning the use and objects
of the faculties of the human soul. That has two
parts, and those most well-known, and received by common
consent

--- Page 310 ---
288          Oɴ ᴛʜᴇ Aᴅᴠ. ᴏғ Lᴇᴀʀɴɪɴɢ.
received; Logic and Ethics: Except that civil doc-

we have already emancipated, and constituted into a complete
doctrine concerning man in society, or in
community; here treating only of man as an
individual. Logic treats of the Intellect and
Reason; Ethics treats of the Will, Appetite, and Af-
fections: the one produces decrees, the other actions.
It is indeed true that imagination in both
provinces, both Judicial and Ministerial,
plays the part of a certain Legate, or Messenger,
or reciprocal Agent. For the senses deliver all sorts of
images to the imagination, concerning which reason
afterwards judges. But reason in turn transmits
chosen and approved images to the imagination,
before the execution of the decree takes place. In-
deed, voluntary motion is always preceded by,
and incited by imagination: so that
imagination is a common instrument to both, both
to reason and to will: except that
this Janus is Bifrons, and turns two
faces: for the face looking towards reason
has the image of truth; but the face looking towards
action, the image of Goodness: which faces never-
theless are,
—— Such as sisters ought to be.
Nor indeed is imagination a mere and bare Messenger;
but it either receives or usurps no small authority,
besides the simple delivery of a command. For Aristotle
rightly says: The soul has such command over the body
as a master over a slave: But Reason over imagination,

For we see that in matters of faith and religion, imagination ascends and is carried above reason itself: Not that Divine illumination has its place in imagination, (but rather in the very citadel of the mind and intellect:) but just as Divine grace in virtues uses the motions of the will; so similarly Divine Grace in illuminations uses the motions of imagination; whence it happens that Religion has always sought for itself an access and a way to the soul, through similitudes, types, parables, visions, dreams. Again, not humble is the kingdom of imagination in persuasions, insinuated by the force of eloquence. For when by the artifices of speech the minds of men are soothed, inflamed, and drawn in whatever direction; all that happens through the excitation of imagination, which, having now become unrestrained, not only insults reason, but in a way does violence to it, partly by blinding, partly by stimulating. Nevertheless, there seems no reason why we should depart from the former division. For imagination does not truly produce sciences: Indeed, Poetry (which from the beginning has been attributed to imagination) is to be regarded as a play of wit rather than a science. Moreover, we have assigned the power of imagination in natural things to the doctrine of the soul a little earlier. CAP. II.
Division of the inventive art, into the inventive art of arts, and of arguments: And that the former of these (which excels) is lacking. Division of the inventive art of arts into literate experience; and a new organon. Delineation of literate experience.

**I**NVENTION has two species, truly very different from each other; One of arts and sciences; the other of arguments and discourses. I declare that the former of these is entirely lacking. Indeed, this seems to me to be such a defect; as if someone, in compiling an inventory of the goods of a deceased person, were to report: "Cash: nothing." For just as all other things are acquired by money; so too are the rest acquired through this art. And just as the West Indies would never have been discovered by us, had not the Invention of the Nautical Needle preceded it: although those regions are immense, and the movement of the compass needle is small: So there is no reason for anyone to wonder why greater progress has not been made in exploring and advancing the Arts; since the Art of inventing and exploring sciences is hitherto unknown. That this part of science is lacking, is plainly acknowledged. For in the first place, Dialectic professes nothing, indeed, does not even think, about inventing arts, whether Mechanical, or (what they call) Liberal.

     Thirdly, if it be granted that the principles of Sciences can be rightly established from *Induction*, as they use it, or from sense and experience, it is nevertheless most certain that lower axioms cannot be rightly and safely deduced from them by *Syllogism* (in Natural matters, which partake of Matter). Yet, just as one can, on his way, proceed in a threefold manner: either when *he himself gropes in the dark*; or when *he is led by another's hand, himself seeing little*; or finally when *he directs his steps with light applied*: similarly, when one *attempts experiments of all kinds without any order or method*—that indeed is mere *groping*. But when he uses some *direction and order* in experimenting, it is as if he is led by hand. And this is what we understand by *Literate Experience*.       The application of experiment is nothing other than its ingenious transfer to some other useful experiment. But there are innumerable such things. Let men only awaken, and continually turn their eyes, sometimes to the nature of things, sometimes to human uses. C A P. III.

Division of the Invention of Arguments, into Promptuary & Topical. Division of the Topical, into General, & Particular. Example of Particular Topical, in Inquiry. On Heavy & Light.

The Invention of Arguments is not Invention properly speaking. For to invent is to discover unknown things, not to receive or recall things previously known. But the use and function of this kind of Invention seems to be nothing other than to skillfully draw forth, from the mass of Knowledge which is stored up and hidden in the mind, those things which pertain to the matter or question proposed. For to him to whom little or nothing concerning the proposed subject is known, the Topics of Invention are of no use; On the contrary, he who has ready at hand what can be brought to bear on the matter, will, even without art and the Topics of Invention, at last find and produce arguments (though not so expeditiously and conveniently). So much so that this kind of Invention (as we have said) is not Invention properly speaking; but merely a reduction to memory, or a suggestion with application. Nevertheless, since the term has gained currency and been received, let it indeed be called Invention; Indeed, even the hunting and finding of some wild animal can be said no less when it is sought within the enclosures of game parks, than when in open forests. But setting aside ver-

314      ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF SCIENCES.
verbal quibbles, let this be established: the aim and
purpose of this matter is a certain readiness,
and a ready use of our knowledge,
rather than its amplification, or
increase.
   And so that a store of material for discussion may be ready, a two-

It seems, however, that this should be briefly noted: that this Topic (or system of Topics) is useful not only in Argumentations, where we engage with others, but also in meditations, when we ourselves ponder or reflect upon something. Indeed, its utility is not confined solely to this, that from it there should arise a suggestion or admonition as to what we should affirm or assert; but also as to what we should inquire about or ask. But a prudent question is, as it were, half of knowledge. Rightly indeed Plato says, "He who seeks something, comprehends that very thing which he seeks by some general notion: otherwise, how can it happen that he recognizes it when it has been found?" Therefore, the more ample and certain our anticipation has been, the more direct and concise will our investigation be. Therefore, those same topics which will be conducive to stirring up the recesses of our intellect within us, and drawing forth the knowledge accumulated there, will also help in drawing forth knowledge from outside: so that if someone knowledgeable and skilled is at hand, he can be conveniently and prudently questioned by us about it; and similarly, authors, and books, and parts of books, which teach and inform us about those things which we seek, can be usefully selected and perused.

      But *Particular Topics* contributes much more to what we are discussing, and is to be considered a most fruitful thing. Certainly, a slight mention of it has been made by some writers, but it has by no means been treated fully and with the dignity due to the subject. But
                                                              missum

--- Page 339 ---
LIBER V. 317
dismissing that vice and arrogance which have reigned too long in the Schools: namely, that they pursue what is at hand with infinite subtlety, but do not even touch what is a little more remote: we indeed embrace *Particular Topics* as a most useful thing; that is, *places of inquiry and invention*, appropriated to particular *subjects and sciences*. But these are certain mixtures of *Logic and the Matter itself*, proper to individual *Sciences*. For it is clearly futile, and characteristic of a narrow mind, to suppose that a *perfect Art of Inventing Sciences* can be devised and proposed from the very beginning, and that the same should afterwards be put into practice and exercised. But let men know for certain that *solid and true Arts of Invention grow and gain increments with the inventions themselves*: So much so that when someone first approaches the investigation of any *science*, he can have some useful *Inventive Precepts*; but after he has made greater progress in the *Science itself*, he can and should also devise new *Precepts of Invention*, which may lead him more successfully to further things. Indeed, this matter is similar to a path begun on a plain: for after we have traversed some part of the path, we have not only gained this, that we have approached closer to the end of the journey, but also that we may see more clearly what remains of the path. In the same way, in *Sciences*, each step of the journey, having passed over those things which it left behind, also brings those things which remain closer into view.

*Particular Topic, or Articles of Inquiry*
*concerning Heavy and Light.*

1. Let inquiry be made as to what sort of Bodies are susceptible to the Motion of gravity, what sort to lightness; and if there are any Intermediates, or of an Indifferent Nature?

2. After inquiry concerning simple Gravity and Lightness, let us proceed to comparative inquiry; Namely, which among Heavy things weigh more, which less, in the same Dimension? Also, which among Light things are carried upwards more quickly, which more slowly?

3. Let inquiry be made concerning what the Quantity of a Body can do and effect regarding the Motion of Gravity? And this might seem at first glance almost superfluous, because the principles of Motion ought to follow the principles of Quantity. But the matter stands otherwise. For although in scales, Quantity compensates for the Gravity of the body itself (the forces of the body everywhere converging through repercussion, or the resistance of the scales or beam), nevertheless, where little resistance is given (as in the Fall of bodies through the air), the Quantity of the body has little power to incite Descent; Since twenty pounds of lead, and one pound, fall in almost the same space?

4. Let inquiry be made, whether the Quantity of a body can be so increased that the Motion of Gravity is entirely laid aside? as happens in the globe of the earth, which is suspended, it does not fall. Whether therefore there can be other masses so great-

--- Page 341 ---
L I B E R V. 319
great, so that they sustain themselves? For motion towards the center of the earth is a fictitious thing: And every great mass shuns any motion of translation, unless it is overcome by another stronger appetite.
   5. Let it be inquired concerning what the resistance of the intervening or opposing body can do and effect for the regulation of the motion of gravity. Indeed, a descending body either penetrates and cuts through the opposing body: Or it is stopped by it. If it penetrates, penetration occurs: Either with slight resistance, as in Air: Or with stronger, as in water. If it is stopped, it is stopped either by unequal resistance, where there is an over-weighting, as if wood is placed upon wax. Or water, as if water is placed upon water; or wood, upon wood of the same kind. That which the School calls (with a certain empty apprehension) that a body does not weigh except outside its own place. And all these things vary the motion of gravity: For heavy bodies move differently in scales, differently in falling: Also differently (which might seem strange) in scales suspended in air, differently in scales immersed in water: differently in falling through water, differently in floating, or carried upon water.
   6. Let it be inquired concerning what the Figure of a descending Body can do and effect for regulating the mode of gravity? such as a broad figure with thinness, cubic, oblong, round, pyramidal: and when bodies turn themselves, when they remain in the same position in which they are released?
   7. Let it be inquired concerning what the Continuation and Progression of the Fall or Descent itself can do and effect, to the end that it may be carried with greater incitation and impetus? and in what proportion, and how far

CHAP. IV.
*Division of the art of Judging, into Judgment by Induction*
*and by Syllogism. Of which the former is assigned to the*
*Novum Organum. First division of Judgment by Syllogism*
*into Direct, and Inverse Reduction. Its second*
*division into Analytics, and the Doctrine of Elenchi. Division*
*of the Doctrine of Elenchi, into Elenchi of Sophisms,*
*Elenchi of Interpretation, and Elenchi of Images, or Idols.*
*Division of Idols, into Idols of the Tribe, Idols of the Cave,*
*and Idols of the Marketplace. Appendix to the Art of Judging,*
*namely concerning the Analogy of Demonstrations according to the Nature of the Subject.*

[Large initial T] Let us now pass to Judgment, or the Art
of Judging, which deals with the nature of proofs,
or demonstrations. But in this art of Judging (as is also
commonly accepted) one concludes either by Induction,
or by Syllogism. For Enthymemes, and Examples,
are merely compendia of those two. But
as far as Judgment, which is made by Induction,
there is nothing that should detain us:
For by one and the same operation of the mind, that
which is sought, and found, and judged.
Nor indeed is the matter transacted through some medium,
but immediately, in almost the same way, as it happens
in sense (perception). For sense in its primary
objects at once grasps the species of the object, and its
P 4 veri-

--- Page 346 ---
324      DE AUGM. SCIENT.
...truth assents: But it is otherwise in Syllogism; whose proof is not immediate, but is perfected through a medium. Therefore, one thing is *Discovery of the Middle Term*, another is *Judgment concerning the Consequence of the Argument*. For first the mind discourses, then it rests. But we bid farewell entirely to the vicious form of *Induction*; we refer the legitimate form to the *Novum Organum*. Therefore, concerning *Judgment by Induction*, enough in this place.

What need is there to speak of that other (judgment) by *Syllogism*? since this matter has been almost worn out by the most subtle files of intellects, and reduced to many minute details. Nor is it strange, since it is a matter that has great sympathy with the human intellect. For the human mind strives and yearns in wondrous ways for this, that it may not be suspended, but may acquire something fixed and immobile, upon which, as upon a firmament, it may lean in its excursions and investigations. Indeed, just as Aristotle tries to prove that in every motion of bodies something is found that rests, and most elegantly transfers the ancient fable of Atlas, who himself upright sustained the Heavens on his shoulders, to the Poles of the World, around which rotations are performed: Similarly, men eagerly desire to have within themselves an Atlas of thoughts, or Poles, which may in some measure govern the fluctuations and giddiness of the intellect, fearing, of course, lest their Heaven should fall. Therefore, they hastened too quickly to establish the Principles of Sciences, around which all variety of disputes might revolve, without danger of ruin and fall: Not knowing

--- Page 347 ---
L I B E R V. 325
indeed, that he who too hastily seizes certainties will end up in uncertainties; but he who has timely restrained judgment will arrive at certainties.

It is therefore manifest that *this Art of Judging by Syllogism* is nothing else than the reduction of propositions to principles through middle terms. Principles, however, are understood as received by consensus, and are exempt from question. But the invention of middle terms is permitted to the free acuteness and investigation of intellects. *Now that reduction is twofold, namely direct and inverse. Direct is,* when the proposition itself is reduced to the principle itself: This is called *ostensive proof*. *Inverse is,* when the contradictory of the proposition is reduced to the contradictory of the principle; which they call *proof by inconvenience*. The number of middle terms, however, or their scale, is diminished or increased, according to the remoteness of the proposition from the principle.

These things having been established, we will divide *the Art of Judgment* (as is commonly almost customary) into *Analytics, and the Doctrine of Elenchi:* The one indicates, the other guards against: For *Analytics* establishes true forms concerning the consequences of arguments; if one varies from these, or deviates, the conclusion is found to be faulty. And this very thing contains in itself a certain elenchus, or refutation. *For the straight (as it is said) is both an index of itself and of the crooked.* Nevertheless, it is safest to employ Elenchi as monitors, so that falla-
            P 5                         cies

--- Page 348 ---
326 ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING
fallacies, which would otherwise ensnare judgment. But in *Analytics* we find nothing lacking; rather it is burdened with superfluities than it needs additions.

We propose to divide the *Doctrine of Elenchi* into three parts: *Elenchi of Sophisms*, *Elenchi of Interpretation*, and *Elenchi of Images or Idols*. The *Doctrine of Elenchi of Sophisms* is exceedingly useful: For although a grosser kind of fallacies is aptly compared by Seneca with the tricks of jugglers—in which we do not know how the thing is managed, yet we know well enough that the matter stands otherwise than it appears—more subtle *Sophisms*, however, not only accomplish that one has nothing to reply, but also seriously confound judgment itself.

This Part concerning the *Elenchi of Sophisms* has been excellently treated by Aristotle, as regards Precepts; and even better by Plato, as regards Examples: Yet not that in the person of the Sophists Ant-

--- Page 349 ---
L I B E R V. 327
to consider the arguments to be constructed and arranged by means of those very sophisms. This kind of ability is also considered excellent, and brings no small advantages. Although that distinction between an orator and a sophist has been elegantly introduced by someone; that the one, like a hound, excels in speed; the other, like the hare itself, in dodging.

Next come the Refutations of Interpretation: for thus (borrowing the word rather than the sense from Aristotle) shall we call them. Therefore, let us recall to men's memory those things which we said above concerning transcendentals, and concerning the adventitious conditions or adjuncts of beings (when we were treating of First Philosophy). These are: greater, lesser; much, little; prior, posterior; same, different; potency, act; habit, privation; whole, parts; agent, patient; motion, rest; being, non-being; and similar things. But first of all, let them remember and note the different contemplations of these things which we mentioned: namely, that they can be investigated either Physically or Logically. We assigned the Physical treatment concerning them to First Philosophy. Logic remains: and this very thing is what we presently call the Doctrine of Refutations of Interpretation. This is certainly a sound and good portion of doctrine. For those general and common notions have this quality, that they run through everywhere in all disputations; so much so that unless they are accurately, and with anxious judgment, well distinguished from the very beginning, they will in wonderful ways cast a mist upon the universal light of disputations,
P 6 and thereby

and will almost bring the matter to the point where disputations cease to be mere battles of words. For equivocations and ill-conceived understandings of words (especially of this kind) are *Sophisms of Sophisms*. Therefore, it has also seemed better to establish the treatment of these separately, rather than to admit it either into *First Philosophy* or *Metaphysics*, or to subject it partially to *Analytics*, as Aristotle rather confusedly did. We have given it a name from its use, because its true use is plainly refutation and caution concerning the use of words. Moreover, we believe that that part concerning *Predicaments*, if rightly instituted, obtains its principal use in cautions against confusing or transposing the terms of definitions and divisions, and we prefer it to be referred here as well. And so much for the *Elenchs of Hermeneutics*.

As for the *Elenchs of Images* or *Idols*, *Idols* are indeed the deepest fallacies of the human mind. For they do not deceive in particulars, like the others, by casting a mist over judgment and setting snares; but plainly from a corrupt and wrongly constituted predisposition of the mind, which, as it were, distorts and infects all anticipations of the intellect. For the *human mind* (veiled and obscured by the body) is so far from being like a plain, even, and clear mirror, which sincerely receives and reflects the rays of things, that it is rather like some enchanted mirror, full of superstitions and specters. Now *Idols* are imposed upon the intellect either by the *very general nature of the human race*: or by the nature—

--- Page 351 ---
L I B E R. V. 329
the individual nature of each person: or through words or communicative nature. The first kind we are accustomed to call Idols of the Tribe, the second Idols of the Cave, the third Idols of the Marketplace. There is also a fourth kind, which we call Idols of the Theater, and it is superinduced by corrupt Theories, or Philosophies, and by perverse Laws of Demonstrations: But this kind can be denied and set aside: Therefore, for the present, we will omit it. But the rest plainly besiege the mind, nor can they be entirely uprooted. Therefore, there is no reason for anyone to expect any *Analytics* in them: but *Doctrine of Elenchi* is, concerning the *Idols* themselves, the *primary Doctrine*. Nor (if the whole truth must be told) can the *Doctrine of Idols* be reduced to an art: but only a certain contemplative prudence must be applied to guard against them. However, a full and subtle treatment of these, to the *New Organ*

had escaped; and being pressed by questioning, whether then at last he would acknowledge Neptune's Divinity? he asked in return, *“But where are those depicted who perished after having made vows?”* And the same is the reasoning for similar superstitions, as in Astrology, Dreams, Omens, and the rest. Another Example is of this kind: *“The human mind (since it is itself a substance equal and uniform) presupposes and attributes to the nature of things a greater equality and uniformity than actually exists.”* Hence the mathematicians' fiction, *“that in celestial bodies all things move in perfect Circles,”* rejecting spiral lines: Hence it also happens that although many things in Nature are singular and full of inequality; human thought nevertheless always attributes *“Relatives, Parallels, and Conjugates:”* For from this source the element of fire with its own sphere was introduced, to constitute a quaternion with the other three, Earth, Water, Air. The Chemists, moreover, constructed a fanatical array of all things, falsely imagining by a most empty fiction that in those four elements of theirs (Heaven, Air, Water, and Earth), each species is found parallel to each other, and conformable. A third Example is very similar to the preceding; *“that man becomes, as it were, the norm and mirror of Nature:”* For it is not credible (if each thing is examined and noted) how great a host of *Idols* has been introduced into Philosophy by the reduction of natural operations to the likeness of human actions: This very thing, I say, that it is thought that nature does such things as man does.

But the *Idols of the Marketplace* are the most troublesome, which, from a tacit agreement among men, concerning *words and imposed names*, have insinuated themselves into the intellect. Words, however, are for the most part imposed according to the understanding of the common people; and they divide things according to the distinctions of which the common people are capable; but when a sharper intellect, or more diligent observation, wishes to distinguish things better, words obstruct. And what is indeed the remedy for this (definitions, namely) in many cases cannot cure this evil, because definitions themselves consist of words, and words beget words. And although we may think that we command our words; and it is easy to say, '*One should speak as the common people; one should think as the wise.*' Moreover, the terms of the arts (which are valid only among experts) might seem to satisfy this matter; and definitions (of which we have spoken) prefixed to the arts (according to the prudence of Mathematicians) might be able to correct the corrupt acceptations of words, nevertheless, all these things are not sufficient to prevent the deceptions and enchantments of words from misleading in many ways, and from doing a certain violence to the intellect, and from turning their attack (after the manner of Tartar archery) back

But its proper treatment we refer to the *Novum Organum*. There still remains a certain notable *Appendix to the Art of Judgment*, which we also deem to be *lacking*. For Aristotle indeed noted the matter, but nowhere pursued its method. It discusses *what kinds of demonstrations ought to be applied to what kinds of matters, or subjects*: so that this doctrine may contain, as it were, judgments *of judgments*. For Aristotle rightly warns that *neither demonstrations should be required from orators, nor persuasions from mathematicians*. So that if one errs in the kind of Proof, the judgment itself may not be absolved. But since there are four kinds of demonstrations, either *by immediate consent and notions*, or *by induction*, or *by Syllogism*, or by that (*which Aristotle rightly calls*) *demonstration in a circle*, (not from the better known, that is, but as it were from a plain,) these individual demonstrations have certain subjects and matters of sciences in which they excel; others, from which they are excluded. For indeed rigor and curiosity, by demanding too severe proofs in some cases, and much more so facility and laxity in acquiescing to lighter proofs in others, are to be numbered among those things which cause very much detriment and impediment

C H A P. V.

*Division of the Art of Retaining or Retentive Art, into the doctrine concerning aids to memory, and the doctrine concerning Memory itself. Division of the doctrine concerning Memory itself, into Prenotion and Emblem.*

**T**he Art of Retaining, or of Keeping, we shall divide into two doctrines: namely, the *Doctrine* concerning *Aids to Memory*; and the *Doctrine* *of Memory itself*. An aid to Memory is plainly *Writing*; and it must be altogether warned, that *Memory* without this aid is unequal to more extensive and accurate matters; nor should it in any way be received, except from writing. Which also holds especially true in *Inductive Philosophy*, and the *Interpretation of Nature*: For one could as easily complete the calculations of an Ephemeris with bare Memory, without writing, as suffice for the interpretation of Nature through Meditations, and native and bare powers of memory; unless that same memory is supplied by *Ordered Tables*. But leaving aside the *Interpretation of Nature*, which is a new Doctrine, even for the Old and Popular Sciences hardly anything could be more useful than a solid and good aid to Memory; that is, a sound and learned *Digest* of *Commonplaces*. Nor does it escape me, that the arrangement of those things which we read, or learn, into *Commonplaces*,

--- Page 357 ---
L I B E R. V. 335
nes, lest it be imputed by some as a detriment to learning, as that which delays the course of reading, and invites *Memory* to idleness. However, since it is a spurious thing to be precocious and quick in the sciences, unless one is also solid and manifoldly instructed; we judge that diligence and labor in collecting *commonplaces* is altogether a thing of great use and firmness in studies; as that which supplies abundance to *Invention*; and concentrates the keenness of *Judgment* into one. It is true, however, that among the methods and syntaxes of *Commonplaces* which it has so far happened for us to see, none is found which is of any value: inasmuch as in their titles they altogether exhibit a face more of the school than of the World, employing vulgar and pedagogical divisions, but not those which in any way penetrate to the marrow and innermost parts of things.

Concerning *Memory* itself, however, it seems that inquiry has been made quite sluggishly and languidly so far. There certainly exist some things concerning that *Art*: But it is clear to us, that both better precepts concerning the strengthening of *Memory* can be had than that art embraces; and that a better Practice of that very art can be instituted than that which is received. Nor do we doubt, however (if anyone pleases to abuse this art for ostentation), that some marvelous and prodigious things can be performed by it: But nevertheless, the thing is, as it were, sterile (in the way it is applied) for human uses. But we do not, in the meantime, impute to it that it destroys and overburdens *Natural memory* (as is commonly objected), but that

For to immediately repeat a huge number of names or words once recited in the same order, or to compose several verses extemporaneously on any subject, or to touch upon whatever occurs with some satirical comparison, or to turn everything serious into a joke, or to evade anything by contradiction and caviling, and similar things (of which there is no small abundance in the faculties of the mind, and which can be elevated to a miraculous degree by ingenuity and practice) — all these things and similar ones we certainly do not value more than the agility and tricks of tightrope walkers and mimes. For if one is stuck on some word, there underlies a *Prenotion*, that the word ought to be such which agrees with the verse. And thus *Prenotion* is the first part of *Artificial Memory*. For in *Artificial Memory* we have *Places* already arranged and prepared; we construct *Images* extemporaneously, as the matter demands. But there underlies a *Prenotion*, that the *Image* ought to be such as in some measure agrees with the *Place*. That which stimulates *Memory*, and in some way fortifies it for the matter which we seek. *Emblem* indeed leads the intellectual to the sensible: but the sensible always strikes *Memory* more strongly, and is more easily impressed upon it, than the intellectual. So much so that even the memory of brutes is excited by the sensible; by the intellectual, not at all. Therefore you would more easily retain the image of a hunter pursuing a hare, or of an apothecary arranging boxes, or of a pedant giving a speech, or of a boy reciting verses by heart, or of a mime acting on stage; than the Notions themselves of Invention, Disposition, Elocution, Memory, Action. There are also other things which pertain to aiding *Memory* (as we just said); but the *Art*, which is now possessed, consists of these two already premised.      Let us now approach the *Art of Transmitting*, or of *Bringing forth*, and *Uttering* those things which have been Invented, Judged, and stored in Memory; which we shall call by the general name *Traditive*. It embraces all arts concerning *words* and *discourses*. For although the reason of discourse is, as it were, its soul, nevertheless, in treating it, reason and discourse must be separated; no less than soul and body. We shall divide the *Traditive* into three parts: *Doctrine concerning the Organ of Discourse; Doctrine concerning the Method of Discourse; and Doctrine concerning the Illustration, or Embellishment, of Discourse.*
     The *Doctrine concerning the Organ of Discourse* commonly received, which is also called *Grammar*, is twofold: One *concerning Speaking*, the other *concerning Writing*. For Aristotle rightly said, *Words are the tokens of thoughts, and letters are the tokens of words*. We shall assign both to *Grammar*. But in order to trace the matter more deeply, before we come to *Grammar* and its parts already mentioned, something must be said in general about the *Organ of the Traditive*. For there appear to be certain other offspring of the *Traditive*, besides *Words and Letters*.

The doctrine of ciphers, however, brought with it another doctrine related to itself. That is about Deciphering, or the unlocking of Ciphers: even if one is completely ignorant of the Cipher's Alphabet, or the agreement concerning the secret. That thing is indeed laborious and ingenious at the same time, and dedicated to the secrets of Princes, just like the former. Yet, by diligent precaution, it could be rendered useless; although, as things now stand, it is of very great use. For if the ciphers introduced were good and reliable, there would be many that would completely elude and exclude the Decipherer's effort; which nevertheless would be convenient enough and easy for reading or writing. But the inexperience and ignorance of Secretaries and Amanuenses in the courts of Princes is so great that most affairs are usually entrusted to weak and futile ciphers.

Meanwhile, it is possible that someone may suspect that we, in this enumeration and as it were census of the arts, are acting so that the abundance of sciences (which we bring forth as if into battle array), being increased and multiplied, may be more a cause for admiration; when, however, their number can perhaps only be displayed, and their strengths can hardly be explained in such a brief Treatise. But we faithfully pursue our purpose, and, in completing this globe of sciences, we do not wish even the smaller or more remote islands to be omitted. Nor indeed (as we believe) do we touch upon these arts superficially, though cursorily; but rather their kernels and marrow, from much

--- Page 376 ---
354          ON THE ADV. OF SCI.
from a great mass of material, we extract with a sharp stylus.
We leave the judgment of this matter to those who are most skilled in such arts. For since most who wish to appear learned almost always do this: by casually throwing around the vocabulary and superficialities of the arts, they are an object of admiration to the ignorant, but of ridicule to the Masters; we hope that our work will have the exact opposite outcome, so that it will particularly engage the judgment of the most skilled in each individual art, and be of less account to others.

But as for those arts which can be seen as belonging to lesser peoples, if anyone thinks that we attribute too much to them; let him look around, and he will see that men who are indeed great and famous in their own provinces, when they happen to migrate to the Metropolis or the seat of empire, are almost always mixed in with the crowd and are of inferior note: similarly, it is not surprising that these lighter arts, when placed alongside the Principal and supreme arts, diminish in dignity; although to those who have especially devoted their efforts to them, these things certainly seem great and excellent. And let these things have been said concerning the *organ of speech*.

The doctrine of the method of speech is established, as a
substantive and principal part of the traditive art: The name
given to it is "Prudence of the Traditive Art." Diverse
Kinds of Method are enumerated; and their advantages
and disadvantages are subjoined.

Let us come to the doctrine of the method of speech. This
part has customarily been treated in Dialectic. It also
finds a place in Rhetoric under the name of Dis-
position. But its placement in the service of other arts
has been the cause that many things pertaining to it, useful
to know, have been omitted. Therefore, it has seemed good
to us to establish a Substantive and Principal Doctrine
concerning Method, which we call by the general name
"Prudence of the Traditive Art." And so, we shall enumerate
the Kinds of Method (since they are various) rather than
divide them. And concerning the single Method, and perpetual
Dichotomies, it is not worth saying anything: For it was a
certain little cloud of Doctrine, which quickly passed
away: A thing certainly at once trivial and most
damaging to the sciences. For such men, when they
twist things by the laws of their Method; and whatever
does not fit aptly into those Dichotomies, they either
omit or bend contrary to Nature; they bring it about
that, as it were, the Kernels and Grains of the Sciences
escape, while they themselves grasp only dry and deserted
Pods. Therefore, this kind of Method produces empty
shortcuts, and destroys the solid substance of the sciences.

356	**On the Advancement of Learning**
	Therefore, let the first distinction of *method* be established, that it is either *magisterial* or *initiative*. Nor indeed do we understand the word *initiative* as if this (method) merely imparted the rudiments of sciences, while that (method imparted) the complete doctrine; But on the contrary (borrowing the term from sacred rites), we call that the *initiative method* which itself reveals and lays bare the mysteries of the sciences. The *magisterial* indeed teaches how to use what is said; but the *initiative* rather, how they may undergo examination: The one imparts sciences to the common run of learners; the other imparts them as if to sons of the sciences: Finally, the one has as its end the use of sciences (as they now are); the other, their continuation and further progress.

Of these, the latter seems a *deserted and blocked* path. For thus have sciences hitherto been accustomed to be taught, as if by agreement, both teacher and learner desiring to embrace errors. For indeed, he who teaches, teaches in such a way that the greatest faith may be given to his words, not in such a way that they may be most conveniently subjected to examination: and he who learns, desires to be made an example for himself, not to await a legitimate inquiry; so that it is dearer to him *Not to doubt, than not to err*. So that both the Master, out of love of glory, takes care not to betray the weakness of his science, and the Disciple, out of hatred of labor, is unwilling to test his own powers.

But science, which is handed down to others as a web to be woven, *must be insinuated into the mind of another by the same Method* (if it can be done) *by which it was first discovered*. And this very thing can certainly be done in science acquired through *induction*; But in anticipated science, that is both premature—

--- Page 379 ---
L I B E R VI. 357

knowledge (which we use), one cannot easily say
by what path one arrived at that knowledge
which one has acquired. Nevertheless, certainly, to a greater or
lesser degree, one can review one's own knowledge,
and retrace the steps of one's cognition, as well as one's assent,
and in this way thus transplant knowledge
into another's mind, just as it grew in
one's own. For the same thing happens to disciplines as to plants:
if you intend to use some plant, it matters not
what happens to the root: but if you wish to transplant it

     There follows another distinction of *Method*, altogether of great importance to the Sciences; namely, when Sciences are handed down either by *Aphorisms* or *Methodically*. For it is especially worthy of note that it has generally become customary for men, from a few axioms and observations, in any given subject, to constitute an art as if complete and solemn, stuffing it with certain Commentaries of their own ingenuity, illustrating it with Examples, and binding it together by *Method*. But that other *Tradition* by *Aphorisms* carries with it many advantages, to which *tradition*

which methodical tradition does not reach. For first, it gives a specimen of the Writer, whether he has lightly, and superficially imbibed Science, or has thoroughly absorbed it. For *Aphorisms*, unless they were utterly ridiculous, must necessarily be composed from the marrow, and innermost parts of the Sciences. For illustration, and digression are cut off; variety of examples is cut off; deduction, and connection are cut off; description of Practice is cut off: so that nothing is left for the matter of *Aphorisms*, except a good ample supply of observations.    Another distinction of *Method* follows, and that too of great importance: namely, when Sciences are delivered, either by assertions with proofs added, or by questions together with determinations. But if anyone pursues this latter *Method* too immoderately, it hinders the progress of the Sciences no less than it would be an impediment and detriment to the fortunes and progress of some army, if it were to constantly get stuck in conquering every small castle or town. For if one is superior in the field, and diligently applies himself to the main objective of the war, those lesser places will voluntarily submit themselves. However, I would not deny that to leave some large and fortified city behind is by no means always safe: In the same way, refutations in the delivery of Sciences should be moderated, and used sparingly: and only for this purpose, that greater preoccupations of minds and prejudices may be broken, but by no means, that lighter doubts may be excited and provoked.
   Another distinction of *Method* follows, namely, that the *Method* should be suited to the subject matter which is being treated. For *Mathematics* are delivered in one way (which among the Sciences are most abstract and simple); in another way *Politics*, which are most immersed and composite. Nor (as we have already said) can a uniform *Method* conveniently apply itself to multiform matter.

--- Page 383 ---
L I B E R VI. 361
Indeed, just as we have approved *particular Topics* for invention, so we wish *particular Methods* to be similarly applied to teaching to some extent.
   Another distinction of *Method* follows, to be applied with judgment in teaching Sciences. But that is governed by the information and anticipations concerning the Science (which is to be taught) previously instilled and impressed in the minds of the learners. For a Science that comes to the minds of men as entirely new and foreign must be taught differently; differently that which is both related and familiar to opinions long since imbibed and received. And therefore Aristotle, wishing to disparage Democritus, in reality praises him; "If (he says) we wish to dispute seriously, we should not follow resemblances, etc.," turning it into a fault for Democritus that he was excessive in comparisons. But those whose doctrines have already established their seats in popular opinions have nothing else to do but to dispute and prove. For those, on the other hand, whose dogmas transcend popular opinions, a twofold labor is necessary: first, that what they put forward may be understood; then, that it may be proven. So that they are obliged to resort to the aids of similarities and metaphors, by which they may insinuate themselves into the grasp of men. We see therefore, in the infancy of doctrines, in ruder ages, when those Syllepses, which have now become common and trite, were new and unheard of, everything was full of parables and similarities. Otherwise it would have happened that what was proposed, either without being understood,

--- Page 384 ---

transmitted without notice, or due attention; or rejected as paradoxes. For it is a certain Rule of the Teaching Method, that every Science which is not *consonant with Anticipations, or presuppositions, ought to seek help from similitudes and comparisons.*
     And let these things be said concerning the different kinds of Methods; namely, those which have not been noted by others before now. For as to those other Methods, the Analytic, the Systematic, the Diaeretic, also the Cryptic, the Homeric, and similar ones, they are rightly invented and distributed; nor does there seem to be a reason why we should dwell on them.
     But the Kinds of Method are of this sort. And there are two parts; One concerns the *disposition of the whole work*, or the argument of some book; The other concerns the *limitation of propositions.* For to Architecture belongs not only the construction of the whole building, but also the shaping and form of columns, beams, and similar things. *Method*, however, is, as it were, the Architecture of the Sciences. And in this respect, Ramus deserved better, in renewing those excellent Rules (καθ' όλου πρῶτον, κατὰ παντὸς, καθ' αὑτὸ, &c.), than in obtruding his single Method and *Dichotomies*. Nevertheless, I know not by what fate it happens that to the most precious human affairs (as poets often feign) are always assigned the most pernicious guardians. Certainly, Ramus's attempt, concerning that refinement of propositions, cast him into those epitomes and shallows of the Sciences.       There remain two more *Limitations of Propositions* besides that they become *Convertible*: One concerning *Extension*; the other concerning their *Production*.
Indeed, *Sciences*, if one rightly observes,
