C A P. III.

On the Foundations, & Function of Rhetoric. *Three*
*Appendices of Rhetoric, which pertain only to the*
*Handbook.* Colors of Good & Evil, *both simple,*
*and Comparative:* Antitheses of Things: Minor
Formulas of Oration.

[Large initial V]E come now to the *Doctrine of the Embellishment*
*of Speech.* This is what is called *Rhetoric*,
or *Oratory*. A *science* certainly both excellent in itself,
and excellently cultivated by writers. *Eloquence*,
however, if one truly estimates the matter, is beyond
doubt inferior to *Wisdom*. For we see by how great
an interval the latter leaves the former behind, in the words
with which *God* addressed *Moses*, when he
had refused the task entrusted to him because of a lack of *Elocution*,
"You have Aaron, he will be to you in place of an Orator,
but you to him in place of God." But in effect, and
popular estimation, *Wisdom* yields to *Eloquence*.
For thus *Solomon* says, "The wise in heart will be called
prudent, but the sweet in speech will find greater things."
Not obscurely implying that *Wisdom* procures a certain
fame and admiration for someone: but in managing
affairs, and in common life, *Eloquence* is especially
effective. As for the cultivation of this *Art*;
*Aristotle's Rivalry* towards the *Rhetoricians* of his time,
and *Cicero's* keen and vehement zeal, applying himself
with all his might to ennobling it, combined with long
practice, were the cause that in their books written
about this *Art* they surpassed them-
                                R                      selves.

--- Page 388 ---
366 ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING.
surpassed themselves. Then, those most brilliant *Examples* of this *Art*, which are found in the *Orations of Demosthenes* and *Cicero*, added to the keenness and diligence of the Precepts, doubled its progress. Therefore, what we find to be *lacking* in this *Art* will consist rather in certain *Collections* which may serve this Art as handmaids, than in the Discipline and use of the Art itself. For even then, when we made mention of a certain *Storehouse* in connection with *Logic*, we promised more abundant *Examples* of that matter in *Rhetoric*.

Nevertheless, as is our custom, let us open up and cultivate the soil a little around the roots of this *Art*; *Rhetoric* certainly serves the *Imagination*, just as *Dialectic* serves the *Intellect*. And it is, if one penetrates the matter more deeply, that the *Office and function of Rhetoric* is nothing else than to *apply and commend the dictates of reason to the imagination, to excite the appetite and the will.* For we see the governance of reason assailed and disturbed in three ways: Either by the *entanglement of sophisms*, which pertains to *Dialectic*; or by the *deceptions of words*, which pertains to *Rhetoric*; or by the *violence of the affections*, which pertains to *Ethics*. For just as in affairs which we contract with others, one is accustomed to be overcome and led astray either by *Cunning*, or by *Importunity*, or by *Vehemence*; so also in that internal negotiation which we carry on with ourselves, either we are undermined by the *fallacies of arguments*; or we are troubled and disquieted by the assiduity of *impressions* and *observations*; or we are shaken by the *impetus of the affections*,

--- Page 389 ---
L I B E R VI. 367
we are shaken, and carried away. Nor indeed is human nature dealt with so unhappily, that those arts and faculties should be powerful for overthrowing reason, but by no means for strengthening and establishing it: But for this purpose much more. For the end of *Dialectic* is, to teach the form of arguments, for the defenses of the intellect, not for snares. Likewise the end of *Ethics* is, so to compose the affections, that they may serve reason, and not invade it. Finally, the end of *Rhetoric* is, to fill the Imagination with observations and images, which may bring aid to reason, and not suppress it. For the abuses of art only intervene indirectly, for caution, not for use.

Wherefore in Plato there was the greatest injustice (although arising from a not undeserved hatred towards the *Rhetoricians* of his time) when he placed *Rhetoric* among the voluptuary arts: saying it was similar to *Cookery*, which would no less corrupt wholesome foods, than it would render unwholesome ones more palatable, by abusing the variety of seasonings and delicacies. But far be it, that speech should not more frequently be employed in adorning honest things, than in glossing over base ones: For this is everywhere at hand: Since there is no one, who does not speak more honorably, than he either thinks or acts. Indeed it was very well noted by Thucydides, that something of this kind was accustomed to be objected to Cleon; because, although he always defended the worse side, he was very much engaged in this, to disparage eloquence and the grace of speech. Rightly so, indeed; since he knew, that concerning sordid and unworthy things no one could speak beautifully.

--- Page 390 ---
368          ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING
who; but about honest things, most easily. Plato elegantly said (though it is already a common saying in the Trivium): *“If virtue were given to be seen, it would excite great loves of itself:”* But *Rhetoric* depicts virtue and the good clearly, and renders them as if visible. For since those things cannot be shown to the senses with a bodily form, it remains that through the adornment of words, they be presented before the Imagination by a representation as vivid as possible. Indeed, the custom of the Stoics was deservedly ridiculed by Cicero; who strove to impose virtue upon the minds of men with concise and acute sentences and conclusions; a method which has little agreement with imagination and will.
     Furthermore, if the affections themselves were compelled into order and were entirely obedient to reason, it is true that there would be no great use for persuasions and insinuations which could provide access to the mind; but it would be enough if the things themselves were presented nakedly and simply, and proven. But affections, on the contrary, make such great secessions; and even stir up such great troubles and seditions (according to that saying:
          ——— *I see the better, and approve it,*
*I follow the worse*) ———
that reason would be entirely carried away into servitude and captivity, unless the Persuasion of Eloquence brought it about that Imagination should not stand on the side of the affections, but rather, by its work, a covenant be entered into between reason and imagination, against the affections. For it must be noted that the affections themselves are always carried towards an apparent good, and in this respect have something
                                                            have

--- Page 391 ---
L I B E R VI. 369
to have in common with reason: but this is the difference; that *Affections look primarily at the good, in the present; Reason looking far ahead, also to the future, and in sum.* And therefore, since what is present fills the Imagination more strongly, reason usually succumbs and is subjugated. But after eloquence and the power of persuasions have brought it about that future and distant things are established and seen as if present, then finally, with the imagination going over to the side of reason, reason becomes superior.
Let us conclude, therefore, that *Rhetoric* ought not to be blamed more for knowing how to adorn the worse part, than *Dialectic* for teaching how to construct Sophisms. For who does not know that the principle of contraries is the same, even if they are opposed in use? Furthermore, *Dialectic* differs from *Rhetoric* not only in that (as is commonly said) the one is like a fist, the other like an open hand; (the one, that is, treats things concisely, the other expansively;) but much more in that *Dialectic* considers reason in its Natural state; *Rhetoric*, as it is situated in the opinions of the common people. Wisely, therefore, Aristotle places *Rhetoric, between Dialectic, and Ethics with Politics*, since it participates in both. Indeed, the proofs and demonstrations of *Dialectic* are common to all people; but the proofs and persuasions of *Rhetoric* ought to vary according to the nature of the audience; so that one, like a Musician adapting himself to different ears, finally becomes
*Orpheus in the woods, Arion among the dolphins.*
R 3 Quæ

--- Page 392 ---
370          ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING.
This application and variation of speech (if one desires its perfection and summit) ought to extend so far that if the very same things are to be said among different people, yet among individuals, different and different words must be used. Although it is certain that the greatest orators are for the most part deficient in this part of eloquence (namely Political and Business-like, in private conversations); while pursuing ornament and elegant forms of speech, they miss that fluent application and characteristics of discourse, which it would be more advisable to use for each individual. Certainly, it would not be amiss, concerning this very thing of which we are now speaking, to institute a new inquiry, and to designate it by the name *Prudence of private discourse*, and to place it among the *Desiderata*: A thing certainly, which the more attentively one considers, the more highly one will value it. Whether indeed this is placed among *Rhetoric* or *Politics*, matters not much.

Let us now descend to the *desiderata* in this *art*, which (as we said before) are of such a kind that they ought to be considered rather as *Appendices* than as portions of the art itself, and all pertain to the *Storehouse*. First therefore we do not find anyone who has well pursued or supplemented that prudence, and at the same time diligence, of Aristotle. He indeed began to collect *popular signs*, or *colors of apparent good and evil, both simple and comparative*, which are truly *Rhetorical Sophisms*. But they are of excellent use, especially for business, and the prudence of private discourse. But the labors of Aristotle concerning these colors in three clau-

--- Page 393 ---
L I B E R VI. 371
Firstly, because although there are many (of them), he enumerates very few. Secondly, because they do not have their Elenchi (refutations) appended. Thirdly, because he seems to have partly ignored their use. For their use serves not so much for proving as for affecting and moving (emotions). Indeed, many forms of speech, which signify the same thing, nevertheless affect differently. For that which is sharpened penetrates much more strongly than that which is blunt; although in the striking itself, the forces are applied equally. Certainly, there is no one who is not more affected hearing, *Your enemies will achieve wondrous triumphs from this;*
*This the Ithacan would wish, and the Atridae would buy it at a great price;*
than if it is simply said, *This will be inconvenient for your affairs.* Therefore, these points and stings of speech are by no means to be neglected. But since we propose this matter as a *Desideratum*, according to our custom, we will support it with *Examples*; for *Precepts* would illustrate the matter less.
*Examples of colors of good and evil, both simple and comparative.*
Sophism.
1. *That which men praise and celebrate, is Good; that which they blame and reprehend, is Evil.*
Elenchus.
The *Sophism* is fallacious in four ways, namely, Either because of ignorance; Or because of bad faith; Or because of biases and factions; Or because of the character of those who praise and blame—
R 4

372          ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING.
of those who praise and blame. Because of *ignorance*; What is the judgment of the common people for the examination of good and evil? Better Phocion, who, when the people applauded him more than usual, asked, *Had he perhaps committed a fault?* Because of *bad faith*; For those who praise and those who blame often act for their own interest, and do not speak as they think.
    *He praises marketable goods, who wishes to push out his*
        *wares.*
Likewise; *It is bad, it is bad, says the Buyer; but when he has*
*gone away, then he will boast.* Because of *factions*; For it is clear to everyone that men are accustomed to extol with excessive praises those who are of their own party; but to depress below their merit those who are of opposing parties. Because of *dispositions*; For some are by nature made and disposed to servile flattery; Others, on the contrary, are fault-finders and morose; So that in praising and blaming, they only indulge their own dispositions, little concerned with the truth.
        Sophism.
2. *What is praised even by enemies, is a great good; but*
*what is blamed even by friends, is a great evil.*
This Sophism seems to rest on this foundation, that what we say unwillingly and against the affection and inclination of our mind, that very thing is easily believed to extort the force of truth from us.
        Elenchus.
The Sophism is fallacious because of the cunning, both of enemies and of friends. For enemies sometimes bestow praises, not unwillingly, nor by the

--- Page 395 ---

compelled by the force of truth, but nevertheless choosing those things which might stir up envy and dangers for their enemies. And so among the Greeks a certain superstition became prevalent, that they believed, if someone were praised by another, with a malevolent mind and the intention of harming, *a pustule was accustomed to grow on his nostrils.* It deceives again, because enemies sometimes bestow praises as certain prefaces, so that afterwards they might calumniate more freely and maliciously. On the other hand, this Sophism also deceives because of the cunning of *Friends*. For they too are accustomed to acknowledge and declare the faults of friends sometimes, not because any force of Truth compels them; but choosing those things which can least harm their friends, as if in other respects they were indeed excellent men. It deceives again, because *Friends* also use their criticisms (just as we said about the praises of *Enemies*) as certain prefaces, so that a little later they may burst forth more effusively into praises.

Sophism,
3. *Whose deprivation is good, that thing itself is Evil; whose deprivation is evil, that thing itself is Good.*
Refutation.
The *Sophism* deceives in two ways: Either because of the *comparison of good and evil:* Or because of the *succession of good to good, or evil to evil.*
Because of *comparison:* If it was good for the human race to be deprived of eating acorns, it does not follow that that thing was evil; but *Dodona* was good, *Ceres* better. Nor if it was bad for the people of Syracuse to be deprived of Dionysius the Elder,

Nor does the privation of some evil always give place
to good, but sometimes to a greater evil. For with the enemy
Clodius removed, Milo at the same time lost his harvest of
glory.
                Sophism.

  This is almost the nature of things, that those which

Since each thing rejoices to associate friends with itself, and to

*Sophism.*

The foundation, however, of this sophism is;
That human actions are so uncertain, and
exposed to dangers, that that seems best
which has the most escapes. To this refer those
formulas which are in use, *You will render yourself plainly bound and*
*restricted: You will not take as much as you*

                              *Refutation.*
  The sophism fails first, because in human
actions fortune urges that something at last be decided.
For as it has been elegantly said by someone;
*Even not to decide, is to decide something:*
So much so that very often the suspension of counsel involves
us in more necessities than if we had
decided something. This seems to be a certain disease
of the mind, similar to that which is found in misers: But
transferred from the desire of retaining wealth; to the desire
of retaining free will and power. Indeed,
the miser does not wish to enjoy, lest anything be subtracted
from the sum; So also a skeptic of this kind wishes to execute nothing,
so that all things may remain whole for him. It fails secondly,
because necessity, and that (which they say) *The die is*
*cast*, adds spurs to minds: as he says:
*Equal to others, you are certainly superior by necessity.*

For, just as we see it happen, that when a fault has been committed, and the perpetrator is unknown, men become excessively enraged and agitated: but if it afterwards comes to be known, that fault to the son

L I B E R VI. 381
*The degree of inception seems greater than the degree of increment.*
   There is a rule in Mathematics: that there are no ratios of nothing to something. Therefore, the degrees of nullity and quiddity seem greater than the degrees of increment and decrement. Just as it is harder for a one-eyed person to lose one eye than for someone having both eyes [to lose one]. Similarly, for someone having several children, it is more grievous to lose the last son who survived, than the remaining earlier ones. And so Sibyl, when she had burned the two previous books, doubled the price of the third: since the loss of that [book] would have been a degree of *privation*, *not diminution*.
*Refutation.*
   The *Sophism* fails first, because of those things whose use consists in a certain sufficiency, or competence, that is, a determined Quantity. For if someone is penalised to pay a certain sum of money by a certain day; it would be more grievous for him to lack a single gold coin, than if, supposing that single one could not be procured, ten others were also missing. Similarly, in the ruin of fortunes, the degree of indebtedness, which first diminishes the principal, seems more damaging; than the last, which reduces [one] to poverty. To this point refer those common sayings; *Parsimony is late at the bottom [of the barrel]: There is little difference whether you have nothing, or what helps nothing, etc.* It fails secondly, because of that Principle in nature; that *the corruption of one is the generation of another.* So much so that the very degree of ultimate *privation*, sometimes less...

--- Page 404 ---
382 ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF SCIENCES.
while it causes inconvenience; because it offers an opportunity and a stimulus for undertaking some new course of action. Hence also Demosthenes often complains among his citizens; *that the less useful and honorable conditions, which they endured imposed by Philip, were nothing other than certain nourishment for their own idleness and sloth; so that it would have been much better for them to be entirely without them, because in this way their industry could be better sharpened for preparing other remedies.* We certainly know a certain Physician, who, to delicate women complaining that they were ill, but nevertheless abhorred all medicines, used to say, no less wittily than peevishly: *You absolutely need to be worse, so that you may willingly tolerate any medicines, even of any kind. Moreover, the very degree of ultimate privation, or indigence, can be salutary, not only for exciting industry, but also for commanding patience.*

As for the second member of this Sophism; that relies on the same foundation as before (concerning the degrees of quiddity and nullity). Hence such great praises are employed concerning the beginnings of undertakings.
*He who has well begun, has half done, etc.*
Hence the superstition of Astrologers, who make a judgment about a person's disposition or fortune, from the moment or point of birth, or conception.

*Refutation.*
The sophism fails first, because in some

--- Page 405 ---
L I B E R VI. 383
...in some cases the first beginnings of things are nothing other than what Epicurus, in his Philosophy, calls *tentamenta*; that is, certain rudiments, which are nothing unless they are repeated or advanced. Therefore in this case, the second step seems more worthy and more powerful than the first: Just as in wagons, the horse which is second to last contributes more to the movement of the wagon than the first. It is also aptly said; *'A returned insult is that which is guilty of a fight.'* For the former perhaps would have flown past. Therefore *the former gave a beginning to evil, but the latter took away the limit.* The Sophism is fallacious secondly, because of the dignity of perseverance; which lies in progress, not in initial attack. For chance or nature can produce the first impulse; but only mature affection and judgment (produce) constancy. It is fallacious thirdly in those things whose nature and ordinary course are carried contrary to the thing begun. So that the first beginning is perpetually rendered void, unless the forces are continued. Just as it is said in those usual formulas; *'Not to advance, is to retreat: And, He who does not profit, fails:'* As in running uphill; (or) rowing against the current: But on the contrary, if movement begins on the slope of a mountain (downhill); or if rowing is done with the current; then the *initiated step* plays a much more powerful role. Furthermore, that *color* is not only extended to the *degree of inception, which is from potentiality to actuality, compared with the degree which is from actuality to increment:* But also to the *degree which is from Impotence to potency, compared*

The refutation, however, is as follows. Granted, that virtue (especially that which undergoes labors and conflicts) would not be chosen, unless praises and fame were accustomed to accompany it; it does not therefore follow that the appetite and impulse towards virtue is not primarily for its own sake. Indeed, fame can be merely an impulsive cause, or a *sine qua non* (that without which not), by no means an efficient or constitutive cause. For example: If there were two horses, one of which, without spurs being applied, would perform everything not sluggishly: but the other; with spurs applied, would far surpass the former: That latter one (I believe) would carry off the prize, and would be judged as the better horse. Nor would that saying move anyone of sound judgment; Away with that horse, whose spirit is thirsty for spurs. For since the spur is the ordinary instrument for a rider, and is in no way a burden or hindrance to him; the horse which is spurred on is not therefore to be esteemed less: Nor indeed the other,

Sophism.
11. *That which is acquired by our own work and virtue is a greater good; that which is bestowed by another's benefit, or by the indulgence of fortune, is a lesser good.*

The reasons for this are these. First, because of *hope for the future*. For indeed, in the favor of others, or in the favorable winds of fortune itself, there is not much certainty; but one's own industry, or virtue, are always at hand. So much so that, after something good has been prepared for us in this way, the same instruments also remain, prepared for new uses, and indeed rendered stronger by habit and success.

Secondly, because that which we acquire *by another's benefit*, of that we are also *debtors to others*; whereas, what we ourselves have acquired, carries no burden with it. Even if divine indulgence has heaped anything upon us, it demands a certain retribution towards God's Goodness. This bites wicked and depraved men, when in the former kind that of the Prophet has come to pass: *They rejoice, and exult, they sacrifice to their traps, and sacrifice to their net.*

Thirdly, because *those things which have not at all proceeded from our virtue, no praise and estimation follow*. For those things which are of fortune, they produce a certain admiration, but by no means praise. As Cicero says to Caesar: *What we may admire, we have; what we may praise, we await.*

Fourthly, because those things which *are acquired by one's own industry*, are almost *joined with labors and struggle*; which has in itself a certain *sweetness*; as Solomon says, *Sweet is food from hunting.*

Elen-

--- Page 409 ---
L I B E R VI.        387
*Elenchus.*

But four opposite arguments are found, which incline the matter to the contrary side; and these can serve as refutations to the former ones. Firstly, because happiness seems to be a certain sign and mark of divine favor; and therefore, it generates both confidence and alacrity in ourselves, and authority and reverence among others. But this happiness also embraces fortuitous things, to which virtue hardly aspires; as when Caesar, encouraging the Ship's Pilot, said: "You carry Caesar, and his fortune." But if he had said, "You carry Caesar, and his virtue," it would have been a completely cold comfort to one in danger in a storm.

Secondly, because those things which proceed from virtue or industry are imitable, and open to others; whereas happiness is an inimitable thing, and a certain prerogative of an individual person. Therefore, in general, we see natural things preferred to artificial ones, because they do not admit imitation. For what is imitable is potentially vulgarized.

Thirdly, those things which arise from happiness seem to be gratuitous goods, not bought by labors; but those which are from one's own virtue are as if acquired at a price. Therefore, Plutarch elegantly, when comparing the affairs of Timoleon, a man by far the most fortunate, with the affairs of Agesilaus and Epaminondas, who lived in the same age, said: that those were like Homer's poems, which, while they excel in other ways, also seem to flow spontaneously, and as it were, taste of genius.

Fourthly, because what happens beyond hope or beyond expectation is more pleasing, and with greater...

--- Page 410 ---
388      Oɴ ᴛʜᴇ Aᴅᴠᴀɴᴄᴇᴍᴇɴᴛ ᴏғ Lᴇᴀʀɴɪɴɢ
*with greater pleasure flows into the minds of men. But that by no means applies to those things which are acquired by one's own care and ambition.*
               Sophism.
   12. *That which consists of many and divisible parts is greater than that which consists of fewer and is more unified: For all things considered part by part seem greater: Therefore, a plurality of parts also presents magnitude: But a plurality of parts operates more strongly if order is absent: For it induces a likeness of the infinite, and hinders comprehension.*
   This sophism seems fallacious even at first glance, and as it were palpable: Indeed, not merely a plurality of parts, but their greater size, will be able to constitute a larger whole. Nevertheless, this very sophism often carries away the imagination; indeed, it even ensnares the senses. For to the sight, a path seems shorter on a plain where nothing intervenes to break the view, than in such a stretch of land where trees, or buildings, or some other sign that can measure and divide the space are simultaneously seen. Thus, for a wealthy person, after he has divided and arranged his chests and purses, a greater imagination of wealth comes to him than before. It also has power in amplifications, if a thing is divided into more portions, and each is treated separately. But this fills the imagination even more if it is done indiscriminately and without order. For the confusion of multitude generates opinion. Indeed, those things which are shown in order, or are proposed...

--- Page 411 ---
L I B E R. VI. 389
...presented in order, then they themselves appear more finite, and then they provide a certain argument that nothing has been omitted. But on the contrary, things that are represented confusedly are not only thought to be numerous in themselves, but also leave room for the suspicion that there are still more things remaining which are omitted.

_Elenchus._

_The Sophism Fails._ Firstly, when someone has conceived a more amplified opinion about something than corresponds to the true magnitude of the thing itself. For when this is the case, distribution will destroy that false opinion, and will show the thing in its truth, not with amplification. Therefore, if someone is seized by illness or pain, the hours will seem longer to them without a clock or water-clock, than if they are measured by these. For if the weariness and vexation of illness make time seem longer than it truly is, yet the computation of time corrects that error, and makes it shorter than that false opinion had conceived. Also on a plain, contrary to what was said above, it sometimes happens. For although sight at first shows the way to be shorter to the sense, because it is undivided: yet if from this an opinion creeps in about a much smaller interval than is found: the frustration of that vain opinion will cause it to appear in the end even longer than it truly is. Therefore, if someone wishes to support someone's false opinion about the magnitude of something, let him beware of distributions, but by all means extol the thing as a whole. _The Sophism Fails_ secondly, if that distribution is drawn out, and not presented simultaneously, or in a single
S glance

--- Page 412 ---
390          ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING.
or strikes the sight in one aspect. Therefore, if flowers in some garden are divided into several beds, they will present the appearance of a greater quantity than if all grew together in one bed; Provided that those beds are simultaneously subjected to the eyes; For otherwise, unity will prevail over distracted distribution. Thus, the incomes of those seem greater for whom their estates and large landholdings are neighboring or conjoined. For if they are situated scattered, they do not come so easily into view. Thirdly, the Sophism is misleading, because of the dignity of unity, above multitude. For every composition is a most certain sign of want in the individual parts; where that applies:

    *And what are not useful individually, are useful in multitude.*

Therefore, Mary's part is better; *Martha, Martha, you are anxious about many things, one thing is sufficient.* Hence that fable of Aesop about the fox and the cat: for the fox boasted how many tricks and escapes it had, by which it might save itself from dogs; But the cat said that it trusted in only one aid, inasmuch as it had the simple ability to climb. Which, however, was a far more excellent defense than those other foxy ones: whence the Adage; *The fox knows many things, but the cat knows one great thing.* Moreover, the same is perceived in the moral meaning of this fable: For to rely on a powerful and faithful friend has more protection than very many tricks and cunning devices.

The second *Collection, which pertains to a storehouse and is desired*, is that which Cicero (as we said above in *Logic*) hints at; when he prescribes that *Commonplaces* be held in readiness, debated and treated on both sides. Such are, *For the words of the law* and *For the spirit of the law*, etc. We, however, extend this precept also to other matters; so that it may be applied not only to the judicial genre, but also to the deliberative and demonstrative. In short, we wish that all *Commonplaces*, of which there is frequent use (whether they pertain to proofs and refutations, or to persuasions and dissuasions, or to praises and censures), should already be meditated upon, and that they should be raised and lowered with the utmost powers of intellect, and as if improperly, and entirely contrary to truth. We deem the best method for this

--- Page 441 ---
L I B E R V I. 419

The third Collection, which belongs to the promptuary and is also needed, is that which it pleases us to call Minor Formulas. These, moreover, are, as it were, vestibules, back doors, antechambers, inner chambers, passages, etc., of discourse, which can indiscriminately apply to all subjects. Such are prefaces, conclusions, digressions, transitions, promises, evasions, and many things of this kind. For just as in buildings it contributes greatly both to pleasure and to utility that frontispieces, steps, doors, windows, entrances, passages, and suchlike be conveniently distributed; in the same way it happens also in discourse that these additions and interpositions (if they are gracefully and skillfully formed and placed) add much both of grace and of convenience to the structure of the entire discourse. We will propose one or two examples of these Formulas, nor will we dwell on them any longer. For although they are things of no small use, yet since we add nothing of our own in these, but merely describe bare formulas from Demosthenes, or Cicero, or some other selected Author, they seem somewhat inferior for us to spend time on them.

C H A P. I V.

*Two General Traditional Appendices: Critical, & Pedagogical.*

**T**here remain two *Traditional* appendices in general;
one *Critical*, the other *Pedagogical*. For just as the principal
*Traditional* part consists in the *Writing of Books*,
so its relative part is concerned with the *Reading of Books*:
but *Reading* is either guided by the help of Masters, or perfected
by each person's own industry; and to this end serve those two
*Doctrines* which we have mentioned.
To *Criticism* pertain, first, the *refined Correction of approved*
*Authors*, and their *amended Edition*; by which both the honor
of the Authors themselves is vindicated, and light is offered to Students.
In which matter, however, it has brought no small detriment to
                                                                           studies.

--- Page 443 ---
L I B E R VII. 421
...has been brought by the rash diligence of certain men. For it is the custom of not a few *Critics*, when they encounter something they do not understand, to immediately assume a fault in the manuscript. As for example in that passage of Tacitus: When a certain Colony asserted the right of Asylum before the Senate, Tacitus relates that what they put forward was heard by the Emperor and Senate with not very favorable ears: Therefore the Legates, distrusting their cause, gave a good sum of money to Titus Vinius, so that he might advocate for them. And so in this way the matter was obtained: "*Then*" (says Tacitus) "*the Dignity and Antiquity of the Colony prevailed:*" as if the arguments, which previously seemed slight, had then received new weight with the addition of a price. But a certain *Critic*, and not one of the lowest rank, expunged the word "*Tum*" and replaced it with "*Tantum*". And by this depraved custom of *Critics* it has come to pass that (as someone wisely noted) "*the most thoroughly corrected manuscripts are very often the least pure of all.*" Indeed, to speak the truth, unless *Critics* are learned in those Sciences of which the Books edited by them treat, their diligence is not free from danger.

Secondly, pertaining to Criticism are, *the Interpretation & Explanation of Authors, Commentaries, Scholia, Notes, Spicilegia,* and similar works. However, in labors of this kind, that worst sort of disease has, as it were, invaded some *Critics*, so that they skip over many of the more obscure points, but dwell and expatiate to the point of tedium on those that are sufficiently clear. Evidently, the aim is not so much that the Author himself be illuminated, as that the *Critic* in question may show his mani-

T 5
fold

--- Page 444 ---
422      ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING.
his manifold erudition and varied reading, seizing every opportunity. It would be especially desirable (although this matter pertains to the principal Traditive [method of delivery], not to appendices) that the Writer who treats more obscure and nobler arguments should himself subjoin his own explanations; so that the text itself is not broken up by digressions or explanations; and that the Notes do not depart from the Writer's mind. We suspect something of this kind concerning *Theon of Euclid*.

Thirdly, it pertains to Criticism (which also gave it its name) *to interpose some brief judgment concerning the Authors they edit;* and to compare them with other Writers who treat the same subjects; so that by such a judgment students may be advised both concerning the choice of books, and may approach their reading itself better instructed. And this last point is, as it were, the *Chair* of *Critics*, which certainly in our age some great Men have obliterated, greater certainly, in our judgment, than befits the measure of *Critics*.

As far as *Pedagogy* is concerned, it would be very brief to say; *Consult the Schools of the Jesuits:* For nothing that has come into use is better than these. We, however, will advise a few things in our own manner, as if gleaning ears of corn. We entirely *approve of collegiate instruction for childhood and youth;* Not in private homes; Not merely under private tutors. There is for adolescents in *Colleges* a greater emulation towards their peers; There is also the very countenance and appeara-

--- Page 445 ---
L I B E R VI. 423.
aspect of serious men; which conduces to modesty, and from the very beginning shapes tender minds to an example: Finally, there are indeed many advantages of *collegiate education*. However, regarding the order and method of instruction, I would primarily advise this: that one beware of *shortcuts*; and of a *certain precocity of doctrine*, which renders intellects audacious, and rather displays great progress than actually makes it. Moreover, some favor should be shown to *the liberty of intellects*, so that if someone does what is customary in instruction, and at the same time steals away time for other things to which he is inclined, he should by no means be restrained. Furthermore, it would be worthwhile to diligently observe (which perhaps has not yet been noted) that there are two methods of *accustoming, exercising, and preparing intellects*, and these as it were *contrasting*. *One begins with easier things, and gradually leads to more arduous ones; The other from the beginning commands and urges harder things*, so that once these are mastered, one can even pleasantly immerse oneself in easier things. For one *Method* is to begin swimming with bladders, which support; Another is to begin dancing with heavy shoes, which weigh down. Nor is it easy to say how much a prudent intermixture of *Methods* contributes to advancing the faculties, both of mind and body. Likewise, the *application and selection of studies*, according to the nature of the intellects being educated, is a matter of singular use and judgment; which Masters also owe to the parents of adolescents, well and truly noted and observed; so that concerning the kind of life to which they destine
T 6 their sons,

--- Page 446 ---
424 ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING.
(so that they might) consult. But, and that too must be observed a little more attentively, that not only in those things to which each person is led by their own nature, are by far the greatest advancements made; but also in those things for which someone might be most unfitted by a defect of nature, remedies and cures are found in studies specifically chosen for this purpose. For example; If someone's intellect is such, as that of birds, so that it is easily carried away, nor can it sustain a discovery for the proper duration; *Mathematics* will provide a remedy for this, in which if the mind wanders a little, the demonstration must be renewed from the beginning. Also, it is clear that the role of *exercises* in education is very great. But that has been noted by few, that there ought to be not only a prudent institution of *exercises*, but also a prudent intermission. Indeed, Cicero very well noted, *that in exercises it generally happens that vices are exercised no less than faculties*; so much so that a bad habit is sometimes acquired simultaneously and insinuates itself with the good. Therefore, it is safer to intermit exercises, and repeat them from time to time, than to continue and urge them assiduously.

But enough of these things. Certainly, these things are at first glance less grand and solemn, but nevertheless fruitful and effective. For just as in plants, for their happiness or unhappiness, injuries or aids which befell them when they were tender, contribute greatly; just as also those immense growths of the Roman Empire are rightly attributed by some to the virtue and prudence of those six Kings, who were, as it were, Tutors to it in its infancy.

--- Page 447 ---

as guardians or nurses. Thus, certainly, the cultivation and instruction of childish or tender years possesses powers, though latent and scarcely noticed by anyone, which neither the passage of time nor the assiduousness and intensity of later efforts in a more mature age can in any way equal. It will not be out of place also to note that even mediocre faculties, if they fall upon great men or great matters, sometimes produce grave and signal effects. We will set forth a memorable example of this; which we adduce all the more because the Jesuits do not seem to despise this same discipline, with sound judgment (as it seems to us). And a thing which, if it is professional, is infamous: but made disciplinary, it is among the best. We mean, however, *Theatrical Action.* For it strengthens memory; tempers the tone and efficacy of voice and pronunciation; composes the countenance and gesture to decorum; conciliates no small confidence; and finally accustoms youths to the eyes of men. The example will be taken from Tacitus, concerning a certain *Vebulenus*, formerly an actor, but at that time serving in the Pannonian Legions. He, at the death of Augustus, had stirred up a sedition; so that Blaesus the prefect cast some of the seditious into prison. But the soldiers, having made an assault, freed them by breaking open the prisons. But Vibulenus, haranguing among the soldiers, thus began: "You (he said) have restored light and breath to these innocent and most wretched men: But who restores life to my brother, who restores my brother to me?"

*Not even enemies begrudge burial.*
*When I have filled my grief with kisses, with tears,*
*order me also to be slaughtered, provided that those who have been killed,*
*for no crime, but because we consulted for the benefit of the Legions,*
*may be buried by these men. By these words he stirred up*
*an excessive amount of envy and consternation.*
*So much so that, had it not shortly afterwards become known that*
*none of these things had happened, and indeed that he never had a brother,*
*the Soldiers would scarcely have kept their hands off the Prefect:*
*He, however, performed the whole affair as if it were*
*a play on stage.*
   Now indeed, we have arrived at the conclusion
of our treatise on rational doctrines. In
which, although we have sometimes departed from accepted *divisions*;
let no one however suppose that we disapprove of all
those *divisions* which we have not used.
For a twofold necessity is imposed upon us
for changing *divisions*: One, because these two things,
namely, to reduce things naturally related into one class,
and to cast things to be brought forth for use
into one heap, are, in themselves and in intention,
entirely different. For example, some *Secretary*
of a *King* or *Republic* undoubtedly arranges his papers in a museum
in such a way; that those which are of a similar
Nature, he puts together, such as treaties separately,
mandates separately; letters from *Foreigners*, domestic
letters, and similar things, all separately. On the
contrary, in some particular cabinet, he puts them together,

--- Page 449 ---
L I B E R VI. 427
places, which, although they are of different kinds, he nevertheless
considers will be useful at the same time: Thus indeed, in this
universal Repository of knowledge, for us, classifications
had to be established according to the nature of the things themselves:
whereas however, if some particular Science
had to be dealt with, we would have followed classifications
rather adapted to use and practice. The second
necessity for changing classifications is, because the addition
of *Desiderata* to the Sciences, and their reduction
with the rest into a complete body, also,
consequently, has shifted the classifications of the *Sciences themselves*.
For (for the sake of demonstration), suppose that the arts
which exist are represented by the Number 15; but with the *Desiderata*
added, by the Number 20. I say that the parts of the Number 15
are not the same parts as those of the Number 20. For the parts
of the Number 15 are 3 and 5. But the parts of the Number 20
are 2, 4, 5, and 10. Therefore it is clear that these things
could not have been done otherwise. And let these things be said
concerning the *Logical Sciences*.

Let us discuss, as much as we please, that moral virtues in the human mind are habitual, not natural: Let us solemnly distinguish between noble spirits and the ignoble common people, that the former are led by the force of reasons, the latter by reward or punishment: Let us ingeniously prescribe that the human mind, to be rectified, ought to be bent like a stick in the opposite direction of its inclination: And let us moreover scatter other things of this kind here and there: Yet it is far from the case that these and other things of that kind excuse the absence of the thing which we now require.

I believe the cause of this neglect to be no other than that hidden rock, against which so many little ships of *Science*, striking, have suffered shipwreck: Namely, that writers disdain to occupy themselves with common and plebeian matters, which are neither subtle enough for disputation, nor illustrious enough for embellishment.    There has been implanted and impressed in every thing an appetite for a twofold *nature of good*; The one, by which *a thing is a whole in itself*: The other, by which *it is part of some greater whole*. And this latter is more worthy and more powerful than the former, since it tends to the conservation of a *more ample form*. Let the first be named, *individual good, or of self-ness*: the latter, *good of communion*. Iron is borne by a particular sympathy to the magnet: but if it is a little heavier, it abandons those affections, and like a good citizen and lover of its country, it seeks the earth, that is, the region of its kindred. Let us proceed a little further; Dense and heavy bodies seek the earth, a great congregation of dense bodies: Nevertheless, rather than the nature of things suffer a divulsion, and a *vacuum* be given (as they say), bodies of this kind will be carried upwards, and will cease from their duty *towards the earth*, so that they may perform their duty owed *to the World itself*. So it almost perpetually holds, that the *Conservation of the more Common Form* brings lesser Appetites into order. But this Prerogative of the *Good of Communion* is especially marked in man, if he has not degenerated, according to that memorable saying of Pompey the Great, who, at a time when famine was pressing upon Rome, having been put in charge of importing grain, but vehemently urged by his friends not to commit himself to the sea, as a fierce storm was approaching, responded only that, "*It is necessary that I go; not that I live*": So that the desire for life (which is greatest in the individual) [is subordinated] to love and faith in the Republic.

Furthermore, he also refutes the *Philosophy of Epictetus*, who uses this presupposition: that happiness ought to be placed in those things which are in our power, lest indeed we be subject to fortune and chance; as if, truly, it would not have been much happier to be deprived of success and frustrated in right and noble intentions and ends which embrace the public good, than to perpetually achieve one's wish in all things which relate only to our private fortune! He likewise refutes that abuse of *Philosophy* which began to spread around the time of Epictetus: Namely, that Philosophy had been turned into a kind of professional way of life, and as it were, into an Art; As if indeed the purpose of Philosophy were not that disturbances should be restrained and extinguished, but that their causes and occasions should be avoided and removed: Therefore

But if it is dear to men's hearts to pursue the duties of society, then that health, finally, is most to be sought after, which can bear and overcome any changes whatsoever and any impulses whatsoever. In the same way, that mind, finally, is to be considered truly and properly sound and strong, which can break through very many and very great temptations and perturbations. So that Diogenes seems to have spoken most excellently; who praised those strengths of mind *which were strong not for cautiously abstaining, but for bravely enduring;* and which can restrain the mind's impulse, even in the greatest extremities; and which (that which is praised in well-trained horses) ensure that in the shortest space they can both stop themselves and turn.

Finally, he also refutes a certain *tenderness* and *unsuitability for compliance,* noted in some of the most ancient Philosophers, and especially in those held in veneration: Who too easily withdrew themselves from civil affairs, so that they might rid themselves of indignities and perturbations, and might live more, in their own opinion, unblemished, and as if sacrosanct: Whereas it would be consistent that the constancy of a truly Moral man would be such,

C H A P.  II.

*Division of Individual Good, or of Self-Good, into Active*
*Good, and Passive Good. Division of Passive Good, into*
*Conservative Good, and Perfective Good.*
*Division of the Good of Communion into General Duties, and*
*Respective Duties.*

Let us therefore now repeat, and pursue first the *individual*
*good*, and *of self-good*. That we will divide into *active good*,
and *passive good*. For this difference of good also (not
unlike certainly those appellations which the Romans in
Economics were familiar with, namely *Promus* and *Condus*)
is found impressed in the whole nature of things: But it
especially reveals itself in the twofold appetite of created
things: the one, *of conserving oneself and fortifying oneself*:
the other, *of multiplying oneself and propagating oneself*: And
this latter, which is *active*, and as it were a *Promus*, seems
more powerful and more worthy: But that former, which is
*passive*, and as it were a *Condus*, can be considered inferior.
For in the universality of things, celestial nature is especially
*active*; but terrestrial nature, *passive*. Also in the delights
of living beings, there is greater pleasure in generating than
in feeding. Also in divine oracles it is pronounced, *It is more*
*blessed to give, than to receive*. Indeed, even in common life,
no one is found of so soft and effeminate a disposition, who
does not value more something that was in his wishes,
                                     V                      perfi-

--- Page 463 ---
LIBER VII. 441
to accomplish and bring to completion, rather than some sensuality or delight. And indeed, this preeminence of *active good* is immensely magnified, when considering the human condition, which is both mortal and exposed to the blows of fortune. For if permanence and certainty could be obtained in human pleasures, great value would accrue to them, due to their security and duration. But since we see the matter come down to this: *We greatly value dying later;* and, *Do not boast about tomorrow; you do not know what the day will bring forth:* it is by no means strange if we are carried by striving towards those things which do not fear the injuries of time. But those can be none other than our works; as it is said, *Their works follow them.* There is also another not insignificant preeminence of *active good*, implanted and sustained by that affection which, as an inseparable companion, adheres to human nature's side: namely, the love of novelty, or variety. But that (love of novelty/variety) is very narrow in the pleasures of the senses (which are indeed the greatest part of *passive good*), nor does it have any significant breadth: *Consider how long you have done the same things; Food, sleep, play; one runs through this circle. To wish to die, not only a brave man, or a wretched man, or a prudent man, but also a disgusted man can.* But in the actions of our life, and in our pursuits, and ambitions, there is significant variety; And this is perceived with much pleasure, while we begin, we advance, we rest intermittently, we retreat to increase our strength, we approach, finally we obtain, and so on;

So that it has been very truly said, *Life without purpose,*
*is languid and aimless.* Which applies equally
to the prudent and the most foolish, as Solomon says; *The*
*fool seeks according to his desire, he meddles in everything.*
Moreover, we see that very powerful Kings,
at whose nod whatever is pleasing to the senses

*Chariot-driving* for *Antoninus*, and other things for others)
which nevertheless were to them more potent than all abundance

that we do something, than that we enjoy.
   Meanwhile, it must be noted a little more carefully,
that *active, individual good* differs entirely *from the good*
*of communion*; although sometimes both coincide.
For although *this individual, active good* often gives birth
to and produces works of beneficence (*which is from the virtues
of communion*); yet it makes a difference that
those works are done by most men, not with the intention
of helping or blessing others, but plainly for themselves
and their own power and greatness.
This is best seen, when *active good* impinges
upon something that is contrary *to the good of communion*.
Indeed, that gigantic condition of mind, by which those great
disturbers of the world are carried away, (such as L. Sulla, and
many others, though in a much smaller degree: who
seem to aspire to this, that all should be happy or
miserable, according as they have been friends or enemies
                                                                      to them;

--- Page 465 ---

enemies; and that the world, as it were, should bear their image: which is true *Theomathia*), this very thing, I say, aspires to *active good*, individual, at least *apparent*, even if it departs most widely from the *good of communion of all*.

But we shall divide *Passive Good* into *Conservative Good* and *Perfective Good*. For a threefold appetite is implanted in every thing, insofar as it pertains to the *Good of its own Being, or of the individual*. First, that it *preserves* itself: Second, that it *perfects* itself. Third, that it *multiplies itself, or diffuses itself*. And this last appetite is referred to *active good*, of which we have just spoken. Therefore, only the remaining two goods, which we mentioned, are left. Of these, the *perfective* excels. For it is a lesser thing to preserve a thing in its own state: but a greater thing, to raise it to a higher nature. Indeed, throughout all things, some nobler natures are found, to whose dignity and excellence, inferior natures aspire, as if to their origins and sources. Thus, he sang not badly of men:
*Fiery is their vigor, and heavenly their origin.*
For to man, the assumption or approximation to the Divine or Angelic nature, is the perfection of his form. Indeed, the corrupt and preposterous imitation of this *perfective good* is the very plague of human life, and a certain rapid whirlwind, which snatches away and overturns everything. Too much, while men, instead of formal and essential exaltation, fly with blind ambition to merely local exaltation. For just as the sick, V 4 reme-

--- Page 466 ---
444 ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING.
not finding a remedy for their ill, toss and turn their body from place to place; as if by change of place they could depart from themselves and escape their internal ill: In the same way it happens in ambition, that men, carried away by a certain false image of exalting their nature, acquire nothing else than a certain height and pinnacle of place.
     But the *Conservative Good* is nothing else than the reception and enjoyment of *things congruent with our nature*. This good, although it is most simple and native, nevertheless seems the softest and lowest of goods. Indeed, this very *Good* admits of some distinction, concerning which partly the judgment of men has wavered, partly inquiry has been omitted. For the dignity and commendation of the Good of *enjoyment*, or, as it is commonly called, of *pleasure*, is situated either in the *sincerity of enjoyment*, or in its *vigor*: Of these, the one is induced and afforded by *uniformity*, the other by *variety and change*: The one has a lesser mixture of evil, the other a stronger and more vivid impression of good. Moreover, which of these is better, is debated: Then, whether human nature can retain both at once within itself, *is not inquired into*.
     And as to that, about which it is debated, that controversy between Socrates and a certain Sophist began to be aired. And Socrates indeed asserted, *that happiness consists in constant peace and tranquility of mind:* but the sophist in this, *That one should desire much, and enjoy much.*

--- Page 467 ---
LIBER VII. 445
...the Sophist, however, in this, *that one should desire much, and enjoy much.* Indeed, they even descended from arguments to insults; the Sophist saying, '*Socrates' happiness is the happiness of a log or a stone;*' and Socrates, on the contrary, saying, '*The Sophist's happiness is that of a person with scabies, who is perpetually itching and scratching.*' Yet neither opinion lacks its own foundations. For even the Epicurean School itself assents to Socrates, which did not deny that virtue plays the greatest part in happiness. And if this is so, it is more certain than certain that virtue has greater use in calming disturbances than in acquiring desired things. To the Sophist, however, that assertion seems to lend some support, *which we just mentioned, namely that perfective good is superior to conservative good;* since the acquisition of desired things seems gradually to perfect nature: which, although they may not truly do so, nevertheless the very movement in a circle presents some appearance of *progressive movement.*

But the second question, (*namely, whether human nature cannot retain both tranquility of mind and vigor of enjoyment at the same time?*) being rightly defined, renders that former one idle and superfluous. For do we not often see the minds of some people so made and composed that they are greatly affected by pleasures when they are present, and yet do not bear their loss with difficulty? So that that philosophical maxim, '*Do not use, so that you may not desire; Do not desire, so that you may not fear,*' seems to belong to a somewhat faint-hearted and distrustful mind. Indeed, most doctrines of philosophers seem to be a little too timid, and to caution humans more than the nature of things demands.

   *Who places the ultimate end of life among the gifts*

   Similarly, in all things, philosophers have striven to render the human mind too uniform and harmonious: by accustoming it least of all to contrary and extreme emotions. The reason for this, I believe, was that they themselves dedicated themselves to a private life, free and immune from business and the services of others. Rather, let men imitate the prudence of jewelers; who, if by chance some cloud or flaw is found in a gem, which could be removed in such a way that the size of the stone is not too much diminished, they remove it; otherwise, however, they leave it untouched: By the same reasoning, the serenity of minds should be consulted in such a way that magnanimity is not destroyed. And so much for *individual good* hitherto.

This part, therefore (when I recall its excellence in my mind), not yet reduced into a *body of doctrine*, I am vehemently surprised by. Therefore, according to our custom, since we place it among the *Desiderata*, we will outline it to some extent.

Therefore, before all things in this matter (as also in all things which pertain to Practice), we must determine what is in our power and what is not. For in the one, alteration is possible; but in the other, only application. The farmer has no control either over the nature of the soil or over the temperatures of the air; likewise, nor has the Physician control either over the temperament and natural constitution of the sick person, or over the variety of accidents. But in the *cultivation of the mind* and in thoroughly healing its diseases, three things come into consideration; *Diverse characters of dispositions; Affections, & Remedies:* Just as also in healing bodies, those three things are proposed: *complexion, or constitution of the sick person, disease & cure.* But of those three, only the last is within our power; the former two are not. But also in those very things which are not in our power, no less diligent inquiry must be made than in those which are subject to our power. For a clear-sighted and accurate knowledge of those must be laid as a foundation for the *doctrine of remedies*, so that the same may be applied more conveniently and successfully. For a garment cannot be fitted to the body unless the measure of the body is first taken.

Therefore, the first article, the *doctrine concerning the cultivation of the*
*mind*, will revolve around the *diverse characters of intellects or dispositions*. Nor, however, are we speaking of those common propensities towards virtues and vices, or even towards perturbations and affections; but of those more intrinsic and radical ones. Indeed, it has sometimes struck me with wonder, even in this respect, that by *Writers*, both *Ethical* and *Political*, it has for the most part been neglected or omitted; since it could shed a most brilliant ray of light upon both sciences. In the *Traditions of Astrology*, the intellects and dispositions of men are not altogether unskillfully distinguished according to the predominance of the Planets; namely, that some are made by Nature *for contemplations*; others *for civil affairs*; others *for military service*; others *for ambition*; others *for loves*; others *for arts*; others *for a varied kind of life*. Likewise, among *Poets* (Heroic, Satirical, Tragic, Comic), images of intellects are scattered everywhere, though almost with excess, and beyond the measure of truth. Moreover, this very topic, *concerning the diverse characters of intellects*, is among those things in which the common discourses of men (which very rarely, yet sometimes happens) are wiser than the books themselves. But by far the best material and store for this Treatise ought to be sought from the more prudent *Historians*: And not only from Elogies, which they are accustomed to append upon the death of some illustrious person, but much more from the entire body of *History*, whenever such a person, as it were, steps onto the stage.     That opinion of Aristotle seems to me clearly to be narrowness...

--- Page 485 ---

certain narrowness of contemplation and negligence: when he asserts that, in those actions which are natural, *Custom* can do nothing; using the example, *That if a stone is thrown a thousand times upwards, it does not even acquire an inclination to ascend spontaneously: moreover, that by seeing or hearing more often, we see or hear no better.* For although this holds true in some cases, where Nature is peremptory; (the reasons for which it is not convenient to give at present) it is nevertheless otherwise in those cases where nature, according to a certain latitude, permits intensity and remission. Indeed, he could have seen that a *Glove* a little too tight, by being frequently put on the hand, becomes looser; a *Staff*, by use and persistence, bent contrary to its natural flex, becomes curved and remains in the same state a little later; a *Voice*, by exercising, becomes more robust and sonorous; *Cold and Heat* are tolerated by custom; and many other things of the same kind. These latter two examples indeed approach the matter more closely than those adduced by himself. However, however this may be; the more true it is that *both virtues and vices consist in habit;* the more he ought to have striven to prescribe rules as to how such habits might be acquired or removed. For indeed, very many precepts could be drawn up concerning the prudent institution of exercises, no less for the mind than for the body. We shall recount a few of them.

of all things is most concise and summary, and again
most noble and efficacious, by which the mind may be formed
to virtue, and placed in a state nearest to perfection. This, moreover, is,
*That we choose the ends of life and actions, and propose to ourselves*
*those that are right and congruent with virtue, which*
*nevertheless are such that we have some ability*
*to attain them.* For if these things are assumed in their proper place:
that both the *ends of actions* are honorable and good,
and the *mind's resolve concerning attaining and obtaining them*,
is fixed and constant, it will follow that the mind continuously
turns and forms itself, in one operation, into
all virtues. And this certainly is that operation
which reflects the *work of Nature itself*, while the others
we have mentioned seem to be merely like *works of the hand*.
For just as a *Sculptor*, when he carves or
cuts some statue, only shapes the figure of that
part around which his hand is occupied, not
however of the others: (as if he shapes a face,
the rest of the body remains a rough and unformed
stone, until he also reaches that part:)
On the contrary, however, *Nature*, when it forms a flower
or an animal, simultaneously brings forth and produces
the rudiments of all parts: In the same way, when
virtues are acquired by habit, while we apply ourselves
to temperance, to fortitude or the other

--- Page 491 ---
LIBER VII. 469
in which we make little progress; but when we shall have thoroughly dedicated and devoted ourselves to *right* *& honest Ends*, whatever virtue those ends shall have commended and commanded to our mind, we shall find ourselves already imbued and predisposed with some aptitude and propensity to attain and express it. And this could be that state of mind which is excellently described by Aristotle: and by him, it is marked not with the character of *virtue*, but of a certain *divinity*. His very words are these: *But it is fitting to oppose to brutality that which is above humanity, heroic or divine Virtue.* And a little later, *For just as a wild beast is neither vice nor virtue, so neither is God.* *But this state is indeed something higher than virtue: that other is something different from vice.* Pliny the Younger, certainly, with the license of pagan grandiloquence, proposes Trajan's virtue as a model, not as an imitation, of divine virtue, when he says: *There is no need for men to pour out other prayers to the Gods, than that they should show themselves as benevolent and propitious lords to mortals;* *as Trajan had shown himself.* But these things savor of the profane boasting of the Pagans, who grasped at certain shadows larger than the body itself. But true Religion, and the holy Christian faith, seeks the very thing itself: by imprinting charity upon the minds of men; which is most aptly called the *bond of perfection*, because it gathers and binds all virtues together. Indeed, it was most elegantly said by Menander, concerning *sensual love,* X 5 which

--- Page 492 ---

who wrongly imitates that *Divine* one: *Love*
*is a better Sophist than a Left-handed one, for human life.*
By which he implies that the grace of character is better
formed by love, than by a Sophist and an inept teacher,
whom he calls *Left-handed*. For indeed, by all
its laborious Rules and Precepts, it cannot fashion a human

Thus, without a doubt, if anyone's soul is inflamed by the fervor

Which indeed has the nature of a *Sophist*, if compared

*other affections, though they elevate the soul, nevertheless*

Thus all other human endowments, which we admire,
while they exalt nature to a greater degree, are meanwhile subject
to excess: but *Charity* alone admits no excess.
Angels, while they aspired to power equal to the divine,
transgressed and fell: *I will ascend, and I will be like the Most High.*
Man, while he aspired to *Knowledge* equal to the Divine,
transgressed and fell: *You will be like Gods, knowing good*

very *Imitation* we are even invited: *Love your enemies,*

[Just as the good of the body consists in] beauty, strength, and pleasure; so the good of the mind, if we contemplate it according to the precepts of moral doctrine, we shall perceive to tend to this: that it renders the mind sound, and free from disturbances; Beautiful; and adorned with the ornaments of true grace; Strong, and agile for performing all the duties of life; finally, not dull, but vividly retaining the sense of honest pleasure and solace.

These things, however, just as in the body, so also in the mind, are rarely all found together at the same time. For it is easy to see many, powerful in intellectual faculties and strength of mind, whom disturbances nevertheless afflict; and whose manners are scarcely sprinkled with any elegance or grace: Others, for whom there is an abundance of elegance and grace in their manners, yet they lack, either integrity of mind, so that they might wish, or strength, so that they might be able to act rightly: Others, endowed with an honest mind, and purged from the stain of vices, who nevertheless are neither an ornament to themselves, nor useful to the Commonwealth: Others, who perhaps possess three of these, but are nevertheless endowed with a certain Stoic sadness and dullness, indeed perform actions of virtue, but do not enjoy pleasures. But if it happens that two or three of these four sometimes coincide, it very rarely happens, as we have said, that all do. Now indeed this principal member of human philosophy, which contemplates man, inasmuch as he consists of body and soul, but nevertheless isolated, and apart from society, has been treated by us.

CHAP. I.
*Division of Civil Doctrine, into the Doctrine of Conver-*
*sation: The Doctrine of Business: & The Doctrine of*
*Empire, or the Commonwealth.*

[Large decorative initial V] There is an old story, (Most Excellent King)
that several Philosophers solemnly met
before the Ambassador of a foreign King,
and each, to the best of his ability, displayed his
Wisdom; so that the Ambassador might have things to report
concerning the wonderful wisdom of the Greeks. One,
however, from their number *remained silent*, and brought
nothing forward: so much so that the Ambassador, turning
to him, said: *What, indeed, do you have that I might report?*
To whom he [replied]: *Report (he said) to your King,*
*that you found among the Greeks someone who knew how to be silent.*
And indeed I had forgotten, in this Synopsis of the arts,
to insert the art of *silence*: Which, however (*since it is
often desired*) I will now teach by my own example.
For indeed, since the order of things has at last brought me to
that

--- Page 496 ---
474        ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF THE SCIENCES.
it has led me, so that a little later the art of *Empire* must be treated; and since I am writing to so great a King, who is so perfect a Master in that art, and has drawn it from its very cradle: Nor can I be entirely unmindful of what place I have held with your Majesty: I have deemed it more fitting to prove myself by *being silent* about this matter before your Majesty, rather than by writing. Indeed, Cicero makes mention not only of an art, but also of a certain eloquence, which is found in *silence*. For when he had mentioned some conversations of his, held back and forth with a certain other person, in a letter to Atticus, he writes thus: "*Here, I have taken something from your eloquence; for I was silent.*" Indeed, Pindar (to whom it is peculiar to strike the minds of men unexpectedly with some wonderful maxim, as if with a divine rod) utters something of this kind: "*Sometimes things not said affect more than things said.*" In this part, therefore, I have decided to *be silent*, or what is nearest to silence, to be very *brief*. But, before I come to the *arts of empire*, not a few things must be premised concerning other *portions of civil doctrine*.
    *Civil science* is concerned with a subject which, of all other things, is most immersed in Matter: and therefore is most difficult to reduce to axioms. There are nevertheless some things which alleviate this difficulty. For first, just as that Cato the *Censor* was accustomed to say about his Romans: "*that they are like sheep, whose flock*"

--- Page 497 ---
LIBER VIII. 475
a whole flock one would manage with less trouble than
a single one: because if you can drive a few from the flock, so that
they enter the right path, the rest will follow of their own accord:
Similarly, in this respect, the task of Ethics is in a way
more difficult than that of Politics. Secondly, Ethics proposes to itself
that the soul be imbued and filled with internal goodness:
But civil science demands nothing more than external goodness:
For this suffices for society. Therefore it not infrequently happens
that the government is good, but the times are bad:
Indeed, in Sacred History, this occurs more than once (when
good and pious Kings are spoken of) "But as yet the people had not
directed their heart unto the Lord God of their fathers."
Therefore, in this respect too, the parts of Ethics are harder. Thirdly,
Commonwealths have this characteristic, that like larger machines
they move more slowly, and not without great effort, whence they are
not so quickly undermined: For just as in Egypt seven fertile years
sustained seven barren ones: in Commonwealths, the good institution
of former times ensures that the errors of subsequent times do not
immediately bring ruin: But the decisions and customs of individual
men are accustomed to be overthrown more suddenly. This finally
burdens Ethics, and aids Politics.

Civil science has three parts, according to
three summary actions of society: The doctrine
of conduct; The doctrine of business; and the doctrine
of Empire or the Commonwealth. For there are indeed
three goods which men seek to procure for themselves from civil
society: Solace against

against *solitude*, aid in *business*,
and *protection against injuries*. And these three
prudences are clearly distinct from each other, and often
separate: *Prudence in social interaction,
prudence in business, and prudence in governing.*
     Indeed, as far as *social interaction* is concerned,
it certainly ought not to be affected, but much less neglected:
since prudence in its management both displays a certain
grace of manners in itself, and greatly helps in conveniently
managing affairs, both public and private. For just as
action is held in such high regard for an orator (although it is
something external) that it is even preferred to those other parts
which seem more weighty and internal; in almost the same way, in
a civil man, *social interaction*, and its management,
(however much it may be concerned with external matters)
finds, if not the highest, then certainly an excellent place. For what
weight does the *countenance* itself, and its composition, hold?
As the Poet rightly says;
     —— *Nor destroy your words with your countenance.*
For one can undermine the *force of speech* with one's
countenance, and plainly betray it. Indeed, *deeds*, no
less than *words*, can likewise be destroyed by the
countenance, if we believe Cicero. He, when he commended
affability to his brother towards the Provincials, said that it was
not primarily situated in this, that he should offer easy
access to himself, unless he also received those approaching
courteously with his very countenance. *It makes no difference
to have an open door, [and] a closed countenance.* We also

--- Page 499 ---
L I B E R V I I I. 477

having met with Caesar, while the war was still raging, Atticus diligently and seriously advised Cicero by letter concerning composing his *face and bearing* for dignity and gravity. But if the moderation of *mouth and face* alone can do so much, how much more *familiar conversation*, and other things that pertain to *social interaction*? And indeed, the sum and epitome of decorum and elegance of manners are almost entirely situated in this: that as if with an even balance, we measure and maintain both our own Dignity and that of others. Which T. Livy also expressed not badly (although intent on another matter) by this characterization of a person: "*Lest (he says) I seem either arrogant or servile: of which the former is forgetting the liberty of others, the latter one's own.*" But on the contrary side, if we too eagerly pursue *urbanity* and external elegance of manners, they pass into a certain Deformed and Spurious affectation. "*For what is more unseemly than to transfer the Stage into Life?*" Furthermore, even if they do not at all fall into that vicious excess, nevertheless, too much time is consumed in such trifles, and the mind is burdened by the care of these things themselves, more than is proper. And therefore, just as in Academies, young men zealous for letters, but indulging too much in the gatherings of companions, are accustomed to be warned by their teachers, "*that Friends are thieves of time:*" so certainly that constant mental attention to decorum in *social interactions* commits a great theft from more serious meditations. Furthermore, those who so excel in *urbanity*, and seem, as it were, born for this one thing, almost always have this, that to themselves

--- Page 500 ---
478      ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING
they please themselves in that alone, and scarcely ever aspire to more solid and higher virtues: Whereas, on the contrary, those who are conscious of their own defects in this regard seek honor from a good reputation. For where a good reputation is present, almost everything is becoming; but where that is lacking, then indeed help must be sought from the agreeableness of manners and *urbanity*. Furthermore, in conducting affairs, you will scarcely find a more serious or frequent impediment than an overly curious observation of this external decorum; and that other thing which serves this very purpose, namely, an anxious selection of time and opportunities. For Solomon excellently says: *He who observes the wind will not sow; and he who regards the clouds will not reap.* Indeed, opportunity must be created by us more often than awaited. In a word, this *urban composition of manners* is like the garment of the mind, and therefore ought to reflect the advantages of a garment. For first, it ought to be such that it is in common use; again, that it be not too delicate or expensive. Next, it should be made in such a way that if there is any virtue in the mind, it may display it most conspicuously; if any deformity, it may supply and conceal it. Lastly, and above all, that it be not too tight, and so constrain the mind that it may restrain and impede its movements in conducting affairs. But this part of *civil science concerning conversation* has indeed been elegantly treated by some, nor should it in any way be set down as *lacking*.

**D**octrine of business we will divide into the doctrine
