      EXAMPLE OF A PORTION
*Of the Doctrine concerning scattered occasions, from some of Solomon's parables.*
            Parable.
1. *A soft answer breaks wrath.*
            Explanation.
  If the *wrath* of a Prince or Superior is kindled against you, and it is now your turn to speak, Solomon prescribes two things: The one, that an *answer be made*; the other, that the same *be soft*. The former contains three precepts. First, that you *beware of a sad and stubborn silence*: For that either takes the whole blame upon yourself, as if you had nothing you could answer; or secretly accuses your Lord of injustice, as if his ears were not open to a defense, even if just. Secondly, that you *beware of postponing the matter*, nor demand other time for defense: For this either brands you with the same mark as before, namely, that your Lord is carried away by excessive mental disturbance; or plainly signifies that you are preparing some artful defense.

--- Page 505 ---
LIBER VIII. 483
to meditate a defense, when you have nothing ready: So much so that it will always be best to bring forward something in the present, and from the matter as it arises, in your excuse. Thirdly, that a response be made altogether: a *response*, I say, not a mere *confession*, or a mere *submission*, but that something of apology and excuse be sprinkled in: For it is not safe to do otherwise, except among very generous and magnanimous natures; which are exceedingly rare. It follows in the latter place, that the *Response be soft*, by no means broken or harsh.

Parable.
2. *A prudent servant will rule over a foolish son; And will divide the inheritance among brothers.*

Explication.
In every troubled and discordant family, there always arises some *servant*, or *humble friend*, powerful, who conducts himself according to his own judgment, to settle the family's disputes, and to whom, on that account, both the whole family and the master himself are beholden. If he pursues his own interest, he fosters and aggravates the family's ills: but if he has truly been faithful and upright, he certainly deserves a great deal: So much so that he ought even to be considered *among brothers*, or at least *to receive the fiduciary administration of the inheritance*.

Parable.
3. *A wise man, if he contends with a fool, whether he is angry or laughs, will find no rest.*

Explication.
We are often warned to avoid an *unequal encounter*, in the sense, *Lest we contend with the more powerful.* But no less useful is the warning, which here

--- Page 506 ---
484 - ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING
here Solomon shows, *Do not contend with the unworthy.* For this matter is settled by a completely unfair lot. Indeed, if we are superior, no victory follows: if we are overcome, great indignity. Nor does it help, in exercising such a contention, if sometimes we act as if *in jest*, sometimes with *pride and contempt.* For wherever we turn, we shall be made less weighty thereby, nor shall we conveniently extricate ourselves. But it is worst if such a person, with whom we contend, (as Solomon speaks,) has something akin to a *fool*, that is, if he is audacious and rash.
Parable.
4. *But also to all words that are spoken, do not apply your ear, lest perhaps you hear your servant speaking ill of you.*
Explanation.
It can scarcely be believed how much *useless curiosity* disturbs life, concerning those things which concern us: Namely, when we strive to pry into those secrets which, when detected and discovered, indeed bring grief to the mind, but help nothing for expediting counsels. For first follows *vexation and disquiet of mind*, since all human affairs are full of perfidy and ingratitude. So much so that, if some magic mirror could be procured, in which we could behold hatreds, and whatever else is stirred up against us anywhere, it would be better for us if it were immediately cast away and shattered. For things of this kind are like the rustling of leaves, and quickly vanish. Secondly, curio-

--- Page 507 ---
L I B E R. VIII. 485
that curiosity burdens the mind with excessive suspicions, which is most hostile to counsels, and renders them inconstant and complicated. Thirdly, the same curiosity very often fixes the evils themselves, which would otherwise fly past: For it is serious to provoke the consciences of men; who, if they think they are hidden, are easily changed for the better, but if they feel themselves detected, they drive out evil with evil. Therefore, the highest prudence was deservedly attributed to Pompey the Great, because he had immediately committed all of Sertorius's papers to the fire, neither reading them himself nor permitting others to do so.
        Parable.
  5. *Poverty arrives like a traveler, and indigence as if an armed man.*
        Explanation.
  It is elegantly described in the parable how the shipwrecks of fortunes supervene upon the prodigal and those careless about their family affairs. For at the beginning, step by step, and with slow paces, like a traveler, indebtedness and a strong diminution of fortune arrive, and are scarcely felt: But not long after, indigence invades like an armed man, with a hand so strong and powerful that it can no longer be resisted: since it was rightly said among the Ancients that necessity is the strongest of all things. Therefore, one must meet the traveler, and fortify oneself against the armed man.
        Parable.
  6. *He who instructs a scoffer, does himself an injury: and he who reproves the impious, generates a stain for himself.*

            Explanation.
   It agrees with the precept of the Savior. *That we do not*
*cast our pearls before swine.* Moreover, in this parable, the actions
of instruction and reprehension are distinguished; Likewise,
the persons of the *scoffer* and the *impious* are distinguished;
Finally, that which is repaid is distinguished. For in the former,

For when someone teaches and instructs a *scoffer*,

of the impious*; who not only does not listen (being *impious*);
but also turns his horns, and either immediately assails
the reprover, now made hateful to him, with insults, or at least
later slanders him among others.

            Explanation.
   The comforts and sorrows of the household,
namely of the father and mother, concerning their children, are distinguished.
For a *prudent and thrifty son* is a special comfort to the father,
who knows the value of virtue better than the *mother*;
and therefore rejoices more in his son's disposition,
inclined to virtue: Moreover, perhaps his own upbringing
brings him joy, because he has educated his *son* so well,
and has impressed upon him integrity of morals, by precepts and example,

impressed. On the contrary, *the mother feels more compassion and grief for the misfortune of her son; partly because of a more gentle and tender maternal affection; partly perhaps conscious of her own indulgence, by which she may have corrupted and depraved him.*

Parable.
8. *The memory of the just is with praises; but the name of the wicked will rot.*

Explanation.
It distinguishes between *the fame of good men and bad men, what sort it is accustomed to be after death.* *For with good men, envy being extinguished (which used to diminish their fame while they lived), their name immediately flourishes, and their praises grow stronger day by day:* *But with bad men (although their fame, through the favor of friends and men of their faction, may have lasted for a short time) a little later a loathing of their name arises, and finally those fleeting praises end in infamy, and as it were, in a heavy and foul odor.*

Parable.
9. *He who troubles his own house, will possess the winds.*

Explanation.
A very useful warning, concerning *domestic discords and troubles.* *For very many people, from quarrels with wives, or disinheritances of sons, or frequent changes of household, promise great things to themselves; as if from these, either tranquility of mind, or a more fortunate administration of their affairs, would come to them.* *But for the most part, their hopes go into the winds.* *For, partly those changes, for the most part...*

firstly, they do not turn out for the better; then also,
these disturbers of their own household very often experience various troubles,

Parable.
10. *Better is the end of a speech than the beginning.*

Explanation.
This *parable* corrects a very common error,
not only among those who are especially devoted to words,
but also among the more prudent. That is,
that people are more anxious about *the approach and entrance*
*of their speeches* than about
*the outcome*, and they meditate more carefully on introductions and prefaces
than on the ends of their speeches.
They ought, however, neither to neglect the former, nor to fail to have the latter,
as far more important, prepared and digested within themselves;
revolving with themselves, and, as far as possible,
looking forward in their mind, what the *outcome of the speech*
will finally be, and how business can thereby be promoted
and brought to maturity. Nor is this the end.
Indeed, it is not only *epilogues* and *the conclusions of speeches*
*which pertain to the business itself* that one ought to meditate upon;
but also the care of those *speeches*
                                        to be undertaken

11. *As dead flies make the best ointment stink; so a little folly makes a man precious in wisdom and glory.*

Explanation.
Very unfair and miserable is the condition of *men excelling in virtue*, (as the *parable* rightly notes) because their errors, however slight, are in no way forgiven. But, just as in a very bright gem, every tiny speck or cloud strikes the eyes and causes a certain annoyance: which, however, if it were found in a more flawed gem, would scarcely be noticed: Similarly, *in men endowed with singular virtue*, every slightest fault immediately falls into the eyes and conversations of men, and is met with harsher censure: which *in mediocre men* would either be entirely hidden, or easily obtain

they were to mix some *absurdities* (which could be done without vice)

                Parable.
  12. *Mocking men destroy a city, but wise men avert calamity.*
                Explanation.
  It may seem strange that in describing the kind of men
who are, as it were, by nature fitted and made to undermine and
destroy republics, Solomon chose the character; Not of a man
proud and insolent; Not tyrannical and cruel;
Not rash and violent; Not impious and wicked;
Not unjust and oppressive; Not seditious

Not finally of a foolish and incompetent man: But of a *mocker*.
But this is most worthy of the wisdom of that King, who best
observes the preservation and overthrow of republics.
For there is scarcely a plague so similar to kingdoms and republics
than if the counselors of kings, or senators, and those who are placed
at the helm of affairs, are *mockers* by disposition.
For men of this kind always diminish the magnitude of dangers,
so that they may appear brave senators; and they insult those
who weigh dangers as is proper, as if they were timid:

They scoff at the mature delays of consulting and deliberating, and at considered discussions, as if they were mere rhetorical exercises, full of tediousness, and contributing nothing to the most important matters: They despise reputation, to which the counsels of Princes ought especially to be directed, as the spittle of the common people, and a thing quickly passing away: They care nothing for the force and authority of laws, as if they were mere nets by which greater matters ought least to be restrained: They reject counsels and precautions that look far ahead, as if they were mere dreams and melancholic fancies: They mock with jests and witticisms truly prudent men, skilled in affairs, and of great spirit and counsel: Finally, they simultaneously undermine all the foundations of political governance. Which ought to be more carefully noted, because this matter is conducted by secret tunnels, and not by open assault: Nor has it begun to be suspected among men (as it deserves).

          Parable.
     14. *A righteous man has regard for the life of his animal; but the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel.*

          Explanation.
     There has been implanted, by Nature itself, in man, a noble and excellent *feeling of compassion*; which also extends to *brute animals*; which, by divine ordinance, are subjected to his dominion. Therefore, this *compassion* has a certain analogy with that of a Prince towards his subjects. Moreover, it is most certain that the more worthy the soul is, the more it sympathizes with many. For narrow and degenerate souls think that such matters do not pertain to them at all: But that soul, which is a nobler part of the universe, is affected by communion.
          Therefore

--- Page 515 ---
**BOOK VIII. 493**
Therefore we see that under the old law there were not a few precepts, not so much merely ceremonial as *instructive of mercy*: Such was that, *concerning not eating flesh with its blood*; and similar things. Also, in the sects of the Essenes and Pythagoreans, they entirely abstained from eating animals. Which also holds true today (their superstition being inviolate) among some inhabitants of the Mogul Empire. Indeed, even the Turks (a people, though, both by race and discipline, cruel and bloodthirsty) are accustomed to bestow alms upon brute animals; nor do they tolerate the vexation and torture of animals. But lest perhaps these things which we have said seem to advocate for every kind of *mercy*, Solomon wisely adds that *the mercies of the wicked are cruel*. Such mercies are when wicked and criminal men are spared, who ought to be struck by the sword of justice: For such *mercy* is more cruel than cruelty itself. For cruelty is exercised against individuals; but that mercy, with impunity granted, arms and unleashes the entire army of criminals against innocent men.

**Parable.**
15. *The fool brings forth his whole spirit; but the wise man reserves something for the future.*

**Explanation.**
The parable corrects chiefly (as it seems) not the futility of vain men, who easily bring forth what should be said and what should be kept silent: not that frankness by which, without distinction and judgment, they rush into all people and all things: not garrulity, by which to the point of nausea
Y 5 seam

--- Page 516 ---
494           On the Advancement of Learning.
...even to the point of annoying others: but another, more hidden vice; namely, a manner of speech least of all prudent and politic; that is, when someone so conducts a conversation (in private colloquies) that whatever he has in mind, which he thinks pertains to the matter, he utters at once, as if with one breath, and in a continuous discourse. For this greatly hinders business. Indeed, first, *speech broken up, and instilled in parts*, penetrates much more deeply than continuous speech; because in continuous speech the weight of things is not distinctly and individually received, nor does it settle in through some delay, but one idea expels another before it has fully settled. Secondly, no one possesses such powerful and felicitous eloquence that, with the first rush of speech, he can *render the person he is addressing completely mute and speechless*: rather, the other will also respond in turn, and perhaps object. Then indeed it happens that what should have been reserved for refutation or reply, having been already put forward and previously touched upon, loses its force and grace. Thirdly, if someone does not pour out all at once what needs to be said, but speaks it in parts, introducing one thing first, and then another; he will perceive from the countenance and response of the person he is addressing how each point has affected him, and in what sense it has been received; so that he may more cautiously suppress or select what still remains to be said.

               Parable.
   16. *If the spirit of him that has power rises upon you, do not leave your place, for com-*
   *posure will allay great offenses.*
                                         Expla-

--- Page 517 ---
**BOOK VIII. 495**
Explanation.
The *parable* teaches how one ought to conduct oneself when one has incurred the anger and indignation of a *prince*. The precept is twofold: First, *that he not leave his place*; Second, *that he diligently and cautiously attend to the cure*, as if in some serious illness. For men are accustomed, after they have perceived their *Princes* to be moved against them, partly from impatience with disgrace, partly lest they reopen the wound by observing it, partly so that their Princes may perceive their sadness and humility, to withdraw themselves from their duties and functions, and even sometimes to restore the magistracies themselves, and the dignities they hold, into the hands of the *Princes*. But Solomon disapproves of this method of healing, as if it were harmful; and indeed with the best reason. For first, *it too much publicizes the disgrace itself*; from which then enemies and the envious become bolder to harm; and friends become more timid to help. Second, in this way it happens that the *Prince's anger*, which perhaps, if it were not divulged, would spontaneously subside, *is more fixed*, and, as if a beginning had already been made to displace the man, it is carried towards his downfall. Finally, *that withdrawal* *tastes of ill-will*, and of being hostile to the circumstances; which adds the evil of suspicion to the evil of indignation. Now, these things pertain to the *cure*. First, let him beware above all, lest by some *stupidity*, or even by *haughtiness of spirit*, he seem *not to feel the Prince's indignation* at all, or not to be affected by it as he ought: That is, that his countenance, not to
Y 6                                     sadness

--- Page 518 ---
496      DE AUGM. SCIENT.
not to a stubborn sadness, but to a grave and modest sadness compose himself: and in whatever matters are to be done, he should show himself less cheerful and joyful than usual: Moreover, it will be to his advantage to use the help and speech of some friend with the *Prince*, who may opportunely insinuate how much he is tormented by a sense of pain in his innermost being. *Secondly, he should diligently avoid all occasions, even the smallest,* through which either the matter itself, which gave cause for indignation, might be stirred up again, or the *Prince* might seize an opportunity to become angry again and rebuke him, for whatever reason, before others. *Thirdly*, he should also diligently seek out all occasions in which *his service might be pleasing to the Prince*; so that he may show a ready will to redeem past fault; and his Prince may perceive what kind of servant, if he dismisses him, he would eventually be deprived of. *Fourthly, he should either shrewdly transfer the fault itself to others; or insinuate that it was not committed with malicious intent; or even point out the malice of those who reported him to the King, or exaggerated the matter beyond measure. Finally, in all things, he should be vigilant, and* be intent *on the cure*.
                Parable.
  *17. The first to plead his case seems just: then comes*
*the other party, and examines him.*
                Explanation.
  The first information in every case, if it has settled for a little while in the mind of the judge, takes deep root, and imbues and occupies him; so much so that it can hardly be washed away, unless either some manifest falsehood
                                  in the ma-

--- Page 519 ---
L I B E R VIII. 497
in the matter of the information, or some artifice is detected in presenting it. For indeed, a bare and simple defense, though it be just and weighty, can scarcely compensate for the prejudice of the first information, or by itself restore the scale of justice, once tipped, to equilibrium. Therefore, it is safest for the judge that nothing pertaining to the merits of the case be prejudged before both parties are heard together; and it is best for the defendant, if he perceives the judge to be prejudiced, to focus on this above all (as far as the case allows), to detect some cunning and malicious deceit employed by the opposing party to abuse the judge.
            Parable.
  18. *He who delicately nourishes a servant from childhood, will afterwards find him rebellious.*
            Explanation.
  A measure must be observed by Princes and Lords, according to the counsel of Solomon, in their grace and favor towards servants. This is threefold. First, that *they be promoted by steps, not by leaps:* Secondly, that *they sometimes become accustomed to refusal:* Thirdly, (which Machiavelli rightly advises) that *they always have before their eyes something to which they can further aspire.* For unless these things are done, Princes will undoubtedly in the end receive from their servants, instead of a grateful and dutiful spirit, disdain and rebellion. For, from sudden promotion, arises *insolence;* from the perpetual attainment of desires, *impatience of refusal;* Finally, if aspirations are lacking, *likewise, alacrity and industry will be lacking.*

          Parable.
  24. A poor man slandering the poor is like

  This parable was anciently expressed and depicted

men; and for peoples, not to allow their Kings
to struggle with excessive poverty.

          Parabola.
  27. *He who conceals a transgression seeks friendship; but he who repeats it in another conversation, separates allies.*
          Explicatio.
  There is a twofold way of treating concord and reconciling minds. One, which begins with *amnesty*; the other, which begins with the repetition of injuries, by adding apologies and excuses. Indeed, I recall the opinion of a very prudent and political man: *He who treats of peace, without repeating the conditions of discord, deceives minds more with the sweetness of concord than he reconciles them with equity.* But Solomon, wiser than that man, is of the contrary opinion; and approves *amnesty*, prohibits *repetition*. For in *repetition* these evils are present; first, because it is like a *nail in a wound*; then because danger threatens from a *new altercation*, (since concerning the reasons for injuries, the parties will never agree;) then finally because it leads the matter to *apologies*; But each party would rather seem to have remitted the offense than to have admitted an excuse.

        Parabola.
  30. The prudent man attends to his steps; The foolish man turns aside to deceptions.
        Explicatio.
  There are two kinds of prudence. One is true and sound: The other is degenerate and false, which Solomon does not hesitate to call by the name of *folly*. He who dedicates himself to the former, guards his own ways and footsteps, foreseeing dangers, meditating remedies: using the works of the upright, fortifying himself against the wicked, cautious in beginning, not unprepared in retreating; attentive to opportunities, strenuous against impediments: with countless other things, which pertain to governing his own *actions* and *steps*. But the other kind is entirely composed of *deceits* and *cunning*, and places its hope entirely in circumventing others, and shaping them at will. The parable rightly rejects this, not only as wicked, but also as *foolish*. For firstly, it is by no means among those things which are in our power, nor does it rely on any constant rule: But new stratagems must be devised daily, as the previous ones fail and become obsolete. Secondly, he who has once incurred the reputation and opinion of being a cunning and subtle man, has entirely deprived himself of the principal *instrument* for conducting affairs, that is, *trust*: And so he will experience everything little in agreement with his wishes. Lastly, *these arts*, however beautiful they may seem, and *please*; yet they very often fail, which well

            Parable.
  32. Give occasion to a wise man, and wisdom will be added to him.
            Explanation.
  The Parable distinguishes between that Wisdom which has grown into a true habit and has matured, and that which floats only in the brain and in conception, or is boasted about in speech, but has not put forth deep roots.                **Parable.**
  34. As faces are reflected in water: so are the hearts of men manifest to the prudent.
               **Explanation.**
  The Parable distinguishes between the minds of the prudent and those of other men; comparing the former to waters or mirrors, which receive the forms and images of things; while the latter are like earth or an unpolished stone, in which nothing is reflected. And for this reason, the mind of a prudent man is more aptly compared to a mirror; because in a mirror one's own image can be seen, together with the images of others: a faculty not granted to the eyes themselves or to a mere mirror. [it is most] suitable; so that if anyone's observation had fallen upon something that would have been conducive to common life, he should reduce and contract it into some brief sentence, or a *Parable*, or even a *Fable*. But, as for fables (as has been said elsewhere), they formerly existed as substitutes for examples and supplements: Now, when the times abound with a wealth of histories, the living aim is pursued more directly and eagerly.

But the mode of writing which best suits an argument so varied and manifold (such as a *treatise on scattered affairs and occasions*) would be that most suitable one which Machiavelli chose for treating political matters; namely, through observations, or *discourses* (as they say) upon *history and examples*. For knowledge, which is recently, and as it were in our sight, elicited from particulars, best knows the way of repeating particulars anew: And certainly it contributes much more to Practice when discourse or disputation serves under an example, than when an example is subjoined to the disputation. For not only is this order regarded, but the matter itself. For when an example is established as the basis of a disputation, it is usually proposed with the entire apparatus of circumstances; which sometimes correct the discourse, sometimes supplement it; whence it becomes a model for imitation and practice: Whereas on the contrary, examples brought forward for the sake of disputation are cited succinctly and plainly, and like slaves, only observe the commands of the disputation.

Moreover, there is to be found a basis for *precepts concerning affairs* even more suitable than either of those *histories*: namely, that discourses be made upon *letters*, but more prudent and more serious ones; such as those of Cicero to Atticus; and others. Indeed, *letters* are accustomed to represent affairs more immediately and vividly than either *Annals* or *lives*. This virtue of being wise for oneself was not unknown even to the Romans themselves, although they were the best guardians of the fatherland: whence the Comic Poet [says], *“For by Pollux, a wise man makes his own fortune.”* Moreover, it was even turned into a proverb among them: *“Each man is the artisan of his own fortune.”* And Livy attributes this very thing to Cato the Elder: *“In this man there was such strength of mind and talent, that in whatever place he had been born, he seemed destined to make his own fortune for himself.”*
This kind of *prudence*, if anyone professes it and openly boasts of it, has always been considered not only un-Political (i.e., not civic-minded), but also something ill-omened and inauspicious: As was observed in the Athenian Timotheus: Who, after he had performed many splendid deeds for the honor and benefit of his state, and rendered an account of his administration to the people (as was then the custom), concluded each point with this clause: *“And in this matter, fortune played no part.”* It happened indeed that after that time, nothing ever turned out fortunately for him. Truly, this is too boastful and too high-minded wisdom, looking to the same thing as that of Ezekiel concerning Pharaoh: *“You say, ‘The river is mine, and I made myself.’”* or that of the Prophet Habakkuk: *“They exult and sacrifice to their net,”* or also that of the Poet, concerning Mezentius, the despiser of the Gods:

But that excess of confidence (as we have said) is a thing as profane as it is always unfortunate. Therefore, it seemed good to great and truly wise men to attribute any successes to their fortune, not to their virtue or industry: For Sulla also called himself *“Felix”* (Fortunate), not *“Magnus”* (Great); and Caesar (better than above) to the ship's pilot: *“You carry Caesar and his Fortune.”*

      Nevertheless, these sayings: *“Every man is the architect of his own fortune,” “The wise man will rule the stars,” “No road is impassable for virtue,”* and similar ones; if they are understood and applied rather as spurs to industry than as stirrups to insolence, and more so that they produce in men constancy and strength of purpose, rather than arrogance and boastfulness, they have deservedly been considered sound and wholesome, and undoubtedly have occupied some place in the hearts of magnanimous men, to the extent that they sometimes with difficulty conceal such thoughts. For we see that Augustus Caesar (who, compared with his uncle, was rather different from him than inferior, but certainly a somewhat more moderate man) at the end of his life asked his friends, who

L I B E R VIII. 513
...when he had breathed his last, they should applaud him, as if he had been conscious of having successfully performed the drama of his *life*. This part of *learning* also is to be numbered among the desiderata: Not that in practice it has not been used and frequently practiced, even excessively more than is proper; but because books are silent about it. Wherefore, according to our custom, as in the former part, we will review some of its chapters: And we will name it *the architect of fortune*, or (as we have said) *the doctrine of the art of rising in life*.

And indeed at first glance, I shall seem to treat a certain new and unusual subject: by teaching men how they can become *the architects of their own fortune*: A *doctrine*, certainly, to which anyone would gladly devote himself as a disciple, until he has clearly perceived its difficulty. For not lighter are, or fewer, or less arduous, the things required for acquiring fortune, than those for *virtue*: And the matter is equally difficult and severe, to become truly *Political* as truly *Moral*. But the treatment of this *doctrine* pertains very much both to the honor and to the weight of learning. For it is especially to the *honor of letters* that those pragmatic men should know that erudition is by no means like a little bird, such as a lark, which is accustomed to be carried aloft and to delight itself by singing; but nothing else: but rather to be of the hawk kind, as one who knows how to fly high, and from time to time, when it seems fit, to descend and seize its prey.

**Dᴇ Aᴜɢᴍ. Sᴄɪᴇɴᴛ.**
Then, too, this very thing pertains to the perfection of learning, because it is the true norm of legitimate inquiry that nothing should be found in the globe of matter which does not have a parallel in the crystalline globe, or intellect. That is, nothing should come into Practice of which there is not also some Doctrine and Theory. Yet learning does not admire or esteem this very architecture of fortune otherwise than as a work of an inferior kind. For one's own fortune, as a gift of itself granted by God, can in no way be a worthy recompense to anyone. Indeed, it not rarely happens that men excellent in virtues voluntarily renounce their fortune, so that they may devote themselves to more sublime matters. Yet fortune is worthy, inasmuch as it is an instrument of virtue and of deserving well, of its own speculation and doctrine too.

    Furthermore, even *actions themselves*, though they are the surest pledges of the human mind, are not to be entirely trusted, unless their *magnitude* and *peculiarity* have first been diligently and attentively weighed. For that is most true: "*Fraud builds up credit for itself in small things, so that it may deceive with greater profit.*" An Italian, however, thinks himself to be *standing on the very stone* where the herald proclaims, if he is treated better than usual without manifest cause. For these minor services make men drowsy and as if lulled to sleep, both regarding caution and industry: And rightly are they called by Demosthenes *the nourishment of idleness*.
    Moreover, the cunning and ambiguous *peculiarity* and *nature* of some *actions*, even those which are considered as benefits, can be clearly seen from what Mutianus perpetrated against Antonius Primus: "*Who, after returning to favor with him, but with the worst faith, elevated many of Antonius's friends to dignities; at the same time bestowing prefectures and tribuneships upon his friends.*" But by this cunning, he did not strengthen Antonius, but utterly disarmed and isolated him, by transferring his friendships to himself.

   Knowledge of others is followed by knowledge of oneself. For
no less diligence must be applied, but rather greater, that we
inform ourselves truly and accurately about ourselves, rather
than about others. Indeed, since that oracle, *Know thyself*,
is not only a rule of universal prudence, but also holds a principal
place in *Politics*. For *Saint James* rightly warns people
that he who has considered his face in a mirror, nevertheless
immediately forgets what he was like: So that frequent inspection
is entirely necessary. And this also holds true in *Politics*.
But mirrors, of course, are different: For the *Divine mirror*,
in which we ought to behold ourselves, is the word of God:
But the *Political mirror* is nothing other than the State of Affairs
and the Times in which we live.

Nor indeed is their number small; who, being by nature more solid, and least boastful, and therefore lacking this art of promoting their own honor, pay the penalty for their moderation, with some loss of dignity.

But however much someone of weaker judgment, and perhaps too much of an *Ethicist*, may disapprove of this kind of *display of virtue*: no one would deny that at least effort must be made so that virtue is not, through neglect, defrauded of its just price, and estimated at less than it truly is. This diminution of price, however, in estimating virtue, usually happens in three ways: First, when someone, in managing affairs, offers and thrusts himself and his service forward, uncalled or unsummoned: for with such services, it is usually considered a reward if they are not rejected. Secondly, when someone, at the beginning of an undertaking, abuses his strengths too much; and pours out in one rush what ought to have been performed gradually; this, while it gains premature favor for well-managed affairs, in the end, however, induces satiety. Thirdly, when someone too quickly

   Indeed, the diligent *concealment of defects* is by no
means of less importance than the prudent and artful *display
of virtues*. Defects, moreover, are concealed and lie hidden mostly
by a certain threefold industry, and as it were, by three hiding places:
*Caution, pretext, and confidence.*
   We call it *Caution* when we prudently abstain from those things
for which we are not equal: Whereas, on the contrary, bold
and restless natures easily thrust themselves, without judgment,
into things to which they are unaccustomed; and consequently
publish their own defects, and as it were, proclaim them. We call it
*Pretext* when we sagaciously and prudently pave and fortify
a path for ourselves, by which a benign and convenient interpretation
may be made of our *vices and defects*; as if they originated
elsewhere, or tended towards something else, than is commonly
supposed. Indeed, concerning the hiding places of vices, the Poet (says) not badly:
   *Often a vice lies hidden by the proximity of good.*
   Therefore, if we perceive any *defect* in ourselves, effort
must be made to borrow the persona and pretext of a *neighboring
virtue*, under whose shadow it may lie hidden. For example,
*gravity* should be used as a pretext for the *slow*, *gentleness* for the
*lazy*, and so for the rest. It is also useful to put forward some
probable cause, and spread it among the populace, by which,
being influenced, we may refrain from exerting our utmost strength;
so that what *we cannot do, we may seem unwilling* to do. As for

As for confidence, it is certainly an impudent remedy, but nevertheless most certain and most effective: Namely, that one should profess to utterly despise and disdain those things which one cannot truly attain: After the manner of prudent merchants, for whom it is customary and characteristic to raise the price of their own goods, and lower that of others. There is nevertheless also another kind of *confidence*, even more impudent than this; To wit, with a brazen front to thrust and hawk one's *defects* even upon public opinion, as if one believes oneself to excel in those very things in which one is most deficient. And so that one may more easily impose this upon others, one feigns diffidence in those things in which one truly excels. Just as we see happen among Poets. For when a poet recites his poems, if he says that one particular verse is not very commendable, you will immediately hear: *“And this verse cost me more than most of the others.”* Then indeed he will bring forward some other verse, as if it were suspect to him, and he will inquire what you think of it, which he knows well enough to be the best among many, and least liable to censure. But above all, for this purpose which is now being discussed, namely, that one should display an illustrious example of oneself before others and maintain one's right in all things, I judge nothing to be more important than that one should not, through excessive goodness and sweetness of one's nature, disarm oneself and expose oneself to injuries and insults: But rather, in all things, one should occasionally emit some sparks of a free and generous spirit, carrying within itself no less sting than honey. The same Caesar, with war already begun, was by no means a dissimulator, if we listen to what Cicero proclaims about him. *The other (alluding to Caesar) does not refuse, but in a certain way demands that, as he is, so he should be called Tyrant.* Similarly we see, in a certain letter of Cicero to Atticus, how little Augustus Caesar was a dissimulator; who, at the very outset of managing affairs, when he was still a favorite of the Senate, nevertheless was accustomed to swear in public assemblies before the people with that formula: *So may it be permitted to obtain the honors of my parent.* But that was no less a certain thing than tyranny itself. It is true that, to somewhat mitigate envy, he was accustomed at the same time to stretch out his hand towards the statue of Julius Caesar, which was placed in the Rostra. But people laughed, and applauded, and admired, and spoke among themselves thus: *What is this? What a youth?* But nevertheless they suspected no malice in him, who so candidly and openly spoke what he felt. And indeed those whom we have named attained complete success: Pompey, on the other hand, who aimed at the same goals, but by more shadowy and obscure paths, (as Tacitus speaks of him, *More hidden, not better:* and Sallust similarly accuses him of the same, *With an honest face, but a shameless mind:* ) he absolutely pursued that, and strove with countless stratagems, so that his desires and ambition

he might be thought to be unwilling and resisting. But when he thought he had achieved this, having been made sole Consul (which had never happened to anyone), he advanced no further towards his aims, because even those who would undoubtedly have helped him did not perceive what he wanted. So much so that he was at last compelled to enter upon the beaten and common path, namely, under the pretext of opposing Caesar, to raise arms and an army. So slow, subject to chances, and for the most part unsuccessful are those counsels wont to be, which are covered by deep dissimulation. Concerning this matter, Tacitus seems to have held the same opinion, when he established *simulations* (artifices) as a kind of *prudence of an inferior kind*, in comparison with *political arts*: attributing the former to Tiberius, but the latter to Augustus Caesar. Indeed, speaking of Livia, he says thus; *That she had been well composed with the arts of her husband, and the dissimulation of her son.*
    As for bending and shaping the mind; one must certainly strive with all one's might, that the mind may be rendered compliant to occasions and opportunities, and in no way hard or resistant towards them. For there will be no greater impediment to managing affairs, or establishing the fortunes of men, than that saying; *He remained the same, and it was not fitting:* that is, when men are the same, and use their own nature, after occasions have changed. Rightly therefore Livy, when he introduces Cato the Elder, as the most skillful architect of his own fortune, adds that he possessed a *na-*

--- Page 555 ---
BOOK VIII. 533
an adaptable mind. And hence it happens, that serious and solemn dispositions, and those unable to change, usually have more dignity than success. But this fault is deeply ingrained in some *by nature*, who by their very disposition are *viscous and knotty*, and inept at adapting. But in others it has prevailed *by custom* (which is a second *nature*) and by a certain opinion (which easily creeps into the minds of men), that they think the method of conducting affairs, which they have previously experienced as good and prosperous, should by no means be changed. For Machiavelli wisely observes concerning Fabius Maximus, *that he stubbornly wished to retain his old and ingrained custom of delaying and prolonging war, when the nature of the war was different, and demanded more vigorous counsels.* Furthermore, in others the same fault arises from a lack of judgment; when men do not timely discern the periods of things and actions; but only then do they adapt, after the opportunity has already slipped away. Demosthenes reproached his Athenians for something of this kind, saying that *they were like rustics who, proving themselves in a gladiatorial show, always transfer their shield to defend the part where they have been struck, after receiving a blow, not before.* In others again, this very thing happens, who are reluctant to lose the effort invested in the path they have once entered, nor do they know how to sound a retreat, but rather, they trust in their own steadfastness that they will be superior to the circumstances. In the first place, I place *the amendment of the mind*. For by removing and smoothing out *the impediments and knots of the mind*, you will open the way to fortune more quickly than you will remove *the impediments of the mind* with the aids of fortune. In the second place, I place wealth, and *money*. Which many perhaps have placed in the highest place, since its use is so great for all things. But that opinion I reject for a similar reason, as Machiavelli did, in another matter not much differing from it. For although it was an old saying, *that money is the sinews of war*; he, on the contrary, asserted *that there are no other sinews of war than the sinews of brave and military men*. In precisely the same way it can truly be asserted: *that the sinews of fortune are not money, but rather the strengths of the mind, ingenuity, fortitude, audacity, constancy, moderation, industry, and similar things*. In the third place, I place *fame and reputation*; all the more because they have certain tides and times, which if you do not use opportunely, it will be difficult to restore the matter to its original state. 	The fifth *precept* is; That we should in some way imitate nature; which *does nothing in vain*. This will not be very difficult to do, if we skillfully mix and weave together our affairs of all kinds. For in every single action, the mind must be so instructed and prepared, and our intentions must be laid beneath and subordinated one to another: so that, if in some matter we cannot achieve our wishes in the *highest degree*, yet it may be permitted to settle for the *second*, or even the *third*: But if we can stick to or settle for no part of the matter at all, then indeed let us direct the effort expended to some other end (besides the intended one): But if we cannot reap any Fruit in the *present*, let us at least extract something from it that will profit in the *future*: If indeed nothing *solid*, neither in the *present* nor in the *Future*, can be drawn from it, let us at least strive that something may accrue to our *reputation* from it: And other things of this kind: always demanding accounts from ourselves, by which it may be clear that we have gained some fruit, more or less, from each of our actions and counsels: and in no way permitting, that as if confused and dismayed, we should immediately lose heart.

The sixth *precept* is, that we do not bind ourselves too peremptorily to any matter: although it may seem, at first glance, less subject to chance: But let us always have either an open window for escape: or some secret back door for return.

The seventh *precept* is that ancient saying of Bias; provided it is applied not to treachery, but to caution and moderation: *Love as if you will one day hate, and hate as if you will one day love.* For in a wonderful way, it betrays and corrupts all advantages, if one immerses oneself too much in unhappy friendships, troublesome and turbulent hatreds, or childish and futile rivalries.

CHAPTER III.

*The Divisions of the Doctrine concerning Empire or the Commonwealth are omitted;*
*Only an Approach is made to two Desiderata, the Doctrine*
*concerning the Extension of the Bounds of Empire, and the Doctrine*
*concerning Universal Justice, or concerning the Sources of Law.*

I come now to the *art of governance*, or the *doctrine*
*concerning the administration of the Commonwealth*: Under which
*Household Management* is also contained, just as the *family* is under
the *state*. In this part, as I have already said before,
I have imposed silence upon myself. Nor, however, ought I to have
entirely despaired that I might perhaps discourse on it not
unskillfully or unprofitably: seeing that I have been taught by long
experience, and through so many degrees of offices and honors to the
highest Magistracy of the Kingdom, having been raised, by the most
indulgent favor of Your Majesty, by no merit of my own, and having
held the same Magistracy for four full years: and what is more,

--- Page 567 ---
LIBER. VIII. 545
is, that I have been accustomed to your Majesty's commands and conversations for eighteen continuous years; (which could also have carved out a statesman from some block of wood:) and who also, among all studies, have spent a great deal of time in Histories and Laws. All these things I do not relate to posterity boastfully, but because I think it pertains somewhat to the dignity of letters, that some man, born for letters rather than for anything else, and snatched away by some fate, I know not what, against his own genius, to manage affairs, nevertheless has been appointed to civil duties so honorable and arduous under a most prudent King. But, if my leisure should hereafter bring forth anything concerning politics, it will perhaps be an offspring either abortive or posthumous. Meanwhile, lest this so exalted Seat should be entirely empty, with all sciences now as it were placed on their own benches, I have decided to set forth only two portions of *civil science*, which do not pertain to the *secrets of empire*, but are of a more common nature,

     *Example of a summary treatise on extending the*

     The saying of Themistocles, applied to himself,
was certainly uncivil and boastful; but if it had
been uttered concerning others, and in general, it
would seem to embrace a truly prudent observation
and a very weighty judgment. Asked at a banquet
to play the lyre, he replied, *that he did not know how*
*to play stringed instruments, but that he could raise a*
*small town into a great city.* These words, certainly,
translated to a political sense, excellently describe
and distinguish two faculties, very different from
each other, in those who handle the helms of affairs.
For if we carefully observe the counselors of kings,
senators, and others appointed to public affairs, who
have ever existed, there will certainly be found (though
very rarely) some who are able to make a kingdom
or a state ample from small beginnings; yet they
may be very unskilled musicians. On the other hand,
very many others are wonderful artists in the *cithara*
or *lyre* (that is, in courtly trifles), who are so far
from being able to *amplify the commonwealth*, that
they rather seem by nature prepared to undermine
and overthrow a happy and flourishing state of the
commonwealth. Truly, those degenerate arts and
deceptions, by which counselors and powerful men
very often gain both favor with their princes and
renown among the populace, deserve no other name
than a certain skill in playing stringed instruments,

L I B E R VIII. 547
inasmuch as these things are more pleasing at present, and an ornament to the artists themselves, than they are useful or suitable for the wealth and greatness of the Republics, whose ministers they are. Doubtless there will also be other Councillors and Governors of the Republic, by no means to be scorned, who are equal to the tasks and can manage affairs conveniently, and preserve them from obvious dangers and disadvantages; yet they are a long way from that virtue which builds up and enlarges republics.

But, whatever kind of workers they may ultimately be, let us cast our eyes upon the work itself; namely, what the true *Greatness of Kingdoms and Republics* ought to be considered, and by what arts it can be obtained: A subject truly worthy for princes to always have in their hands and diligently meditate upon; by which they may neither, overestimating their strength, involve themselves in vain and overly arduous undertakings; nor again, despising them more than is right, descend to pusillanimous and timid counsels.

The *Greatness of Empires*, as to mass and territory, is subject to measurement; as to revenues, to calculations. The number of citizens, and heads, by census; the multitude and greatness of cities and towns can be recorded in tables. Yet among civil matters, no thing is found more prone to error than to ascertain the true and intrinsic value concerning the strength and resources of any empire. The *kingdom of heaven* is likened not to an acorn, or to some larger nut, but to a *grain of mustard seed*, which among seeds

--- Page 570 ---
548          ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING
among grains is the smallest, which nevertheless has within
itself a certain property and innate spirit, by which it raises itself
more quickly and spreads more widely: In the same way, one finds Kingdoms and
States, indeed very ample in extent and tract of regions,
which nevertheless are less apt for *further extending their borders*;
or for ruling more widely; Others, on the contrary, of sufficiently small
dimension, which nevertheless can be bases upon which the greatest Monar-
chies may be built.
     1. Fortified cities, full armories, noble breeds of
horses, armed chariots, elephants, machines and all kinds of war
engines, and similar things, are certainly all these nothing
other than a sheep clothed in a lion's skin, unless
the nation itself, by its stock and character, is strong and
military. Indeed, nor does the mere number of troops
help much, where the soldiers are unwarlike and
cowardly. For rightly says Virgil;
—— *The wolf cares not for the number of sheep.*
The army of the Persians in the plains of Arbela was presented to the eyes
of the Macedonians as a vast sea of men,
so much so that Alexander's Generals,
somewhat struck by the spectacle itself, interrupted the King,
and advised him to engage in battle by night:
To whom he said, *'I do not wish to steal a victory.'*

spirited and military, let him estimate his power
very soberly: And conversely, Princes who rule
over spirited and martial nations, let them know
their strength sufficiently, if other things do not fail
them. As for mercenary troops (which is usually
employed as a remedy when native forces are lacking),
history is full of examples by which it is clearly
evident that whatever state relies on them will
perhaps be able to spread wings, for a short time,
larger than its nest, but they will fall off a little later.
2. The blessing of Judah and Issachar will never
come together into one: Namely, that the same

--- Page 572 ---
550          ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING.
the same Tribe or Nation, be at the same time, both a Lion's cub, and an Ass lying down among burdens. Nor will it ever happen that a people oppressed by taxes should be strong and warlike. It is true that contributions made by public consent depress and deject the spirits of subjects less than those which are imposed by mere command. This is clearly to be seen in the taxes of Lower Germany, which they call excises: and on the other hand in those which are called subsidies among the English. For it is to be noted that the discussion is now about the spirits of men, not about wealth. But taxes, which are contributed by consent, and which are imposed by command, although they are the same thing as far as exhausting wealth is concerned, yet they affect the spirits of subjects entirely differently. Let this therefore also be established, that a people burdened by taxes is not fit to rule.

     3. For Kingdoms and States aspiring to greatness, it is absolutely to be avoided that Nobles and Patricians, and (whom we call) Gentlemen, should be excessively multiplied. For this leads to the result that the common people of the Kingdom are humble and abject; and almost nothing else than the bondmen and laborers of the Nobles. We see something similar happen in coppice woods; where, if a greater number of trunks or larger trees than is proper is left, the wood will not regenerate purely and cleanly; but the greater part will degenerate into thorns and bushes. In the same way, in nations where the nobility is more numerous than is just, the common people will be vile and idle: and ultimately the situation will come to this, that neither

--- Page 573 ---
L I B E R VIII. 551

nor will even one in a hundred be fit to bear a helmet: especially if you consider the infantry; which army is generally the principal strength. Hence will follow a large population, but meager forces. Nowhere in the world has this which I say been more clearly proven than by the examples of England and France. Of which, England, although far inferior in territory and number of inhabitants, nevertheless almost always obtained the upper hand in wars: for this very reason, that among the English, farmers and men of the lower order are fit for military service, which the peasants of France are not. In this matter, it was devised by King Henry VII of England with a certain wonderful and profound wisdom (as we have treated more fully in his *History of Life*) that smaller estates and farmhouses should be established, which should have a certain and moderate measure of land annexed to them, which could not be alienated, to the end that it might suffice for a more liberal sustenance; and that agriculture should be practiced by those who were owners of the land, or at least usufructuaries, not hired laborers or mercenaries. For only thus will any region deserve that character with which Virgil distinguished ancient Italy:
—— *A land mighty in arms, and rich in soil.*
Nor should that part of the people be passed over, (which is almost peculiar to England, nor elsewhere (as far as I know) in use, unless perhaps among the Poles) namely the servants of the *nobles*: For even the lower ranks of this class, as regards infantry, are not at all inferior to the farmers themselves.

   4. Every effort must be made, that that tree *of Monarchy, such as Nebuchadnezzar's was, should have a sufficiently ample and robust Trunk to sustain its branches and leaves: That is, that the number of natives, for restraining foreign subjects, should amply suffice. Therefore, those states are well-prepared for the greatness of empire, who easily and willingly grant citizenship rights.* For it would indeed be a vain opinion, that a handful of men, however much they excel in spirit and counsel, could restrain and curb with the yoke of empire regions excessively vast and spacious. They might perhaps do this for a time, but this matter does not achieve permanence. *The Spartans* were sparing and difficult in admitting new citizens. Hence, as long as they ruled within small limits, their affairs were firm and stable. But after they began to extend their borders and to rule more widely than the Spartan stock could conveniently restrain the multitude of foreigners by their rule, their power suddenly collapsed. No Republic ever so profusely opened its bosom for receiving new citizens as the *Roman Republic.* And so it was fitting, for such a prudent institution, that fortune, when into empire

...the most ample in the whole world grew up.
It was their custom to readily grant *the right of citizenship*: and that in the highest degree: That is, not only *the right of commerce, the right of marriage, the right of inheritance*; but also *the right of suffrage, and the right of petition*, or of holding offices: And this again, they communicated not only to individual persons, but to entire families, indeed to cities, and sometimes to whole nations. To this add the custom *of founding colonies*, by which Roman stock was transplanted into foreign soil. If you combine these two institutions, you will certainly say that the Romans did not spread themselves over the whole world: but rather that the whole world spread itself over the Romans: Which is the most secure method of extending empire. One often comes to wonder at *the Spanish empire*; that with so few natives it could embrace and restrain so many Kingdoms and Provinces. But certainly Spain itself ought to be considered a sufficiently large trunk for the tree, since it contains a far wider tract of regions than had fallen to Rome or Sparta in their beginnings. Furthermore, although the Spanish are accustomed to impart *the right of citizenship* quite sparingly, they do what is next best; Namely, they promiscuously admit men of any nation to their ordinary military service. Moreover, they not infrequently entrust the supreme command in war to leaders who are not Spanish by birth. However, they themselves also seem not so long ago to have felt that very scarcity of natives, and to have wished to remedy it; as appears from the *pra-gmatic sanction*

--- Page 576 ---

pragmatic sanction, promulgated this year, can
be seen.
     5. It is most certain that *sedentary mechanical*
*arts*, which are practiced not outdoors, but under a roof,
and *delicate manufactures* (which require the finger
rather than the arm) are by their nature contrary
to military spirits. In general, warlike peoples delight in leisure, and dread
dangers less than labors. And in this their natural
disposition, they are not to be greatly repressed,
if it is our desire to preserve their spirits in vigor.
Therefore, it was of great help to Sparta,
Athens, Rome, and other ancient republics,
that they had for the most part not *freemen*, but
*slaves*, by whose labors such
crafts were carried out. But the use of slaves,
after the reception of the Christian law, has for the most
part fallen into disuse. From this, therefore, the next
thing is that these arts should be permitted only to foreigners;
who for that reason are to be attracted, or
at least easily received. But the *common people* of the
*natives* ought to consist of three kinds of men;
namely, of *farmers*: *free servants*: and
*artisans*; whose work demands strength and manly
sinews; such as are *blacksmiths*, *stone-*
*cutters*, *carpenters*, and similar trades; not counting
the *enlisted military*.

10. Modern wars can be considered as if fought in darkness, compared to the varied glory and honor which, in ancient times, used to accrue to military men from warlike deeds. Today we have, perhaps for inspiring spirits, certain honorary military orders, which nevertheless have now become common to both military and civilian life. Also, we have some coats of arms on family shields; furthermore, certain public hospitals intended for veteran and disabled soldiers, and suchlike. But among the Ancients, there were trophies erected in places where victories were won; funeral orations, and magnificent monuments for those falling in war. The civic crown, military crowns, granted to individuals. The very name of Imperator; which afterwards the greatest Kings borrowed from military commanders; celebrated triumphs of returning commanders, after wars successfully concluded. Donations, and immense largesses to soldiers; upon the disbanding of armies. These (I say) were so many and so great, and gleaming with such remarkable splendor, that they could inject sparks into the breasts of mortals, even those most frozen, and inflame them for war. But above all, that custom of triumphing among the Romans was not a matter of mere pomp, or some empty spectacle, but truly to be counted among the most prudent and noble institutions. Inasmuch as it contained these three...

--- Page 582 ---
560      On the Advancement of Learning.
it had three things; the honor and glory of the Generals; the enrichment of the treasury from spoils, and gifts for the soldiers. But perhaps the honor of a triumph is not suitable for Monarchies, except in the persons of the king himself, or the king's sons. This also held true in the times of the Roman Emperors; who reserved the honor of the triumph itself, for themselves and their sons, for wars which they themselves had personally conducted, as a special privilege: but they granted only the triumphal robes and insignia to other Generals.
    But, to conclude these remarks; No one is there (as Sacred Scripture testifies) who by anxious thought can add one cubit to his stature; that is, in the small measure of the human body: But, in the great fabric of Kingdoms and Commonwealths, to enlarge empire and extend its boundaries, is in the power of Kings and Rulers. For by wisely introducing laws, institutions, and customs, such as we have already proposed, and others similar to these, they will have sown the seeds of greatness for posterity and future ages. But these counsels are rarely considered by Princes, but the matter is usually committed to fortune.
    And these are the things we had to say, which occur to us at present concerning the extension of the empire's boundaries. But to what purpose is this discussion; since the Roman Monarchy is to be (as is believed) the last among earthly ones? Unless it be that for us, faithful to our purpose, and nowhere deviating from the path, (inasmuch as the amplification of empire has been the third among the three offices of Politics) that must by no means be omit-

--- Page 583 ---
LIBER VIII. 561
to omit that entirely. There now remains the other *desired* thing out of those two which we have set forth, namely, concerning *Universal Justice, or the sources of law.*
Those who have written about *Laws*, all have treated that subject either as *Philosophers* or as *Jurists*. And *Philosophers* propose many things, beautiful in theory, but remote from practice. Jurists, however, bound and devoted to the tenets of the laws of their own country, or even Roman or Pontifical laws, do not employ sincere judgment, but speak as if from chains. Certainly, this knowledge properly belongs to civil men: who best know what human society requires, what the welfare of the people, what natural equity, what the customs of nations, what the diverse forms of Republics; and therefore can decide concerning *laws*, from the principles and precepts, both of natural equity and of politics.
Wherefore, let this now be done, that the *sources of justice, and of public utility,* may be sought, and in each *part of law a certain character and idea of justice may be exhibited,* by which the *Laws* of particular kingdoms and Republics may be tested, and from that (standard) anyone, to whom this shall be a matter of heart and care, may be able to undertake amendment. Therefore, of this matter, in our manner, we shall propose an *example, in the title*.

An Example of a *Treatise on Universal Justice*,
     or on the Sources of Law, in one Title,
               by Aphorisms.

          P R O E M.

               Aphorism I.
**I**N civil society, either law or force prevails. But
there is also a certain force simulating law: and some
law savouring more of force than of the equity of
right. Therefore, the source of injustice is threefold: mere force;
malicious ensnarement under pretext of law; and the harshness
of the law itself.

               Aphorism 2.
The foundation of private law is this. He who
commits an injury gains utility or pleasure from the deed,
but danger from the precedent. Others are not partakers
of that utility or pleasure, but they consider the example
to pertain to themselves. Therefore, they easily come together in
agreement, that they may be protected by laws; lest injuries
by turns revert to individuals. But if, by reason
of the times, and a community of guilt, it should happen
that, by some law, more danger is created for the many
and the more powerful than is provided against, a faction dissolves
the law; Which also often happens.

               Aphorism 3.
But private law lies hidden under the protection of public law.
For law protects citizens, Magistrates protect Laws.
But the authority of Magistrates depends on the ma-
jesty of the empire, and the structure of the Polity, and the
Fundamental Laws. Wherefore, if from that quarter, *soundness*

--- Page 585 ---
LIBER VIII. 563
soundness, and a right constitution, Laws will be in good use; but if not, there will be little protection in them.

Aphorism 4.
However, public law does not look only to this, that it be added as a guardian to private law, lest that be violated, and injuries cease; but it extends also to religion, and arms, and discipline, and adornments, and wealth, finally, to all things concerning the well-being of the State.

Aphorism 5.
For the end and scope which laws ought to regard, and to which they ought to direct their commands and sanctions, is no other than that citizens may live happily. This will happen if they are rightly instructed in piety and religion; honorable in morals; safe by arms against external enemies; protected by the aid of laws against seditions and private injuries; obedient to government and magistrates; and rich and flourishing in resources and wealth. But the instruments and sinews of these things are Laws.

Aphorism 6.
And the best laws achieve this end; but most of them deviate. For laws differ remarkably among themselves, and by a very great interval: so that some excel, others are mediocre, and others are entirely faulty. Therefore, according to the measure of our judgment, we will dictate certain laws, as it were, of laws; from which information can be sought as to what in individual laws has been well or wrongly placed or constituted.

Concerning proceeding to similar cases, and extensions of laws.

Aphorism 11.
In omitted cases, the norm of law is to be deduced from similar cases, but cautiously and with judgment. Regarding which, the following Rules are to be observed. Reason is prolific; custom should be sterile, and not generate cases. Therefore, what has been received contrary to the reason of law, or even where its Reason is obscure, is not to be drawn to a consequence.

Aphorism 12.
A significant public good attracts omitted cases to itself. Wherefore, when any Law notably and in a greater manner regards and promotes the advantages of the Commonwealth, its interpretation should be extensive and amplifying.

Aphorism 13.
It is harsh to torture Laws, so that they may torture men. It is not pleasing, therefore, to extend penal Laws, much less Capital ones, to new offenses. But if the crime be old, and known to the laws, but its prosecution falls into a new case, not provided for by the Laws; let it be entirely departed from
Bb 5

one should depart from the dictates of the law, rather than offenses remain unpunished.
          Aphorism 14.
  In Statutes which plainly abrogate the Common Law (especially concerning those matters which frequently occur and have long been established), it is not advisable to proceed by analogy to omitted cases. For when the State has entirely lacked a law, and that in expressed cases, there is little danger if omitted cases await a remedy from a new Statute.
          Aphorism 15.
  Statutes which were manifestly laws of their time, and born from the then prevailing circumstances of the State; when the reason of the times has changed, they are sufficient if they can sustain themselves in their own cases: but it would be preposterous if they were drawn in any way to omitted cases.
          Aphorism 16.
  A consequence is not consequence: but extension ought to be stopped within proximate cases: Otherwise it will gradually slide to dissimilar cases, and the subtleties of intellects will prevail more than the authorities of laws.
          Aphorism 17.
  In Laws and Statutes of a briefer style, extension is to be made more freely. But in those which are enumerative of particular cases, more cautiously. For just as an exception strengthens the force of the Law in cases not excepted, so enumeration weakens it in cases not enumerated.
          Aphorism 18.

Aphorism 19.
The solemnity of words and acts does not admit of extension to similar cases. For that which passes from custom to discretion loses its solemn nature: And the introduction of new things corrupts the majesty of the old.
Aphorism 20.
The extension of Law to cases arising subsequently, which did not exist in the nature of things at the time the Law was enacted, is readily made. For either the case could not be expressed, because it did not then exist, or the omitted case is held to be expressed, if the reason was similar.

Concerning examples, and their use.
Aphorism 21.
Now we must speak of examples, from which Law is to be drawn, where the Law is deficient. But concerning custom, which is a species of Law, and concerning examples which, through frequent use, have passed into custom, as if a tacit Law, we will speak in their proper place. Now, however, we speak of examples which occur rarely and sparsely, and have not coalesced into the force of Law, when, and with what caution, a rule of Law is to be sought from them, when the Law is deficient.
Aphorism 22.
Examples are to be sought from good and moderate times.

must be sought, not from tyrannical, or factious, or dissolute ones. Examples of this kind are spurious offspring of time, and do more harm than good.
          Aphorism 23.
  In examples, more recent ones are to be considered safer. For what was done a little while ago, from which no inconvenience followed, why should it not be repeated again? But nevertheless, recent examples have less authority. And if perchance it is necessary for things to be restored for the better, recent examples savor more of their own age, than of right reason.
          Aphorism 24.
  But older examples are to be received cautiously and with selection: For the passage of time changes many things, so that what seems old in time, that, by disturbance and shapelessness in relation to present circumstances, may be plainly new. Therefore, examples from the middle period are best, or even of such a time that greatly agrees with the current time; by which sometimes a more remote time is preferable, rather than one in the immediate past.
          Aphorism 25.

          Aphorism 26.

Aphorism 27.
In examples, it matters greatly through whose

Aphorisism 35.
Similarly, let the praetorian courts have the power, both to relieve against the rigor of the law, and to supply the defect of the law. For if a remedy ought to be extended to him whom the law has overlooked, much more to him whom it has wounded.
Aphorisism 36.
Let these censorial and praetorian courts confine themselves entirely within enormous and extraordinary cases, and not invade ordinary jurisdictions; lest perchance the matter tend to the subversion of the law, rather than to its supplementation.
Aphorisism 37.
Let these jurisdictions reside only in the supreme courts, and not be communicated to inferior ones. For the power of supplying, or extending, or moderating laws is little short of the power of making laws.
Aphorisism 38.
But let not those courts be committed to one man, but let them consist of several. Nor let Decrees issue in silence; but let the judges adduce the reasons for their sentence, and that openly, and with the crowd present: so that what is free by its very power, may nevertheless be circumscribed by reputation and public opinion.
Aphorisism 39.

Aphorism 44.
Praetorian courts shall not have the right to decide against an express statute under any pretext of equity. For if this were to happen, the judge would entirely transform into a lawgiver, and everything would depend on arbitrary judgment.
Aphorism 45.
Among some, it is accepted that the jurisdiction which decides according to what is fair and good, and that other one which proceeds according to strict law, be assigned to the same courts; but among others, that they be assigned to different ones; the separation of courts is entirely preferred. For the distinction of cases will not be preserved if there is a mixing of jurisdictions; instead, arbitrary judgment will eventually dictate the law.
Aphorism 46.
Not without reason had the Praetor's album come into use among the Romans, in which he prescribed and published how he himself would administer justice. By which example, judges in Praetorian courts ought to propose certain rules for themselves (as far as possible) and publicly affix them. For the best law is that which leaves least to the judge's discretion; the best judge is he who leaves least to himself.
But we will treat more fully of these courts when we come to the section on judgments; we have spoken of them only incidentally now, insofar as they expedite and supply what is omitted by law.
On the Retroactivity of Laws.
Aphorism 47.
There is also another kind of supplement for omitted cases, when one law supersedes another, and at the same time draws in the omitted cases. This happens in laws, or statutes,

--- Page 596 ---
574          On the Advancement of Learning.
tutes, which are retrospective, as they commonly say. Laws of this kind are rarely, and with great caution, to be applied: for Janus is not pleasing in laws.
               Aphorism 48.
   He who, by trickery and fraud, evades and circumvents the words or the meaning of a law, is worthy to be ensnared by a subsequent law. Therefore, in cases of fraud and deceitful evasion, it is just that laws be retrospective, and that they be mutual aids to one another; so that he who devises frauds and the subversion of present laws, may at least fear future ones.
               Aphorism 49.
   Laws which strengthen and confirm the true intentions of acts and instruments against defects of forms or solemnities, most rightly embrace past matters. For the chief fault of a law which is retrospective is that it disturbs. But laws of this confirmatory kind aim at the peace and stability of those things which have been transacted. However, care must be taken lest settled judgments be overturned.
               Aphorism 50.
   It must be diligently observed lest those laws only be thought to look to the past which invalidate past acts: but also those which prohibit and restrict future things, when necessarily connected with past things. For example, if some law forbids certain artisans from selling their wares in the future: this applies to the future, but operates on the past: For it is no longer open to them to seek a livelihood by another means.
                                                  Apho-

--- Page 597 ---
