Aphorism 51.
Every declaratory law, although it does not have words concerning the past, is nevertheless, by the very force of the declaration, entirely drawn to past matters. For interpretation does not then begin when it is declared, but it is made as if contemporary with the law itself. Therefore, do not ordain declaratory laws, except in cases where laws can look back with justice.

Here indeed we conclude that part which treats of the uncertainty of laws where no law is found. Now we must speak of that other part, where, namely, some law exists, but it is perplexing and obscure.

On the obscurity of laws.
Aphorism 52.
The obscurity of laws derives its origin from four things: either from an excessive accumulation of laws, especially with obsolete ones mixed in; or from their ambiguous, or less clear and lucid description; or from neglected or poorly established methods of elucidating the law; or finally, from the contradiction and vacillation of judgments.

On the excessive accumulation of laws.
Aphorism 53.
The Prophet says; "He will rain snares upon them." But there are no worse snares than the snares of laws, especially penal ones; if, immense in number and useless in the course of time, they do not provide a lamp for the feet, but rather cast nets.

Aphorism 54.
A twofold method of enacting a new statute comes into use. One, previous statutes concerning the same subject.

--- Page 598 ---
576          ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING.
confirms and strengthens; then adds or changes some things. The other abrogates and deletes all things that were previously ordained, and entirely substitutes a new and uniform law. The latter method is preferred. For by the former method, ordinances become complicated and perplexing: and what is urgent, is indeed dealt with, but the body of laws is meanwhile rendered defective. In the latter, however, greater diligence must certainly be applied, while the law itself is being considered; And previous acts must certainly be reviewed and weighed, before the law is passed: But by this, the harmony of laws in the future proceeds optimally.
               Aphorism 55.
  It was customary among the Athenians that conflicting heads of laws (which they call antinomies) should be examined annually by six men, and those which could not be reconciled should be proposed to the people, so that something certain might be decided concerning them. Following their example, those who have the power of enacting laws in individual Polities should review antinomies every three or five years, or as it shall seem fit. These, moreover, should first be inspected and prepared by men delegated for this purpose, and finally presented to the Assemblies, so that what is approved may be established and fixed by votes.
               Aphorism 56.
  Nor indeed should there be too diligent or anxious a care for reconciling conflicting heads of laws, and (as they say) saving everything, through subtle and far-fetched distinctions. For this is a snare of ingenuity: And however much it may present a certain modesty and reverence, it must nevertheless be reckoned among harmful things;

--- Page 599 ---
LIBER VIII. 577
is to be considered; inasmuch as it renders the entire body of laws varied and ill-stitched. It is altogether better that the worse (laws) succumb, and the better (laws) stand alone.

Aphorism 57.
Obsolete laws, and those which have fallen into disuse, no less than antinomies, should be proposed (for removal), to be abolished by delegates ex officio. For since an express statute is not regularly abrogated by disuse, it happens that from the contempt of obsolete laws, some loss of authority occurs even in the remaining (laws): And that kind of torment of Mezentius follows, that living Laws perish in the embrace of dead ones. And altogether, gangrene in laws must be avoided.

Aphorism 58.
Moreover, in obsolete laws and statutes, and not (those) newly promulgated; let the praetorian courts have the right, in the interim, to decide against them. For although it has been not badly said, that no one ought to be wiser than the laws, nevertheless, let this be understood of laws when they are awake, not when they are slumbering. Against more recent statutes, however (which are found to harm public right), not indeed to praetors, but to kings and more sacred councils, and supreme powers, let the right of offering assistance belong: suspending their execution by edicts or acts, until the assemblies return, or such gatherings, which have the power to abrogate them; lest the safety of the people be endangered in the interim.

               On new digests of laws.
                    Aphorism 59.
   But if laws accumulated one upon another,
have grown into such vast volumes, or have labored under such great
confusion, that to revise them completely,
and to reduce them into a sound and manageable body, is
expedient; do that above all things, and let such a
work be a heroic work: And the authors of such a
work are rightly and deservedly numbered among legislators and restorers.
                    Aphorism 60.
   This kind of purification of laws, and a new
digest, is accomplished by five things. First, let
obsolete laws be omitted, which Justinian calls "ancient
fables." Next, from among the antinomies, let the
most approved be received, and the contrary ones be abolished. Third, let homoeonomies,
or laws which sound the same, and are nothing else than repetitions of the same thing,
be expunged; and let one of them, which
is most perfect, be retained in place of all.
Fourth,

--- Page 601 ---
LIBER VIII. 579
in the administration of justice, the interpretation and administration of common law and statutes. This is what Trebonianus did in the Digest and Code.

Aphorism 62.
Truly, in this kind of regeneration of laws, and new structure of old laws and books, I entirely retain the words and text of the law, even if it was necessary to excerpt them through fragments and small portions: These are then woven together in order. For even if perhaps more conveniently, and also, if you regard right reason, this could be better accomplished through a new text, than through such a patchwork; nevertheless, in laws, not so much style and description, as authority, and its patron antiquity, must be regarded. Otherwise, such a work might seem rather something scholastic, and a method, than a body of commanding laws.

Aphorism 63.
It would be advisable that in the new digest of laws, the old volumes not be entirely destroyed, and fall into oblivion, but at least remain in libraries; even if their common and indiscriminate use is prohibited. For in more serious cases, it would not be without purpose to consult and inspect the changes and series of past laws; and certainly it is customary to sprinkle antiquity upon present matters. Moreover, such a new body of laws must be entirely confirmed by those who have legislative power in individual polities: lest perchance, under the pretext of digesting old laws, new laws be secretly imposed.

Concerning the perplexed and obscure description of laws.
Aphorism 65.
Obscure description of laws arises either from their
loquacity and verbosity; or again from excessive
brevity; or from the prologue of the law conflicting with the body
of the law itself.
Aphorism 66.
But concerning the obscurity of laws which arises from their
faulty description, we must now speak. Loquacity, which
comes into use in writing laws, and prolixity, is not approved.
For it does not in any way achieve what it wants and desires, but rather
the opposite. For when it strives to pursue and express
individual particular cases with appropriate and proper words,
hoping for greater certainty therefrom; on the contrary, it gives birth to
multiple questions about the words; so that interpretation according
to the meaning of the law (which is sounder
and truer/more correct —

and truer) because of the noise of words.
Aphorism 67.
Nor, for that reason, is excessively concise and affected brevity to be approved, for the sake of majesty, and as if more imperious; especially in these ages, lest perchance the law be like a Lesbian rule. Moderation, therefore, must be sought; and a well-defined generality of words must be sought out; which, although it does not diligently pursue the cases comprehended, yet it sufficiently and clearly delimits the comprehended cases.
Aphorism 68.
In ordinary and political laws and edicts, however, in which, for the most part, no one employs a jurist, but trusts to his own understanding, all things ought to be explained more fully, and shown to the grasp of the common people, as if with a finger.
Aphorism 69.
Nor indeed would the prologues of laws, which were once considered inept, and which introduce laws as disputing, not commanding, please us, if we could bear ancient customs. But these prologues of laws are for the most part (as times now are) necessarily employed, not so much for the explanation of the law, as by way of persuasion, for carrying the law in the assemblies. And again, for satisfying the people. As far as possible, however, prologues should be avoided, and the law should begin with a command.
Aphorism 70.
The intention and meaning of a law, although it may sometimes be not badly elicited from prefaces and preambles (as they say); nevertheless, its breadth or extension ought by no means to be sought from them. For often the preamble seizes upon some things from the most plausible

                Aphorism 71.
  There is indeed a very faulty kind of drafting laws.

On the transcription of judgments.
Aphorism 73.
First of all, let judgments rendered in supreme and principal courts, and in more serious cases, especially doubtful ones, and which have something of difficulty or novelty, be diligently and faithfully recorded. For judgments are the anchors of laws, as laws are of the Commonwealth.
Aphorism 74.
Let the method of recording such judgments and committing them to writing be as follows. Precisely describe the case, exactly transcribe the judgments themselves. Add the reasons for the judgments which the judges brought forward. Do not mix the authority of cases adduced as examples with the principal cases. Be silent about the perorations of advocates, unless something in them was very exceptional.
Aphorism 75.
Let the persons who record such judgments be from among the most learned advocates, and let them receive a generous fee from the public treasury. Let the judges themselves abstain from such transcriptions, lest perhaps, addicted to their own opinions and relying on their own authority, they overstep the limits of a reporter.
Aphorism 76.
Arrange those judgments in order and sequence of time, not by method and titles. For such writings are like histories, or narratives of laws. And not only the acts themselves, but also their times, provide light to a prudent judge.

          Aphorism 83.

          Aphorism 85.

          Aphorism 87.

But care must be taken lest these Summaries make men quick in practice, but idle in the science itself. For their function is such that law is recalled from them, not learned thoroughly. Moreover, Summaries must be compiled with great diligence, fidelity, and judgment, lest they steal from the laws.

         Concerning Responses & Consultations.

Concerning Lectures.
Aphorism 93.
Lectures on law, and the exercises of those who apply themselves to legal studies and give their effort, are to be so instituted and ordered, that all things tend towards settling questions and controversies of law, rather than exciting them. For a game (as it now happens) is instituted and opened among almost everyone, for multiplying altercations and questions of law, as if for the sake of displaying ingenuity. And this is an old evil. For even among the ancients it was a glory, as if through sects and factions, to foster many questions of Law rather than extinguish them. Let it be provided that this does not happen.
Concerning the Instability of Judgments.
Aphorism 94.
Judgments waver, either because of an immature and premature sentence; or because of the rivalry of the courts; or because of a bad and unskillful drafting of judgments; or because of a path provided for their too easy and expeditious rescission. Therefore, it must be provided that judgments are issued, with mature deliberation first having been held, and that courts respect each other, and that judgments are drafted faithfully and prudently: and that the way to rescind judgments,

## CHAP. I.

*Divisions of Inspired Theology are omitted: Only*
*an approach is made to three desiderata: The Doctrine concerning the Legitimate*
*Use of Human Reason in Divine Matters: The Doctrine concerning the*
*Degrees of Unity in the City of God: & the Emanations*
*of the Scriptures.*

[Large initial J]Now indeed (O excellent King), since a small keel,
such as ours could be, has sailed around the entire
circuit, both of the old and the new World, of the Sciences,
(how [well] with favorable winds, and course, let it be the judgment
of posterity) what remains, but that, having at last fulfilled our
vows, we should pay them? But there still remains *Sacred Theology*,
or *Inspired Theology*. Nevertheless, if we proceed to treat
of it, we must depart from the *small boat of human reason*,
and pass into the *Ship of the Church*

--- Page 617 ---
L I B E R IX.                                  595
no longer the *Star of Philosophy*, which has hitherto especially shone upon us. Therefore it would be fitting to observe silence in this matter also. Wherefore we will omit *legitimate divisions* concerning it: Nevertheless, we will contribute a few things to this, according to our humble capacity, in place of offerings. We do this all the more because in the Body of Theology we have found no region or tract whatsoever that is completely deserted or uncultivated: So great has been the diligence of men in sowing either wheat or tares.
   Therefore we will propose three *Appendices to Theology*, which deal not with *matter* informed or to be informed by *Theology*, but only with the *mode of information*. Nor, however, concerning these *Treatises*, (as we have been accustomed in other matters) will we subjoin *examples* or give *precepts*. We will leave this to theologians. For those things (as we have said) are merely in the nature of offerings.
   1. The *Prerogative of God* embraces the whole man: and extends no less to *reason* than to *human will*: so that man indeed may entirely deny himself, and approach God. Wherefore, just as we are bound to obey the *Divine Law*, although *will* may resist, so also to have faith in the *Word of God*, although *reason* may resist. For indeed, if we believe only those things which are agreeable to our *reason*, we assent to the things themselves, not to the *author*: Which we are accustomed to grant even to witnesses of suspect credibility. But that *Faith*, which *was imputed to Abraham for righteousness*, was concerning a matter of this kind, which *Sarah* held in derision: Which in this part ima-

--- Page 618 ---
596          On the Advancement of Learning.
...was a certain image of natural reason. Therefore, the more absurd and incredible a *Divine Mystery* is, the more honor is shown to God in *believing* it, and the more noble the *victory of faith* becomes. Even sinners, the more their conscience burdens them, and nevertheless they place their Faith concerning their salvation in God's Mercy, the more they honor God: for all *Despair* is an insult to God. Moreover, if we carefully consider the matter, what is more worthy than to believe, than to *know* in the way we now *know*. For in *Knowledge*, the human mind is affected by the senses, which recoil from material things; but in *Faith*, the soul is affected by the soul, which is a more worthy Agent. The matter is different in the *State of Glory*: For then *Faith* will indeed cease, and we shall know, *even as we are known*.
     Let us conclude, therefore, that *Sacred Theology* ought to be drawn from the *Word and Oracles of God*, not from the *light of nature*, or the *dictate of reason*. For it is written, *The heavens declare the glory of God*: But nowhere is it found written, *The heavens declare the will of God*. Concerning that [will], it is declared, *To the Law and to the Testimony: if they speak not according to this word*, etc. Nor does this hold true only for *those great Mysteries* concerning the Godhead, Creation, Redemption; but it also pertains to the more perfect interpretation of the Moral Law; *Love your enemies; Do good to those who hate you*, etc. *That you may be children of your Father who is in heaven, who rains upon the Just and Unjust*. Which words certainly deserve that applause; *Nor voice of man-*

--- Page 619 ---
**BOOK IX. 597**
sounds human. Indeed, it is a voice that surpasses the light of nature. Moreover, we see pagan poets, especially when they speak passionately, not infrequently protest against moral laws and doctrines (which nevertheless are much more indulgent and less strict than divine laws), as if they resist the liberty of nature with a certain malice:
—— *And what nature allows,*
*Envious laws deny.* ——
Thus Dendamis the Indian, to Alexander's messengers: *That he had indeed heard something of the name of Pythagoras, and of other wise men from Greece; and that he believed them to have been great men; but to have suffered from that fault, namely, that they had held in excessive reverence and veneration some fantastic thing, which they called Law and Custom.* Wherefore, nor is it to be doubted that a great part of the moral Law is more sublime than to where the light of nature can ascend. Nevertheless, what is said, that men have, even from the light and law of nature, some notions of virtue, vice, justice, injustice, good, evil; that is most true. It must be noted, however, that the light of nature is understood in a twofold sense. Firstly, inasmuch as it arises from sense, induction, reason, arguments, according to the laws of heaven and earth: Secondly, inasmuch as it shines internally upon the human soul by instinct, according to the law of conscience, which is a certain spark, and as it were the remnants of pristine and primitive purity. In which latter sense the soul is especially a partaker of light

598          ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF LEARNING.
of some light, for contemplating and discerning the perfection of *moral law*; Which light, however, is not entirely clear, but such that it rather reproves vices to some extent, than fully informs about duties. Therefore, *Religion*, whether you consider its Mysteries or its morals, depends on *Divine revelation.*

     Yet the *use of human reason* in spiritual matters, certainly exists in many forms, and extends very widely. For it is not without cause that the Apostle called Religion a *Rational Worship of God.* Let one recall the ceremonies and types of the old Law. *Those were Rational and Significant*, far different from the ceremonies of idolatry and magic, which were as if deaf and mute, teaching nothing for the most part, indeed not even hinting at anything. Especially *Christian faith*, as in all things, so in this very thing it excels, in that it preserves a golden mean concerning the *use of reason and disputation* (which is the offspring of reason) between the Laws of the Gentiles and of Mahomet, which pursue extremes. For the Religion of the Gentiles had nothing of constant Faith or Confession; on the contrary, in the Religion of Mahomet, all disputation is forbidden: so that the one bears the face of vague and manifold error; the other, of a certain cunning and cautious imposture; while holy *Christian Faith both accepts and rejects the use of reason and disputation* (but according to due limits).

     The *use of human reason*, in matters pertaining to *Religion*, is twofold: one, in the *explanation of My-*

--- Page 621 ---
LIBER IX. 599

...stery, the other, in the *inferences* which are deduced therefrom. As far as the *explanation of Mysteries* is concerned, we see that *God* does not disdain to lower Himself to the weakness of our understanding; explaining His *mysteries* in such a way that they can be best perceived by us; and, as it were, inoculating His *revelations* into the *preconceptions* and notions of our *reason*; and accommodating His *inspirations* to open our intellect, just as the shape of a key is fitted to the shape of a lock. In this respect, however, we ourselves ought by no means to be lacking. For since *God* Himself uses the works of our *reason* in His *illuminations*, we also ought to turn it in all directions, so that we may be more capable of receiving and imbibing *Mysteries*. Provided that the mind, according to its measure, is expanded to the amplitude of *Mysteries*, not that *Mysteries* be confined to the narrowness of the mind.

As for the *inferences*, however, we ought to know that the use of *reason* and *reasoning* is left to us (as regards *Mysteries*) as something secondary and *relative*, not primitive and absolute. For after the *articles* and *principles of Religion* have already been placed in their proper seats, so that they are entirely exempt from the examination of *reason*, then and only then is it permitted to derive and deduce *inferences* from them, according to their analogy. Indeed, this does not hold true in *natural things*. For even the *principles* themselves are subjected to examination; by *induction*, I say; though by no means by *Syllogism*: And those very things have no connection with reason

--- Page 622 ---
600        On the Advancement of Learning.
repugnance with reason, so that both the primary propositions and the intermediate ones are deduced from the same source.
It is otherwise in *Religion*; where both the primary propositions are self-subsistent, and subsisting by themselves; and again, they are not governed by that reason which deduces consequent propositions. Nor, however, does this happen in *Religion* alone, but also in other *Sciences*, both more serious and lighter, where, namely, the primary propositions are *assumptions*, not *posited*: Since in those too, the absolute use of reason cannot exist. For we see in *Games*, for instance, *Chess*, or similar ones, that the primary rules and laws of the Game are merely positive and arbitrary; which must absolutely be accepted, not called into question: But to win, and skillfully conduct the game, that is artful and rational: In the same way it is also in *Human Laws*: In which there are not a few *Maxims*, (as they say) that is, mere *Tenets of Law*, which rest more on *Authority* than on reason; Nor do they come into dispute; But what is most just, not absolutely, but relatively; (that is, by analogy with those *Maxims*; ) that finally is rational, and offers a wide field for disputation. Such, therefore, is *that secondary reason*, which has a place in *Sacred Theology*, which, namely, is founded upon the *Decrees of God*.
    But just as the use of human reason in *Divine matters* is twofold; so also in the same *use* there is a twofold excess. One, when a *Mystery* is inquired into more curiously than is proper. The other, when, in *inferences*...

--- Page 623 ---
L I B E R IX. 601
authority is attributed to inferences, and to principles themselves. For he might seem a disciple of Nicodemus who too stubbornly asks; How can a man be born when he is old? And he can by no means be considered a disciple of Paul, who does not sometimes insert into his doctrines, "I, not the Lord:" Or that, "According to my counsel." Indeed, to most inferences, this style will be appropriate. Therefore, it seems to us a salutary thing, and especially useful, if a sober and diligent treatise were instituted, which would usefully instruct concerning the use of human reason in theological matters, as a kind of Divine Dialectic. Inasmuch as it would be like a kind of Opiate Medicine, which not only lulls to sleep the empty speculations with which the school sometimes labors, but also somewhat mitigates the furies of controversies, which stir up tumults in the Church. We place such a treatise among our desiderata; and we name it *Sophron*, or *Concerning the Legitimate Use of Human Reason in Divine Matters*.

    2. It greatly concerns the peace of the Church, that the covenant of Christians, prescribed by the Savior in those two Chapters, which seem somewhat divergent, be well and clearly explained: Of which one defines thus; "He who is not with us, is against us:" The other, however, thus; "He who is not against us: is with us." From these it is clearly evident, that there are some articles in which he who dissents must be placed outside the covenant: but others, in which it is permitted to dissent, with the covenant preserved. For the bonds of Christian communion are established as, One Faith, One Baptism, etc. Not one rite, one

--- Page 624 ---
602      On the Advancement of Learning.
one opinion. We also see that the Savior's tunic was seamless; but the Church's garment is many-colored. Chaff in the ear must be separated from the grain; but tares in the field are not to be immediately uprooted. Moses, when he found an Egyptian contending with an Israelite, did not say, "Why are you contending?" But drawing his sword, he killed the Egyptian: But when he saw two Israelites contending, although it could not be that a just cause belonged to both, yet he addressed them thus: "You are brothers, why are you contending?" Therefore, having weighed these things, it seems to be a matter of great moment and utility that it be defined what those things are, and of what breadth, which utterly tear men from the body of the Church, and cut them off from the Communion of the faithful. But if anyone thinks that this has already been done long ago, let him consider again and again how sincerely and moderately. Meanwhile, it is probable that he who mentions Peace will receive that reply of Jehu to the Messenger, ("Is it peace, Jehu?") "What have you to do with peace? Turn behind me and follow me:" since not peace, but factions are dear to most. Nevertheless, it has seemed good to us to place a Treatise on the Degrees of Unity in the City of God among the things desired, as salutary and useful.
   3. Since the Sacred Scriptures have such great parts in shaping Theology, their Interpretation must first be considered. Nor do we now speak of the Authority to interpret them, which is established in the consensus of the Church, but of the method of interpreting. This is twofold; Methodical,

--- Page 625 ---
L I B E R IX. 603
...cal, and *Loose*. For indeed, these Divine streams, which infinitely surpass those waters from Jacob's wells, are drawn and presented in almost similar ways as natural waters usually are from wells: These, indeed, are either received into cisterns upon the first drawing, from where they can be conveniently distributed for use through many pipes; or they are immediately poured into vessels, to be used as needed, from time to time. And *that former methodical mode* *finally gave birth to Scholastic Theology for us;* *through which the Doctrine of Theology was collected into an art, as into a cistern;* *and from there streams of Axioms and Positions were distributed into all parts.* But in the *Loose* mode of Interpreting, two excesses occur. The first, *presupposes such a Perfection in the Scriptures,* that even all Philosophy ought to be sought from their sources, as if any other Philosophy were a profane and heathen thing. This intemperance prevailed especially in the school of Paracelsus, and also among others: its beginnings, however, are from the Rabbis and

*Interpreting* (which we establish as an excess) seems
at first glance sober and chaste; but nevertheless it
both dishonors the *Scriptures* themselves, and afflicts

But it is necessary to remember that to God, the *Author*
*of the Scriptures*, those two things are open, which human

the *successions of time*. Wherefore, since the *dictates*

interpreted only according to the breadth

occasion from which the words were uttered: or
precisely from the context of the preceding and
following words: or by contemplating the principal

them to embrace, not only totally, or collectively,

innumerable streams and veins of doctrine
for irrigating the individual parts of the Church, and the souls of the faithful.

...from the grape and skin of the grape have a taste of something. Similarly, doctrines are very wholesome and sweet which emanate from Scriptures gently drawn out, and do not lead to Controversies or Commonplaces. We will name a treatise of this kind *Emanations of the Scriptures*.

Now therefore I seem to have completed, as faithfully as I could, a small globe of the *intellectual world*; together with the designation and description of those parts which, by the industry and labors of men, I find either not constantly occupied or not sufficiently cultivated. In which work, if anywhere I have departed from the opinion of the ancients, let it be understood that this was done with the intention *of advancing for the better, not of innovating, or migrating to something else.* For I could not be consistent with myself, or with the argument I have in hand, unless I had plainly resolved to add to *the inventions of others*, as much as was in my power; although I have no less wished that *my own inventions* also be surpassed by others in the future. How fair I have been in this matter appears even from this: that I have everywhere proposed my opinions naked and unarmed, nor have I contended to prejudice the liberty of others by pugnacious refutations. For in those things which have been rightly set forth by me, there is hope that it will happen that if a doubt or objection arises in the first reading, yet in a repeated reading the answer will spontaneously present itself. But in those things in which it happened to me to err, I am certain that no violence has been inflicted by me upon the truth through contentious arguments: Of which [arguments] such is almost the natu-

nature, that they lend authority to errors, and detract from rightly discovered things. For indeed, error gains honor from doubt; Truth suffers rejection. Meanwhile, there came to my mind that reply of Themistocles, who, when a certain Ambassador from a small town had delivered some grand speeches, rebuked the man; *Friend, your words lack a City.* Certainly, I believe it can be most justly objected to me, that my words *require an Age.* *Perhaps an entire Age,* to prove, but several *Ages* to perfect. Nevertheless, since even the greatest things owe their existence to their beginnings, it will be enough for me to have sown for posterity, and for the immortal God: Whose Divine Power I humbly implore, through His Son and our Savior, that He would graciously deign to accept these, and similar ones, *victims of human intellect,* sprinkled with Religion, as with Salt, and offered to His Glory.
